stem: Which term best describes her tendency to change rapidly between topics of conversation?
explanation:
Flight of ideas
Flight of ideas occurs when patients flit rapidly between subjects only every few seconds. It is a very prominent feature of mania, the likely diagnosis here. She should be reviewed by the psychiatry service, and considered for mood stabilising medication over the longer term. In the short term atypical anti-psychoticsChat and with benzodiazepines may both be of value.

Auditory hallucinations
Auditory hallucinations is incorrect. Auditory hallucinations are seen in association with mania, but don’t result in flight of ideas as described here.

Clang association
Clang association is incorrect. Clang associations occur when patients group similar sounding words together, even though there is no logical reason to group the words together in a sentence.

Grandiose speech
Grandiose delusions is incorrect. Grandiose delusions occur when patients over-claim as to their status, for example believing they are the messiah.

Pressure of speech
Pressure of speech is incorrect. Pressure of speech is where patients speak in a rapid and frenzied way, the speech produced is difficult to interrupt and may be too fast or too tangential for the listener to understand.

stem: You are asked for advice in the management of an 84-year-old woman who is currently an inpatient on the oldage psychiatry ward. She was admitted a few days earlier following a period of low mood, self-neglect, poor sleep and poor appetite. She is started on treatment for depression with a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI). A few days later is it noted that she has become drowsy, confused and has had a seizure. None of these symptoms were present on her admission. On examination there is no evidence of infection, she does not appear dehydrated and has no focal neurological signs, but she does have a reduced GCS as she is responding to pain, is confused and disorientated and localising to painful stimuli. What would be the most important blood test to carry out to establish the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Electrolytes
A full history, physical examination and appropriate investigations should be carried out for this patient. Special attention should be paid to her electrolytes as hyponatremia has been associated with the prescription of all types of antidepressants. Hyponatremia has been reported most frequently with the SSRIs than with any other type of antidepressant. Hyponatremia is particularly common in the elderly and is probably due to the syndrome of inappropriate [secretion of] antidiuretic hormone (SIADH). Severe hyponatremia causes drowsiness, nausea, vomiting, confusion and seizures. The CSM (Committee on Safety of Medicines) has advised that hyponatremia should be considered in all patients who develop drowsiness, confusion or convulsions while taking an antidepressant.

Clotting function
Clotting function is incorrect. Although a bleeding disorder could predispose the patient to intracerebral haemorrhage, it is less likely given the history of the patient being admitted to an old-age psychiatry ward and therefore likely having being started on a medication relating to her mental health.

Liver function
Liver function is incorrect. Deranged liver function is unlikely to present with drowsiness, confusion and seizures.

Full blood count
Full blood count is incorrect. Although CNS infection could present with drowsiness, confusion and seizures, this is less likely given the history of the patient being admitted to an old-age psychiatry ward and therefore likely having being started on a medication relating to her mental health. Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuretic Hormone A 45-year-old man with mild learning difficulties and a known genetic syndrome has been noted by his family to be developing problems with his memory and communication. He is seen in the memory clinic and is diagnosed with Alzheimer’s dementia. What genetic syndrome is most likely to be linked to Alzheimer’s dementia?

Thyroid function
Thyroid function is incorrect. Hyper/hypothyroidism would not present with drowsiness, confusion and seizures.

stem: A 27-year-old female, who gave birth to a baby boy 5 days previously, reports that she feels tearful, anxious and emotionally labile. When questioned she says that although her sleep is disturbed by the baby waking in the night, she is otherwise sleeping and eating well and has had no ideas of self-harm or suicide. She comes back the following week and says she feels much better. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Baby blues
The most likely diagnosis in this case is baby blues. Typical clinical features include tearfulness, emotional lability, irritability, apparent confusion and anxiety; it occurs in about 50% of all women following childbirth. It typically starts 4–5 days following the birth and lasts for about 2–3 days. It resolves spontaneously and medication is unnecessary. Support and reassurance should be offered. The temporal relationship of ‘baby blues’ to childbirth and the frequency of the ‘blues’ together suggest that a biological cause is likely, but no definite hormonal difference between those with and without the ‘blues’ has been demonstrated. It is important to monitor the mood of all mothers post-delivery to ensure that postnatal depression in detected and treated adequately.

Postnatal depression
Postnatal depression is incorrect. The patient’s symptoms resolved spontaneously within 2 weeks, and the baby blues do not usually last longer than 2 weeks following the birth. Postnatal depression should beTutor considered in any patient who presents within 1 year of giving birth with low mood, loss of interest in usual activities, poor sleep, difficulty bonding with their baby and frightening thoughts such as thinking about harming their baby.

Postnatal anxiety
Postnatal anxiety is incorrect. The patient’s symptoms resolved spontaneously within 2 weeks, and the baby blues do not usually last longer than 2 weeks following the birth. Postnatal anxiety should be considered in any patient who presents within 1 year of giving birth with symptoms of anxiety, including worrying all the time, disturbing thoughts that something bad is going to happen and a sense of dread.

Postpartum thyroiditis
Postpartum thyroiditis is incorrect. Postpartum thyroiditis typically occurs 2-6 months postpartum and can present with symptoms of hyperthyroidism or hypothyroidism. Although hyperthyroidism may present with anxiety and irritability, there are no other symptoms reported to suggest hyperthyroidism such as weight loss, tremor or heat intolerance. Depression

Bipolar affective disorder
Bipolar affective disorder is incorrect. This would present with episodes of depression and mania/hypomania.

stem: A 22-year-old woman comes to the Diabetes Clinic for review. She has recently been admitted for the third time in the past seven months with diabetic ketoacidosis, she admits to missing doses of insulin, has recently lost her job and her relationship has broken down over the same period of time. She is not eating properly and wakes around 5 am. Current therapy includes basal-bolus insulin and Ramipril 2.5mg started after she developed microalbuminuria 3 years earlier. Her BP is 123/72 mmHg, pulse is 72/min and regular, her BMI is 20. There is 1+ of protein on urine dipstick and a most recent HbA1c is 88 mmol/mol (10.2%). An appointment with the counsellor is booked. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Arrange a 72hr continuous glucose monitoring system
explanation:
Start Citalopram
Citalopram is an appropriate selective serotonin-reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) for treatment of depression, the likely underlying cause of this patient’s presentation. This should, of course, be accompanied by the access to talking therapies and to a psychologist specialising in the management of patients with type 1 diabetes where possible.

Arrange a 72hr continuous glucose monitoring system
Arrange a 72hr continuous glucose monitoring system is incorrect. A 72hr CGMS is only useful in patients who are motivated to change their glucose regimen in response to the results, and inject multiple times per day.

Reassure her that things will
Reassure her that things will is incorrect. It’s highly unlikely, versus targeted therapy for depression, that reassurance alone will this patient’s clinical situation.

Refer for insulin pump therapy
Refer for insulin pump therapy is incorrect. Insulin pump therapy requires significant patient input with respect to continuing care. Given this patient’s current personal situation, insulin pump therapy therefore isn’t an option.

Start Amitriptyline
Start Amitriptyline is incorrect. Tricyclic anti-depressants are associated with sedation and have a poor profile with respect to CNS and anti-cholinergic adverse events. As such they are usually avoided in young patients.

stem: A 30-year-old lawyer complains of increasing anxiety over the past 2 years. She feels inadequate in social situations and worries about her career. She also complains of insomnia, problems with concentration, tenseness and irritability. There is no other medical problem, and no substance abuse, hallucinations, delusions or psychomotor retardation. She is well dressed, does not feel frustrated and has no suicidal intent. What is the probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Generalised anxiety disorder
This is the most likely cause of this woman’s symptoms. She presents with progressive increase in anxiety that appears to be present in the absence of triggers or distressing thoughts, and is impaired by her symptoms. The first-line management for most anxiety disorders is SSRI medications, but psychological treatments can play a very important role.

Adjustment disorder with anxious mood
Adjustment disorder with anxious mood is incorrect. This may present with anxiety or depressive symptoms, but the diagnosis requires a recent significant life event and symptoms to be within three months of the significant event. In this scenario, symptoms have persisted for over 2 years and there is no evidence of a significant life event.

Social phobia
Social phobia is incorrect. This is unlikely as the patient does not describe a specific anxiety reaction to social situations - rather, a more generalized anxiety state. Social phobia results in a very severe anxiety response to social situations and can be very disabling.

Obsessive–compulsive neurosis
Obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD) is incorrect. This is not likely in this case as neither obsessions nor compulsions are described in the vignette. Obsessions do not mean repeatedly thinking of the same topic; rather they describe intrusive anxiety-provoking thoughts that require the patient to carry out the compulsion to deal with the anxiety induced by the obsession.

Major depressive disorder
Major depressive disorder is incorrect. There is no evidence from the vignette that the primary problem with this patient is low mood or depression. Anxiety and depression are often found together, however, and when assessing an anxious patient an assessment of depressive symptoms should also be performed. Anxiety Generalised anxiety disorder is characterised by excessive anxiety, which is difficult to control, along with restlessness, irritability and sleep disturbances. The anxiety does not appear to be related to a specific stressor or exclusively to social situations, and there is no evidence of specific obsessions or compulsions. The symptoms are better accounted for by generalised anxiety disorder than major depressive disorder.

stem: A 37-year-old woman is referred to your clinic with two episodes of sudden-onset limb paralysis at night-time over the last 4 months. She describes waking shortly after falling asleep and being aware of an inability to move her limbs or to speak, associated with a feeling of suffocation lasting for about a minute. Her father recently died from an intracerebral haemorrhage during sleep. She has no other symptoms other than daytime sleepiness, which she puts down to looking after her two young children. There are no abnormalities on examination. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Sleep paralysis
Sleep paralysis reflects the atonia of REM sleep. Awareness is preserved during the attack, which heightens the sense of terror and anxiety, especially if a feeling of suffocation is present (although the respiratory muscles are only ever mildly affected in comparison with the limbs). Sleep paralysis may be isolated or occur in the context of narcolepsy, in which it affects 15–45% of patients. There are no reported symptoms of narcolepsy (sudden ‘attacks’ of sleep in the daytime) so nocturnal seizures is less correct.

Brainstem transient ischaemic attack
Brainstem transient ischaemic attack (TIA) is incorrect. Brainstem TIAs are not usually stereotyped recurrent attacks and do not produce isolated paralysis wih preserved awareness.

Depression and anxiety
Depression and anxiety is incorrect. Depression and anxiety may present with sleep disturbance, as well as otherbiological symptoms such as altered appetite, but there are no clear markers for a significant affective disorder here.

Narcolepsy
Narcolepsy is incorrect. As described this is less likely than sleep paralysis due to the absence of any symptoms of narcolepsy. NarcolepsyA 30-year-old man with resistant schizophrenia has been switched to a new drug as he is intolerant of chlorpromazine and risperidone. He has been told he has to have regular blood tests to look for ‘low blood cell counts’. On which antipsychotic has he been started?

Nocturnal seizures
Nocturnal seizures is incorrect. Nocturnal seizures are very unlikely given the preserved awareness and memory for the attacks. In addition, nocturnal seizures are likely to result in generalisedtonic–clonic attacks or attacks characterised by hyperkinetic automatisms.

stem: A 35-year-old woman has an intense fear of birds and becomes extremely distressed when in situations where she encounters them. Which of the following treatments is best suited to her condition?
explanation:
Graded exposure
This patient has a simple phobia, which is restricted to a highly specific situation. Graded exposure would be the treatment of choice. This involves drawing up a hierarchy of feared situations and confronting them one by one, starting with the easiest. This is done in conjunction with relaxation and anxiety management training.

Benzodiazepines
Benzodiazepines is incorrect. These should be avoided due to the high risk of dependence and the very specific nature of the patient’s phobia.

Antidepressants
Antidepressants is incorrect. These can be helpful for some people with phobias but are more suited to those with more generalised phobias such as social phobia and agoraphobia. Graded exposure is, therefore, a more appropriate treatment than antidepressants.

Psychoanalytical psychotherapy
Psychoanalytical psychotherapy is incorrect. It has been shown to be ineffective in the management of phobias. Phobic DisordersFlooding
Flooding is incorrect. This describes the now less-favoured treatment of maximal exposure to the feared stimulus until anxiety reduction occurs: for example, locking the patient in a room full of birds.

stem: A 32-year-old woman is started on lithium therapy for bipolar disorder. Which one of the following is the most important side effect of therapy that you should warn her about?
explanation:
Hypothyroidism
Lithium-induced hypothyroidism occurs in approximately 5% of individuals on lithium maintenance therapy. The prevalence of thyroid abnormalities overall is up to 20% of patients on long-term treatment, (includes goiter and thyrotoxicosis).

Abnormal liver function
Abnormal liver function is incorrect. Abnormal liver function tests (LFTs) are not normally a consequence of lithium therapy.

Fever
Fever is incorrect. Excessive sweating and fever may be reported with lithium therapy but they are only rarely seen.

Leukopenia
Leukopenia is incorrect. Leukocytosis rather than leukopenia is more likely to be reported in association with lithium therapy.

stem: A 17-year-old male, who has difficulty concentrating on things for long periods of time and is hyperactive, has recently been prescribed a drug for treatment of his ‘hyperactivity’. What drug is most likely to have been prescribed?
explanation:
Methylphenidate
NICE guidance has recommended that methylphenidate (Ritalin), a central nervous system stimulant, should be used as part of a comprehensive treatment programme for children and adolescents with a diagnosis of severe attention deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). A specialist should initiate this treatment.

Modafinil
Modafinil is incorrect. This is another central nervous system stimulant that is used for the treatment of daytime sleepiness associated with narcolepsy or obstructive sleep apnoea.

Sildenafil
Sildenafil is incorrect. Sildenafil is the generic name for Viagra. This is a PDE5 inhibitor used in the treatment of erectile dysfunction and pulmonary arterial hypertension.

Diazepam
Diazepam is incorrect. This is a benzodiazepine and can be used in the short-term management of anxiety.

Fluoxetine
Fluoxetine is incorrect. This is a selective serotonin-reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) used in the treatment of depression. Some trials of SSRIs, including fluoxetine, in this age group suggested an increase in the risk of harmful outcomes, eg suicide and self-harm. Overall the balance of risk and benefit for fluoxetine in the treatment of depressive illness in those under 18 years of age is considered favourable.

stem: A 35-year-old woman is referred to the Rheumatology Clinic for review. She reports multiple joint and muscle aches, which have worsened over the last 2 years. There is also a history of unexplained tiredness and palpitations, and she takes Omeprazole for gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD) and peppermint oil for irritable bowel syndrome. Multiple medical consultations with colleagues have progressively increased her health concerns and she admits to worries at home about an abusive partner. On examination her BP of 122/82 mmHg, pulse is 72/min and regular. BMI is 28. There is no obvious joint pain and no muscle pain on palpation. Routine bloods are entirely normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Somatisation disorder
Somatisation disorder is a condition characterised by complaints of multiple medical problems, stretching over many years, without any identified physiological basis. They occur against a background often of physical or sexual abuse.

Delusional disorder
Delusional disorder is incorrect. There are no features here consistent with delusional disorder such as being poisoned, being followed, or deceived by others.

Depression
Depression is incorrect. Although the patient does complain of fatigue, there are no other pointers towards a significant mood disorder.

Malingering
Malingering is incorrect. This implies that symptoms are under conscious control and for personal gain, neither of which is relevant here. Somatoform DisordersObsessive compulsive disorder
Obsessive compulsive disorder is incorrect. Obsessive compulsive disorder is incorrect. is characterized by repeated cycles of behavior that the individual feels compelled to carry out, and they have little or no control over.

stem: A 25-year-old woman presented complaining of various physical symptoms. These have included low back pain, muscle aches, reflux oesophagitis, and irritable bowel syndrome during the course of the past 2 years. She denies any other symptoms, and physical examination is entirely normal. How would you best describe her condition?
explanation:
Somatisation disorder
Somatisation disorder is characterised by multiple, changing physical symptoms. Most patients have had multiple contacts with primary and specialist health services. The WHO International Classification of Disease, 10th revision (ICD-10) requires the presence of: two or more years of multiple and variable complaints persistent refusal to accept the advice of several doctors impairment of functioning owing to the symptoms and resultant behaviour.

Personality disorder
Personality disorder is incorrect. A personality disorder is a deeply ingrained maladaptive pattern of behaviour, a number of subtypes are well described, examples include borderline and schizoid personality disorder.

Hypochondriacal disorder
Hypochondriacal disorder is incorrect. Hypochondriacal disorder is the persistent preoccupation with the possibility of having a serious disease

Dissociative disorder
Dissociative disorder is incorrect. Dissociative disorders are presumed to be psychogenic in origin and associated with traumatic events. They are associated with a breakdown of memory, awareness, identity or perception. Somatoform DisordersA lady loses her husband in a traumatic road traffic collision. Three months afterwards she says she regularly hears his voice when alone at home. She is not eating very well, has lost 5 kg of weight in this time and she never sleeps after 4.30 am in the morning. She has lost interest in all her previously normal activities and does not find any pleasure in hobbies or pastimes anymore. She says she often feels his presence around her and sometimes sees him when she goes outside; she is reassured by these feelings. What diagnosis should be suspected?

Depersonalisation
Depersonalisation is incorrect. Depersonalisation disorders are associated with detachment either from reality or from oneself.

stem: Some three months after suffering a serious assault, a 45-year-old man complains of having vivid dreams of the incident, flashbacks of the assault and intrusive thoughts. He has noticed he is more ‘jumpy’ than before and avoids going out at night as it makes him anxious and reminds him of the attack. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Post-traumatic stress disorder
The most likely diagnosis in this case is post-traumatic stress disorder. It arises as a response to a stressful event of a threatening or catastrophic nature. Typical features include episodes of repeated reliving of the trauma (as flashbacks or nightmares), avoidance of circumstances resembling or associated with the stressor and a state of autonomic hyperarousal – with hypervigilance, an enhanced startle reaction and insomnia.

Generalised anxiety disorder
Generalised anxiety disorder is incorrect. The clinical features of generalized anxiety disorder are persistent and generalised symptoms of anxiety that occur across a range of daily circumstances and are not related to particular events or circumstances.

Social phobia
Social phobia is incorrect. This typically presents with symptoms of fear and avoidance relating to social situations and the patient’s fear of humiliation or embarrassment in social situations.

Agoraphobia
Agoraphobia is incorrect. This is anxiety and fear about being in places or situations from which escape may be difficult, e.g. in crowded places or public transport.

Acute stress reaction
Acute stress reaction is incorrect. Although this also occurs in individuals in response to exceptional stress, it is a transient disorder that usually subsides within hours or days. The symptoms in an acute stress reaction typically show a mixed and changing picture.

stem: A 17 year old woman comes to the clinic for review. She is some 3 months away from her A-levels and is depressed and anxious about her potential grades. She is currently waking at 4:30am, and is findng it difficult to eat. She has thought that it might be easier to just take an overdose of paracetamol, and end it all, but has so far resisted the urge to do so. She has no physical health problems and is predicted to achieve 4 A grades. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation:
Cognitive behavioural therapy
Pharmacotherapy is not recommended for teenagers with depression because of increased risk of suicide in this population. CBT is therefore the intervention of choice.

Amitriptyline
Amitriptyline is incorrect. This is a sedating tricyclic anti-depressant and is normally used in the elderly population for treatment of depression.

Citalopram
Citalopram is incorrect. Citalopram may be associated with a lower rate of anxiety and increased activity in teenagers with depression than other SSRIs, although it is still considered a second line option in patients who fail to respond to CBT alone.

Counselling
Counselling is incorrect. Unfocussed counselling used alone is unlikely to significantly impact on symptoms of depression.

Zopiclone
Zopiclone is incorrect. Used short term to sleep zopiclone may have a role, although it is inferior to a CBT intervention for depression.

stem: A 21-year-old business major at a large university presents. Over the past few weeks his family and friends have noticed increasingly unusual behaviour. On many occasions they have overheard him whispering in an agitated voice, even though there is no one nearby. He has refused to answer his mobile phone, claiming that if he does it will activate a chip that was implanted in his brain by aliens. His parents have tried to get him to go with them to a psychiatrist for an evaluation, but he refuses. He has accused them on several occasions of conspiring with the aliens to have him killed so they can remove his brain and put it inside one of their own. He has stopped attending classes altogether. He has become increasingly socially isolated. Although Martin occasionally had a few beers with his friends, he has never been known to abuse alcohol or use drugs. He does, however, have an estranged aunt who has been in and out of psychiatric hospitals over the years due to erratic and bizarre behavior. Which one of the following characteristics would indicate an unfavourable prognosis?
options: A prolonged pre-morbid history of social withdrawal
explanation:
A prolonged pre-morbid history of social withdrawal
A prolonged pre-morbid history of social withdrawal is consistent with a diagnosis of schizophrenia and raises the possibility of negative symptom predominance, which is associated with a less positive response to intervention, this drives the correct answer here.

A normal MRI brain scan
A normal MRI brain scan is incorrect. MRI changes are associated with more severe symptoms and clinical course in people with schizophrenia.

A schizophrenic second-degree relative
A schizophrenic second-degree relative is incorrect. This is commonly found in second-degree relatives and has little prognostic significance.

Catatonia
Catatonia is incorrect. The presence of catatonic symptomatology is not associated with any particular clinical course.

Rapid onset of illness
Rapid onset of illness is incorrect. This has a more favourable prognosis than when the onset is insidious.

stem: A 28-year-old man with schizophrenia who was intolerant of chlorpromazine due to dystonic side-effects was switched to clozapine. To what class of drugs does clozapine belong?
explanation:
Atypical antipsychotic
Clozapine is an atypical antipsychotic licensed for the treatment of schizophrenia in patients who are unresponsive to or intolerant of conventional neuroleptics. It causes fewer extrapyramidal side-effects.

Phenothiazine
Aripiprazole Amisulpride Clozapine Olanzapine Quetiapine Risperidone Phenothiazine Phenothiazine is incorrect. The most commonly used example of a phenothiazine neuroleptic is chlorpromazine.

Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI)
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) is incorrect. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are antidepressants: examples include fluoxetine and paroxetine.

Thioxanthene
Thioxanthene is incorrect. Thiozanthenes are structurally related to neuroleptic drugs: examples include chlorprothixene and flupenthixol.

stem: A 17-year-old girl has been experiencing disturbing auditory hallucinations for the past year, in which voices utter derogatory statements at her. Initially, the voices were occasional, but they have now become more frequent. She has withdrawn from social contact. She has no medical history of note, denies recreational drug abuse and there are no physical abnormalities on examination. Which of the following would you advise her parents?
options: Her younger sister will not be affected by the condition
Parenting skills are likely to have accelerated her presentation
Psychological rehabilitation has no impact on the condition
The early use of antipsychotic medication will alter the course of the illness
There will inevitably be a deterioration in her condition over time
explanation:
The early use of antipsychotic medication will alter the course of the illness
Early treatment for schizophrenia is associated with better long-term outcomes. Risperidone and olanzapine are usual first-line pharmacological interventions, with early intervention with a multidisciplinary and pharmacological approach resulting in fewer readmissions and less long-term disability.

Her younger sister will not be affected by the condition
Her younger sister will not be affected by the condition is incorrect. There is increased risk of schizophrenia in first-degree relatives of an affected patient.

Parenting skills are likely to have accelerated her presentation
Parenting skills are likely to have accelerated her presentation is incorrect. In all likelihood parenting skills will not have impacted on her time to presentation.

Psychological rehabilitation has no impact on the condition
Psychological rehabilitation has no impact on the condition is incorrect. Rehabilitation, via a multidisciplinary team approach, is a crucial brick in the management of schizophrenia.

There will inevitably be a deterioration in her condition over time.

stem: A recently bereaved man visits his GP as he reports hearing the voice of his dead wife as he drops off to sleep. What is this symptom called?
explanation:
Hypnagogic hallucination
Hypnagogic hallucinations are transient hallucinations that occur as the patient is going to sleep; they can be visual, auditory or tactile.

Audible thoughts
Audible thoughts is incorrect. Audible thoughts is a type of auditory hallucination when one hears their own thoughts or beliefs as if they were being spoken aloud by an inner voice. This is a ‘first-rank’ symptom of schizophrenia.

Haptic hallucination
Haptic hallucination is incorrect. Haptic hallucinations are experienced as sensations of being touched, strangled or the feeling that insects are crawling beneath the skin. These can occur in schizophrenia, cocaine abusers or alcohol withdrawal.

Hypnopompic hallucination
Hypnopompic hallucination is incorrect. Hypnopompic hallucinations are experienced on waking. Both hypnopompic and hypnagogic hallucinations often occur as auditory perceptions, but they can also occur as visual perceptions (eg a recently bereaved person may transiently see the image of the recently deceased person). These can occur as part of a normal grief reaction.

Thought broadcast
Thought broadcast is incorrect. Thought broadcast is a type of delusion when one believes external forces are broadcasting their thoughts such that others can read their minds. This is another ‘first-rank’ symptom of schizophrenia.

stem: An 18-year-old girl presents via her GP who is concerned that she may have an underlying endocrine problem. She is a good student and has just won a place at university. She weighs only 38 kg (6 stone) and is 1.78 m (5ft 10 inches) tall. She is emaciated; her skin is dry and she has excessive growth of lanugo hair. She has been amenorrhoeic for 9 months. Her cortisol level is elevated, her free T4 is normal. She has an anaemia and associated reduced white cell and platelet count. Which one of the following diagnoses is most likely to fit with this clinical picture?
explanation:
Anorexia nervosa
The severe weight loss coupled with elevated cortisol and normal free T4 in a high performing student fits well with a diagnosis of anorexia. It has a female-to-male preponderance of 9:1 and a prevalence of between 0.5% and 1% in young women. Typical laboratory tests include decreased follicle-stimulating hormone, luteinising hormone, oestrogens and 17-hydroxy steroids. Free T4 and thyroid-stimulating hormone levels are usually normal. Anaemia with decreased white and platelet cell count may also occur. There may be metabolic alkalosis, hypocalcaemia, hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia, related to abuse of diuretics or laxatives. Treatment may involve complex psychotherapy for a number of years, and referral to a specialist in the field is recommended.

Addison’s disease
Addison’s disease is incorrect. The elevated cortisol counts against Addison’s disease where cortisol levels are signficiantly reduced.

HIV
HIV is incorrect. There are no risk factors to suggest a diagnosis of HIV, and significant weight loss in the context of HIV would in all likelihood be associated with opportunistic infection.

Occult carcinoma
Occult carcinoma is incorrect. In this patient’s age group the probability of occult carcinoma is much less than that of an eating disorder, and the lack of other symptoms apart from weight loss also count against this as the underlying diagnosis. Anorexia Nervosa

Hypothyroidism
Hypothyroidism is incorrect. The normal free T4 counts against a diagnosis of hypothyroidism, and weight gain rather than weight loss would be more usual.

stem: A 28-year-old man comes to the clinic for review. He has stable bipolar disorder and has been taking lithium for the past 10 years. His current lithium levels are within the normal range. Kidney and thyroid function tests are also normal. Which of the following is the current recommedations on monitoring of lithium levels according to the British National Formulary?
explanation:
6-monthly
6-monthly is correct. The british national formulary states that measuring 6-monthly is adequate as long as they are below 65, lithium levels are below 0.8 mmol/l, have good adherence and no renal or thyroid concerns. Routine serum-lithium monitoring should be performed weekly after initiation and after each dose change until concentrations are stable, then every 3 months for the first year, and every 6 months thereafter.

Monthly
Monthly is incorrect. As regular monitoring as that is unnecessary under current guidelines.

2-monthly
2-monthly is incorrect. Current guidance on lithium suggests that levels should be every six months in stable long-term patients who are under 65 and no adherence or interaction concerns. Guidelines also point out the need for more frequent monitoring if medication is introduced that may alter lithium levels.

12-monthly
12-monthly is incorrect. Monitoring less frequently than every three months runs the risk of toxicity, diabetes insipidus or changes in thyroid status going unrecognised.

No need to check
No need to check is incorrect. Not monitoring the levels of lithium is potentially dangerous due to the likelihood of the above-mentioned complications.

stem: A 17-year-old girl, with no previous history of mental illness, suffers an emotional breakdown with partial speech loss. She deliberately avoids talking about the death of her grandfather. When confronted with similar situations she cannot control her emotions and shows avoidance behaviour. How would her emotional reaction best be described?
explanation:
Repression
The use of conscious efforts to forget unpleasant events is called ‘repression’. Although it is not a sign of psychiatric illness, prolonged repression may cause behavioural and emotional problems if untreated. Repression can lead to disorganised thought processes and social isolation. If repression persists for a long time it can lead to depression, anxiety and even paranoia. Usually an undesirable, unpleasant event leads to a traumatised emotional state, and, as such, it has a pathogenic effect on the thoughts and emotions of the individual subjected to such an experience.

Catharsis
Catharsis is incorrect. This describes the process of releasing strong or repressed emotions or feelings by bringing them into consciousness, resulting in relief.

Retrogression
Retrogression is incorrect. This describes the process where an individual returns to a state of earlier development, often adopting child-like characteristics. It is often a form of defence in response to a difficult or traumatic situation.

Depression
Depression is incorrect. A diagnosis of depression should be considered if a patient has persistent low mood or loss of interest or pleasure in their normal activities, alongside other symptoms such as disturbed sleep, loss of appetite, agitation, poor concentration and ideas of self-harm or suicide. You review a 78-year-old woman who is deeply withdrawn owing to severe depression. You are considering electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). Which of the following factors absolutely precludes the use of ECT?

Amnesia
Amnesia is incorrect. This is the loss of memory where an individual is unable to recall or consolidate information that they would normally be able to recall.

stem: A 59-year-old woman who is taking long term lithium for bipolar disorder comes to the psychiatry clinic for review. She has been diagnosed with nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and the plan is to switch the lithium for an alternative. Which of the following is considered as the next most appropriate intervention?
explanation:
Sodium valproate
Valproate is the second line therapy for bipolar disorder in patients who don’t tolerate lithium or where it’s contraindicated. It shouldn’t be used in patients of childbearing potential because of the risk of teratogenicity, in this case contraception should be offered.

Carbamazepine
Carbamazepine is incorrect. Carbamazepine is considered as a third or fourth line therapy and is usually instigated by specialist psychiatry services for patients who fail to respond to alternative interventions.

Citalopram
Citalopram is incorrect. Citalopram, an SSRI, runs the risk of exacerbating an episode of mania.

Lamotrigine
Lamotrigine is incorrect. Lamotrigine is considered for patients in whom lithium and sodium valproate are contraindicated or unsuitable.

Topiramate
Topiramate is incorrect. Topiramate is not recommended by NICE for the treatment of patients with bipolar disease.

stem: A patient with low mood, poor sleep, loss of interest in her usual activities and some thoughts of self-harm has been taking an antidepressant prescribed by her GP. She complains of having noticed that she gets a dry mouth and has also been constipated since starting the medication. Which of the following medications has she most likely been taking?
explanation:
Amitriptyline
Amitriptyline is the most likely medication that she has been taking. This is a tricyclic antidepressant that can commonly cause anticholinergic side effects, such as dry mouth, urinary retention, acute glaucoma and constipation. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are now used as a first line and are better tolerated than tricyclic antidepressants.

Fluoxetine
Fluoxetine is incorrect. This is a SSRI antidepressant; common side effects include nausea, sexual dysfunction, headache and increased anxiety (in the early stages on taking SSRIs).

Citalopram
Citalopram is incorrect. This is a SSRI antidepressant; common side effects include nausea, sexual dysfunction, headache and increased anxiety (in the early stages on taking SSRIs).

Venlafaxine
Venlafaxine is incorrect. This is a serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor (SNRI) antidepressant; common side effects include nausea and hypertension. Depression

Phenelzine
Phenelzine is incorrect here because it is now a typical third-line agent for the treatment of depression, although it does cause anti-cholinergic side-effects. This is a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) antidepressant; common side-effects also include anticholinergic side effects as seen with tricyclics, but patients are also at risk of hypertensive reaction with tyramine-containing foods (chicken liver, cheese, red wine), also known as the cheese effect.

stem: An 83-year-old man is undergoing cognitive assessment in a psychogeriatric clinic. He was referred because of a change in his behaviour, and his wife has noticed a few aggressive outbursts over the past months. His mini mental test score is 18. Which patterns of cognitive deficit would favour a dementia of subcortical origin?
explanation:
Reduced verbal output
The distinction between cortical and subcortical dementia is not absolute but may be clinically useful, particularly in the early stages. However, as dementia progresses, the symptoms of both groups tend to occur. Cortical dementia: Damage to the cerebral cortex – the outer grey-matter layer of the brain. This area plays a critical role in memory and language, and therefore patients usually have severe memory loss and cannot remember words or understand language. Causes: Alzheimer’s Frontotemporal dementia Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease Subcortical dementia: Damage to areas beneath the cortex and disruption in the frontostriatal connections. Results in early frontal lobe problems such as planning difficulties, poor verbal fluency, personality change and task switching. Typically, the ‘cortical’ functions of correct word use and complex motor tasks (praxis) are preserved in earlier stages. Basal ganglia involvement results in ‘psychomotor’ slowing with reduced verbal output, slowed rate of response and reduced alertness. Common causes of subcortical dementia include: Parkinson’s Disease Vascular dementia Multiple sclerosis Rarer causes include: Normal pressure hydrocephalus Huntington’s disease Wilson’s disease HIV dementia complex.

Constructional apraxia
Constructional apraxia is incorrect as constructional apraxia is the inability to accurately copy drawings or threedimensional constructions. Typically, complex motor functions are preserved in subcortical dementia.

Poor visuospatial performance
Poor visuospatial performance is incorrect as visuospatial performance can be poor in both cortical and subcortical dementia, so it is less helpful for use in trying to differentiate between them.

Preserved verbal fluency
Preserved verbal fluency is incorrect as subcortical dementia is associated with poor verbal fluency. Dementia

Severe memory disturbance
Severe memory disturbance is incorrect as severe memory disturbance is more often seen in cortical dementia.

stem: A 78-year-old man is brought to his GP by his wife. She reports an 18-month history of progressive memory impairment (especially for recent events), worsening apathy and occasional disorientation in previously familiar environments. He scores 21/30 on the mini mental state examination (MMSE). His BP is 150/90 mmHg, and pulse 80 bpm and regular. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Alzheimer’s disease
His presentation is most typical of Alzheimer’s disease (AD). AD is the most common type of dementia, accounting for 60% of all causes of dementia. Cardinal features include an insidious onset of symptoms, progressive memory loss (with memory of recent events most affected) and impaired executive function. Neuropsychiatric symptoms are common in AD, including apathy, irritability and depression. Language tends to be relatively preserved until the later stages of the disease.

Depression
Depression is incorrect. Although depression is an important differential in an elderly personChat presenting with with memory impairment or apathy, the extent of the symptoms here are more suggestive of a primary dementia.

Lewy body dementia
Lewy body dementia is incorrect. Lewy body dementia (LBD) has other characteristic features that this man does not display (eg associated parkinsonian symptoms, greater fluctuations in cognition and alertness, visual hallucinations, hypersensitivity to neuroleptic medication and repeated falls). LBD is the second most common cause of dementia after AD and memory loss may not be as apparent in the early stages.

Mild cognitive impairment
Mild cognitive impairment is incorrect. For a diagnosis of mild cognitive impairment (MCI), a person is defined as having a degree of cognitive impairment that is greater than expected for their age and educational level, but not causing a significant impact on their usual activities of everyday life. It may be thought of as an intermediate zone between normal aging and dementia. The risk of developing dementia in a person with MCI is 5–10 times greater compared to cognitively healthy individuals.

Multi-infarct dementia.

stem: A woman is continually worried that she may be contaminated with industrial chemicals in her workplace. She showers longer and longer every night to remove the chemicals, timing her showers and always using a special towel afterwards. She works with cleaning products but has a normal level of contact with them, using them to clean floors. Which of the following is most likely to be effective in managing her symptoms?
explanation:
Citalopram
Citalopram is an SSRI, and serotonin has been closely implicated in the pathophysiology of obsessive compulsive disorder. The range of SSRIs has been shown to positively impact on OCD, and is therefore considered to be the first line pharmacological intervention.

Amitriptyline
Amitriptyline is incorrect. Amitriptyline is a tricyclic anti-depressant, and it is primarily used for the treatment of depression where nocturnal sedation is also required.

L-dopa
L-dopa is incorrect. L-dopa is used as a treatment for Parkinson’s disease and doesn’t have a role in the treatment of OCD.

Pramipexole
Pramipexole is incorrect. Pramipexole may actually induce obsessive compulsive behavior, indeed use of dopamine agonist therapy is recognised as a risk factor for gambling addiction.

Sodium valproate
Sodium valproate is incorrect. Sodium valproate is used as a mood stabilizer in the treatment of bipolar disorder.

stem: A 30-year-old man with resistant schizophrenia has been switched to a new drug as he is intolerant of chlorpromazine and risperidone. He has been told he has to have regular blood tests to look for ‘low blood cell counts’. On which antipsychotic has he been started?
explanation:
Clozapine
Clozapine is an atypical antipsychotic licensed for the treatment of schizophrenia in patients who are unresponsive to or intolerant of at least two other neuroleptics. It causes fewer extrapyramidal side-effects; the most important side-effect of clozapine is neutropenia and agranulocytosis. This is not dose-related and occurs in 1–2% of patients. Weekly blood counts are required for the first 18 weeks of treatment, then every 2 weeks up to a year, and then monthly maintenance blood tests. All patients on clozapine have to be registered with the Clozaril Patient Monitoring Service. Other side-effects of clozapine include hypersalivation, sedation, weight gain and reduce seizure threshold. Any patient on clozapine who presents with signs of neutropenia, such as sore throat or fever, needs an urgent full blood count.

Chlorpromazine
Chlorpromazine is incorrect. Chlorpromazine does not cause agranulocytosis; it’s most common side-effects are extrapyramidal symptoms and photosensitivity.

Olanzapine
Olanzapine is incorrect. Olanzapine side-effects include drowsiness, weight gain, dizziness, increased appetite, postural hypotension and altered diabetic control.

Quetiapine
Quetiapine is incorrect. Quetiapine side-effects include sedation, dry mouth, dizziness and altered lipid metabolism. Schizophrenia

Risperidone
Risperidone is incorrect. Risperidone side-effects include weight gain, postural hypotension and hyperprolactinaemia, which can lead to impotence, galactorrhoea and amenorrhoea.

stem: A 31-year-old woman is seen at home by her GP 12 weeks post-partum. She is tearful, has lost her appetite and fears that she is worthless and will never amount to anything again. There are no features of delirium. She has a history of illicit drug use and her older brother has depression. There are no features to suggest infection and there are no focal neurological signs. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Postpartum depression
Postpartum depression occurs within the first year of pregnancy and is similar to major depression. It occurs in 10 – 15% of pregnancies. The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) is a screening questionnaire used in the identification of women with postnatal depression.

Drug-induced psychosis
Drug-induced psychosis is incorrect. There is no suggestion of current drug use.

Postpartum blues
Postpartum blues is incorrect. Postpartum blues is a mild, transient disturbance in mood typically occurring between the 3 rd & 6 th day after delivery. Symptoms can include: crying, fatigue, sensitivity to criticism, anxiety, irritability, helplessness and labile mood. Symptoms usually last from hours to a few days.

Postpartum psychosis
Postpartum psychosis is incorrect. Postpartum psychosis usually occurs within the first 2 weeks after delivery and is often associated with confusion, disorientation, delusions and hallucinations. Although delusions of something being wrong with the baby are relatively common in postpartum psychosis, depression is also associated with delusions including nihilistic delusions that body parts are missing.

Schizophrenia
Schizophrenia is incorrect. This lady does not display any of the typical features of schizophrenia (eg: hallucinations, delusions, thought disorder) and in any case this would be much less likely in her case than a postpartum psychiatric disorder. Depression A 23-year-old woman who presented with an acute psychotic episode has been started on Risperidone. She has a significant improvement in her mental state, but asks on discharge about long term physiological effects of her treatment. She has no significant past medical history and takes only the oral contraceptive pill. Her BP is 115/72 mmHg, BMI is 23 and there are no abnormal findings on physical examination.

stem: The CAGE questionnaire is a screening questionnaire for which disorder?
explanation:
Alcohol dependence
The CAGE questionnaire is an extremely brief (four-item) tool used for screening people for alcohol misuse or dependence. A positive response (ie two or more questions answered ‘Yes’) is an indicator of probable caseness and indicates probable need. A definitive diagnostic evaluation is required to confirm a diagnosis in a person who has screened positive, and to establish that person’s actual treatment needs.

Dementia
Dementia is incorrect. For demenetia, cognition is assessed by a standardized cognitive assessment tool such as the Mini-Mental state Examination (MMSE), the six-item Cognitive Impairment Test (6-CIT), the General Practitioner Assessment of Cognition (GPCOG) or the Seven-Minute Screen. However, there is no specific scfreening test for dementia as a whole.

Depression
Depression is incorrect. Depression is screened for by using the PHQ-9 (patient health care questionnaire) screening tool.

Eating disorders
Eating disorders is incorrect. Eating disorders are screened by the SCOFF questionnaire.

OCD
OCD is incorrect. People with symptoms of depression, anxiety, alcohol or substance misuse, body dysmorphic disorder or an eating disorder for obsessive compulsive disorder (OCD) using the following questions: Do you wash or clean a lot? Do you check things a lot? Is there any thought that keeps bothering you that you would like to get rid of, but cannot? Do your daily activities take a long time to finish? Are you concerned about putting things in a special order, or are you upset by mess? Do these problems trouble you?

stem: Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this case?
explanation:
Mefloquine-related psychosis
Psychiatric reactions may occur uncommonly in patients taking mefloquine. Where there is a previous history of with Tutor psychiatric disturbance, mefloquine is not recommended at all; the following adverse effectsChat have allAIbeen reported: depression, mood changes, anxiety, confusion, hallucinations, panic attacks, restlessness, forgetfulness, psychosis and paranoia, emotional instability, aggression and agitation. Mefloquine has also been implicated in cases of suicidal ideation and is known to reduce the seizure threshold, for this reason it should not be used by patients with a history of epilepsy.

Acute schizophrenia
Acute schizophrenia is incorrect. The proximity to use of mefloquine, in the absence of other previous symptoms suggestive of schizophrenia, points us towards a diagnosis of drug-induced psychosis rather than schizophrenia.

Manic depressive psychosis
Manic depressive psychosis is incorrect. Manic depressive psychosis is associated with repeated episodes of depression and hypomania; although this episode may represent a first episode of hypomania, drug-induced psychosis as a result of the mefloquine would need to be excluded first.

Acute alcohol withdrawal
Acute alcohol withdrawal is incorrect. Acute alcohol withdrawal is associated with agitation, and sympathetic activation, rather than the specific features of psychosis seen here.

Illicit drug use
Illicit drug use is incorrect. This is a possible alternative diagnosis, and urine testing for drugs of abuse is advised, in conjunction with appropriate measures for mefloquine-related psychosis including withdrawal of the offending agent.

stem: A 19-year-old man presents to the General Practitioner. He reports that he can hear people talking about him and that someone is making him move his arms and legs like a puppet. He also mentions that these people must be aliens because he found two coins in the street this morning. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for his symptoms?
explanation:
An oral atypical antipsychotic
Atypical antipsychotics (amisulpride, olanzapine, quetiapine, risperidone and zotepine) are generally used as first-line treatment for a newly diagnosed patient with schizophrenia. This is based on the side effect profile compared to typical antipsychotics. Patients would be offered oral medication initially, but if they failed to comply with this then depot medication (either typical or atypical) could be considered.

Reboxetine
Reboxetine is a noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor medication that can be used in the treatment of depression.

An oral typical antipsychotic
Typical antipsychotics such as chlorpromazine and haloperidol are no longer used as first line in the treatment of schizophrenia, due to their extrapyramidal and cardiac side effects.

A depot typical antipsychotic
A depot typical antipsychotic is not used as first-line in schizophrenia. This answer is incorrect because of both the type of antipsychotic and the route. A depot atypical medication is normally used if patients fail to comply with oral medication.

A mood stabiliser
A mood stabilizer would be used in the treatment of bipolar affective disorder, not schizophrenia.

stem: A 32-year-old fireman presents with insomnia, recurrent bad dreams and depressive symptoms after witnessing the death of a colleague during an incident they attended. You understand that he was distressed at the time as he was unable to help his friend, and had to be withdrawn from the building. He admits to drinking a glass of wine each evening to help him sleep and has been violent and aggressive towards his girlfriend. This happened over 2 years ago, yet he is still suffering symptoms now and has missed a significant amount of time off work. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD)
Three key criteria form the basis of the diagnosis of PTSD. These include experiencing a traumatic event where the response was fear or helplessness, persistent re-experiencing of the event and avoidance of stimuli associated with the original event. There is a suspicion that his persistent sick days represent avoidance of the situation in which his friend/colleague died. There are key components to successful treatment in this man, and he should clearly be encouraged to seek help if his alcohol problem is considerable. He should be offered access to psychotherapy, and any underlying depression should be managed with pharmacological intervention if necessary.

Adjustment disorder
Adjustment disorder is incorrect. Adjustment disorder cannot be diagnosed in the presence of alternative explanations for the psychiatric illness, and where symptoms persist for longer than a 2-year period.

Alcoholism
Alcoholism is incorrect. Although this person is self-medicating with alcohol, this isn’t the primary diagnosis, with alcohol merely being used to mask other symptoms.

Reactive depression
Reactive depression is incorrect. Although reactive depression may occur in response to the death of a colleague, the other features, including preoccupation with the event, avoidance of triggers and aggression towards loved ones, are not features of reactive depression alone.

Obsessive compulsive disorder.

stem: A 28-year-old man complains of being extremely unhappy with his appearance. He feels that his nose is disproportionately large and ugly, and he feels distressed if he sees his reflection in a mirror. He is anxious about going out in public and tends to stay in his house, and at times he has been so unhappy that he has thought of suicide. On questioning he tells you that he has had these ideas for many years, but that recently they have got a lot stronger. On examination his nose is slightly large, but his overall facial appearance is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Body Dysmorphic Disorder
This disorder presents as a preoccupation with a presumed defect in appearance that may be an overvalued idea, or may be delusional. The onset of the idea is often in adolescence and it may vary in intensity. The pathology of the disorder is probably close to that of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), and the symptoms respond to treatment with an selective serotonin-reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) but not a neuroleptic.

Hypochondriacal Disorder
Hypochondriacal disorder is also similar but the content of the idea is that there is a specific physical illness.

Obsessive Compulsive Disorder
Obsessive Compulsive Disorder is characterised by uncontrollable recurring thoughts (obsessions) and behaviors (compulsions), that the sufferer is compelled to repeat over and over.

Gilles de la Tourette Syndrome
Gilles de la Tourette is a syndrome of motor and vocal tics. Body Dysmorphic DisorderA 55-year-old woman with a long history of well-controlled paranoid schizophrenia, treated with chlorpromazine, presents to her follow-up outpatient psychiatry appointment with repeated abnormal stereotyped movements localised to the lips, jaw and tongue. She states that friends had brought it to her attention and that she herself had not noticed it. Basic bloods done by the GP showed:

Social Phobia
On the surface the presentation is similar to social phobia, but in this disorder the anxiety and avoidance are rooted in a fear of embarrassment or humiliation in certain social interactions.

stem: A 24-year-old man is newly diagnosed with schizophrenia. He is commenced on treatment, but shortly after starting he develops a resting tremor, slowed movements and a shuffling gait. On which class of drug has he been started that would most likely explain his symptoms?
explanation:
Typical antipsychotics
This man’s symptoms are an example of an extrapyramidal side-effect. Antipsychotics are first-line treatment for schizophrenia; they are commonly divided into ‘typical’ antipsychotics, which are the older drugs and associated with more side-effects – in particular extrapyramidal side-effects (EPS) – and ‘atypical’, which are the newer second-generation drugs. There are four types of EPS: akathisia – the most common type of EPS. Usually presents as motor restlessness with a compelling urge to move and inability to sit still Parkinson syndrome – mask-like facies, resting tremor, rigidity, shuffling gait and bradykinesia dystonias – involuntary contractions of major muscle groups (eg eye muscles, leading to oculogyric crisis; neck muscles, leading to torticollis; etc). Tardive dyskinesias – involuntary movements, particularly of the face and sometimes trunk. Usually occur after many years of treatment with antipsychotic medication

Atypical antipsychotics
Atypical antipsychotics is incorrect. Atypical antipsychotics have less extrapyramidal side-effects.

Dopamine agonists
Dopamine agonists is incorrect. Dopamine agonists (eg cabergoline, ropinirole, etc) are used in the management of primary Parkinson’s disease, so would not be relevant here.

Lithium
Lithium is incorrect. Common side-effects of lithium include tremor, muscular weakness, nausea, polyuria and polydipsia. In lithium toxicity, symptoms can include ataxia, nystagmus, dysarthria, confusion, vomiting and diarrhoea. Lithium is not used in schizophrenia.

Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors is incorrect. Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are used in depression not new-onset schizophrenia; second, their typical side-effects include gastrointestinal (GI) upset, anxiety, tremor, hypotension, etc.

stem: A 57-year-old man is brought to clinic with his wife, who is concerned about a change in his personality. Over the past 2 years she has noticed that he appears less empathetic, irritable, easily distracted and laughs inappropriately. On examination he appears to have muscle wasting and fasciculations. What mutations in which gene may be responsible?
explanation:
C9orf72
The answer is C9orf72 (Option B). In this scenario this patient has features of behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia and motor neurone disease. Although the clinical overlap has been recognised for some time, a hexanucleotide repeat expansion of the GGGGCC repeat in the C9orf72 gene has been shown to be associated with this clinical link. Insight is often lacking in FTD, and carers often voice concerns before the patient about changes in personality.

App
APP (Option A) is incorrect. The amyloid precursor protein gene and mutations in this gene and in PS1 (Option D) are associated with familial onset Alzheimer’s disease. Although personality changes do occur in AD, they are rarely the presenting feature. Motor neurone signs are not present in AD until later in the illness.

MAPT
MAPT (Option C) is incorrect. Mutations in MAPT are also associated with FTD, but not with clinical overlap with ALS. MAPT mutations are associated with FTD with parkinsonism, progressive supranuclear palsy and corticobasal degeneration.

PS1
PS1 (Option D) is incorrect. The PS1 gene (presenilin 1), is involved in the pathogenesis of familial Alzheimer’s disease. The presence of the PS1 gene leads to defective activity of gamma secretase which in turn drives accumulation of amyloid pre-cursor protein. The presence of predominant personality changes wouldn’t fit with a diagnosis of Alzheimers.

Huntingtin
Huntigntin (Option E) is incorrect. Mutations in the Huntingtin gene are associated with Huntington’s disease. Like C9orf72, Huntington’s is a repeat expansion disorder with both psychiatric and motor phenotypes. However, patients with Huntington’s do not typically present with frontal personality changes or signs of upper motor neurone damage. They commonly show apathy, depression, aggression and are at high risk of suicide.

stem: A 27-year-old unemployed man is referred by his GP for investigation of haematemesis. He describes a history of fluctuating mood dating back to his late teens, chronic feelings of emptiness and repeated deliberate selfharm by cutting. He occasionally uses cocaine and cannabis, and admits to occasionally drinking up to 10 pints in a day. He confides he has recently been arrested for hitting his most recent girlfriend after she threatened to leave him. He is angry for having had to wait 20 minutes before seeing you in outpatients, and storms off when asked to wait for blood tests. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Borderline personality disorder
This man displays several of the typical features of borderline personality disorder including: unpredictable behaviour, impulsivity, emotional outbursts and loss of temper rapid fluctuations in emotional state, chronic feelings or loneliness, and boredom strong tendency towards suicidal thinking and deliberate self-harm unstable personal relationships some patients may also have transient psychotic symptoms such as brief delusions or hallucinations

Alcohol dependence syndrome
Alcohol dependence syndrome has specific features that include tolerance, craving, withdrawal symptoms, continued use despite harmful effects and inability to control alcohol use. Although this man at times drinks large amounts, the use is described as ‘occasional’, with none of the other features described.

Cyclothymia
Cyclothymia is a diagnosis in which an individual has mood swings cycling from hypomania and mild depression; it resembles a mild form of bipolar affective disorder. This man does not have any symptoms of hypomania (elevated mood and overactivity without psychotic features or significant functional impairment). Once more, the extent of his symptoms is more fitting for a personality disorder.

Antisocial personality disorder
This man does not meet the description for antisocial personality disorder as well as for borderline personality disorder. Typical symptoms include: persistent aggressive, antisocial or defiant behaviour impulsivity and lack of remorse, deceitfulness unstable interpersonal relationships and disregard for the feelings of others failure to learn from experience and disregard for the consequences of one’s behaviour criminal behaviour is central to the definition of antisocial personality disorder. It is sometimes difficult to differentiate between antisocial personality disorder and borderline personality disorder. However, the key here is that this patient frequently engages in self-destructive tendencies, such as his history of self-harm. This is not seen in antisocial personality disorder, which is why this is not the answer here.

Dysthymia
Dysthymia is a diagnosis when an individual experiences persistent (more than two years) of chronic low-grade depression. The symptoms of dysthymia do not meet the full criteria of major depression. Although this man does have chronic feelings of emptiness, his symptoms are more extensive than would be explained by dysthymia. Personality Disorders A 23-year-old woman requests reduction mammoplasty because she is convinced her breasts are grossly large and misshapen. She dresses in elaborate clothing to hide her shape and although she swims well, has stopped going to the pool. Physical examination reveals breasts well within the normal range of size and shape.

stem: A 28-year-old man presents to the outpatient department complaining of a 6-year history of severe tiredness. This has rendered him essentially bed-bound for the past year. He has been extensively investigated by colleagues in Infectious Diseases, Rheumatology and Neurology, with no clear diagnosis. You decide, after taking a history, examining the patient and reviewing the notes, that he is suffering from chronic fatigue syndrome (CFS). The patient asks you which treatments have been shown to work for his condition. On the basis of current evidence, which one of the following treatments is most suitable for him?
explanation:
Cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT)
On the basis of current evidence, only CBT focusing on graded increments in his activity, with concurrent examination of his attitudes and beliefs towards illness can be confidently recommended by a physician practising evidence-based medicine. A randomised controlled trial (RCT) examining CBT, by Sharpe et al., shows the benefits derived from CBT: The behaviour component is a graded increase in exercise. The cognitive element involves changing nihilistic beliefs about illness and instilling hope, and addressing perfectionist tendencies.

Analytical psychotherapy
Analytical psychotherapy is incorrect. Psychoanalytical psychotherapy may be of help in some cases, but there are no RCTs to support its use in this disorder.

Antidepressant medication
Antidepressant medication is incorrect. It is now clear that antidepressants are of no benefit in CFS unless the patient is also depressed.

Bed rest with passive physiotherapy
Bed rest with passive physiotherapy is incorrect. Complete bed rest is only likely to exacerbate the adverse physiological sequelae of inactivity, and thus worsen symptoms. Active, graded, activity is the key to CFS management.

Family therapy
Family therapy is incorrect. Family therapy is probably of benefit, but the studies have been confined to children and adolescents with CFS, and so do not apply to this patient.

stem: A 60-year-old man is admitted because his wife can no longer cope with him at home. He was fit and well until three months ago, but now has severe cognitive impairment and is bed-bound. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease
The biggest clue towards Creutzfeldt–Jacob disease (CJD) is the rapid progression of symptoms: from fit and well to severe mental and physical impairment within 3 months. This is too quick a deterioration for any of the other conditions listed. The characteristic symptoms of CJD include a history of rapidly progressive dementia, ataxia, rigidity, myoclonus and finally, akinetic mutism and death. CJD is caused by the deposition of an abnormal prion protein in the brain that leads to a process of neuronal loss. Clinically it can present with a non-specific prodromal phase with anxiety, malaise and forgetfulness. Patients can go from normality to death within months.

Alzheimer’s disease
Alzheimer’s disease is incorrect. Alzheimer’s disease is usually insidious in onset and develops slowly over a period of several years. In addition, it does not usually cause patients to become bedridden, although this can occur in the very late stages of the disease after many years.

Gerstmann–Straussler–Scheinker syndrome
Gerstmann–Straussler–Scheinker syndrome is incorrect. Gerstmann–Straussler–Scheinker disease is an extremely rare autosomal dominant prion disease that usually presents in adult life (ages 35–55) with a progressive cerebellar syndrome and later, speech disturbance, myoclonus and dementia. It progresses more slowly than CJD, with a disease course between 2 to 10 years rather than months.

Pseudodementia
Pseudodementia is incorrect. Pseudodementia has symptoms of cognitive impairment resembling dementia, but is due to another underlying cause – most commonly depression, but it can also be seen in severe hypothyroidism. The symptoms usually after treatment of the underlying cause.

Wilson’s disease
Wilson’s disease is incorrect. Wilson’s disease would not explain such a rapid deterioration in physical and mental condition, and usually presents in children or young adults. Wilson’s disease is a rare autosomal recessive disorder of copper metabolism leading to copper accumulation in the liver, basal ganglia, eye, joints and other organs. It typically presents in childhood or adolescence with hepatic manifestations, and in adults with more pronounced neuropsychiatric manifestations such as personality change, dysarthria, ataxia or tremor. It does not cause a rapidly progressing dementia. 310 Prion InfectionsA woman is continually worried that she may be contaminated with industrial chemicals in her workplace. She showers longer and longer every night to remove the chemicals, timing her showers and always using a special towel afterwards. She works with cleaning products but has a normal level of contact with them, using them to clean floors.

stem: An 18-year-old man with a diagnosis of fetal alcohol spectrum disorder comes to the clinic for review. He has responded well to socialization behavioural therapy, and some anger management classes, but is finding it difficult to stick to tasks with respect to the job he’s been given at the local McDonald's. According to his bosses he appears to get bored and has been known to throw food around the restaurant. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation:
Methylphenidate
Aspects of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, (ADHD), are seen in patients with fetal alcohol spectrum disorder, and a similar response to stimulants is observed. As such in this case a trial of an agent such as methylphenidate is most appropriate.

Amitriptyline
Amitriptyline is incorrect. Amitriptyline is a tricyclic anti-depressant with effects on improving sleep quality in the elderly.

Citalopram
Citalopram is incorrect. Citalopram may be of value in patients with fetal alcohol spectrum disorder who have aspects of depression, but there is nothing to suggest depression in the clinical scenario as described here.

Diazepam
Diazepam is incorrect. Diazepam may be useful for short term sedation, but is addictive and should therefore be avoided in this situation.

Venlafaxine
Venlafaxine is incorrect. Venlafaxine is used to reduce REM sleep in patients with hypnogogic hallucinations, and is used as an anti-depressant.

stem: A 23-year-old woman requests reduction mammoplasty because she is convinced her breasts are grossly large and misshapen. She dresses in elaborate clothing to hide her shape and although she swims well, has stopped going to the pool. Physical examination reveals breasts well within the normal range of size and shape. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Body dysmorphic disorder
The symptoms exhibited by this patient are most suggestive of body dysmorphic disorder, a pathological preoccupation with an imagined or minor defect in appearance. The increased availability and effectiveness of reconstructive surgery have made the diagnosis of this disorder more important.

Delusional disorder, somatic type
Delusional disorder, somatic type is incorrect. Delusional disorder, somatic type, is distinguished from body dysmorphic disorder by the presence of patently false beliefs about one’s body. This woman’s beliefs about her breast size are quite far away from frank delusions.

Hypochondriasis
Hypochondriasis is incorrect. Hypochondriasis is characterised by inaccurate perception of signs and symptoms, and the belief that there is an underlying significant illness.

Major depressive disorder,single episode
Major depressive disorder, single episode is incorrect. There are no symptoms of low mood or somatic symptoms of depression to fit with this as the diagnosis.

Somatisation disorder
Somatisation disorder is incorrect. Somatisation disorder is characterised by the presence of a range of physical symptoms for which no organic cause can be found over a considerable period of time (2 years or more).

stem: An 87-year-old woman has symptoms of severe depression: she is eating poorly, neglecting herself and cannot sleep. She states that she is about to die and has no money. What type of delusions are these?
explanation:
Nihilistic delusions
Nihilistic delusions are very negative beliefs about oneself (eg there is no future, they are about to die, their organs are rotting, etc), which are associated with extremes of low mood.

Delusions of guilt
Delusions of guilt is incorrect. Delusions of guilt are false feelings of remorse or guilt (eg that they have committed a horrible crime and should be punished, or are responsible for a disaster such as a flood or earthquake), which are also found in severe depressive illness.

Delusions of reference
Delusions of reference is incorrect. Delusions of reference are the belief that a special meaning lies behind something ‘innocent’ in the public domain (eg a song, book, newspaper or TV programme is about them, or the way objects are arranged in a room or cars parked in the street has a specific reference to them).

Grandiose delusions
Grandiose delusions is incorrect. Grandiose delusions are the belief that they have exceptional talent, abilities, worth or that they may be famous (eg patients may believe themselves to be God, a billionaire or have superpowers). These tend to occur in mania. Depression A 74-year-old lady who is known to enjoy 3-4 glasses of wine per evening as well as gin and tonic is admitted to hospital. She has a past history of hypertension, an MI 6 years ago, and 2 previous admissions for urinary tract infection. The nurses ask you to see her as she appears to be acting strangely. Blood pressure is slightly elevated at 149/89, pulse is 91 and regular. Investigations:

Persecutory delusions
Persecutory delusions is incorrect. Persecutory delusions (also known as paranoid delusions) often involve the theme of being followed, harassed, conspired against or the belief that people or organisations (eg MI5, police, employer) are plotting to harm the patient. A delusion is defined as a strongly held false belief that is not typical of the patient’s cultural or religious background. A patient will not acknowledge the belief as false despite evidence to contradict it, and will often change their other beliefs to keep their whole belief system consistent.

stem: An 85-year-old female with advanced Alzheimer's disease (mini mental state examination 16/30) has inhaled a foreign body. She doesn’t recognise her husband or understand what is proposed. What is the best approach to obtaining permission for the bronchoscopy?
options: No consent needed although legal authority should be obtained
Doctor performing the procedure takes responsibility in her best interests
explanation:
Doctor performing the procedure takes responsibility in her best interests
For a mentally impaired adult, the clinician takes responsibility to do his or her best for the patient. Of course the clinician should discuss the issues in detail with next of kin and carers, but a third party should not be asked to sign a consent form. The clinician should write in the case record what he or she has done and why, especially if parents or carers express misgivings. For difficult cases it is prudent to get the support of an appropriately trained clinical colleague, and this is especially so if the opinion of a parent/carer is to be overridden. Normally this should be the responsibility of a consultant. Although the mini-mental state examination (MMSE) cannot be used to determine capacity to consent, studies generally show good agreement between clinicians’ assessment of incapacity and MMSE <20. For MMSE 21–25 the agreement with clinical judgement as to capacity is less clearly defined.

Psychogeriatrician gives permission
Psychogeriatrician gives permission is incorrect. Involving a third party will cause a potential delay in relieving distress, and he is only likely to concur that the patient does not have capacity.

No consent needed although legal authority should be obtained
No consent needed although legal authority should be obtained is incorrect. A patient who has inhaled a foreign body is likely to be in significant distress and, as such, her best interests are not served seeking Chatby with legal authority.

Relative gives consent
Relative gives consent is incorrect. Although relatives should be consulted, it is up to the clinician to act in the patient’s best interests.

The patient gives consent
