The patient gives consent is incorrect. It is clear with a MMSE score of 16 that she lacks capacity to make a decision with respect to consent.

stem: A 27-year-old male is arrested by the police while trying to smash the window of the local department store. He says a story on the news about people who claim they are in contact with aliens is directed just towards him, and he wants to smash up the television set showing the news in the store window. Which one of the following best describes his symptom?
explanation:
Reference delusion
Reference delusions are associated with paranoid schizophrenia; they refer to the belief that a normal everyday occurrence (in this case broadcasting the news) has particular reference to the patient.

Grandiose delusion
Grandiose delusion is incorrect. An irrational belief that one is on a special mission, particularly important or has unique powers is considered a grandiose delusion.

Bizarre delusion
Bizarre delusion is incorrect. This is fixed belief that cannot possibly be true, for instance that his whole life is a play and he is continually being recorded for television.

Somatic delusion
Somatic delusion is incorrect. A somatic delusion is one that refers to body functioning or appearance. Schizophrenia An 85-year-old woman, who recently moved to a nursing home, complains of feeling lonely, not sleeping well and loss of her appetite over the past month. You suspect she is suffering from depression. She has declined psychological interventions. What would be the preferred treatment of choice?

Auditory hallucination
Auditory hallucination is incorrect. Auditory hallucinations are common in patients with psychotic disorders and are often characterised by voices describing the person in the third person.

stem: A 32-year-old man comes to the clinic for review. His family was lost in a terrorist attack some 9 months earlier, and the coroner’s inquest and possible compensation is still pending. They died on a train and since the event he has suffered multiple flashbacks of the moment when the police came to tell him, and has avoided using the train or the underground since then. He is also obsessed with researching the event on the internet, is unable to sleep and is losing weight. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
Eye-movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR)
The history as described here is entirely consistent with a diagnosis of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). A cornerstone of the management of PTSD is eye-movement desensitisation and reprocessing (EMDR), a technique which uses eye movements to process flashbacks and make sense of the traumatic experience. Conventional CBT is also recognised to have a positive impact on symptoms. Debate exists that exposure alone is responsible for the positive effects of EMDR in managing the condition, and that eye movements may not actually be integral to its success.

Acceptance and commitment therapy
Acceptance and commitment therapy is incorrect. Acceptance and commitment therapy involves teaching acceptance while at the same time working on behavior change towards value-driven goals. There are no randomized clinical trials supporting the efficacy of ACT in PTSD.

Mindfulness based stress reduction
Mindfulness based stress reduction is incorrect. Although patients in mindfulness based stress reduction study did show a reduction in self-reported symptoms of PTSD, there was no difference in the percentage of patients who continued to meet the diagnostic criteria.

Paroxetine
Paroxetine is incorrect. Although SSRIs may form a part of the package of therapy for PTSD, it is CBT, EMDR and other evidence based therapies which form the backbone of treatment.

Interpersonal therapy
Interpersonal therapy is incorrect. Interpersonal therapy isn’t effective for PTSD, although it is effective for patients with depression and eating disorders. Post-Traumatic Stress DisorderA 25-year-old female student nurse is brought to the Emergency Department by her family after experiencing sudden neurologic symptoms. She had been on a home visit when she reported ‘suddenly passing out for a couple of seconds while on the elevator’. She stated that she woke up with blurred vision that developed into loss of vision in both eyes. She also reported an inability to stand due to weakness in her left leg. While in the Emergency Department, the patient described seeing only shadows. She stated that she was generally in good health, without significant medical issues or any history of chronic medical conditions or surgeries, which was confirmed by her mother. There was no psychiatric history or substance misuse. The patient’s family history was not significant for medical or psychiatric diseases, including anxiety, depression and psychosis; however, the patient’s mother reported that her daughter was experiencing significant situational stressors from work, with accompanying financial and relationship stresses. On physical examination, the patient was alert, awake and oriented to person, time and place. Her vital signs were stable, with a blood pressure of 122/70 mm Hg and no orthostatic changes, a heart rate of 80 beats per minute, and a temperature of 36.2 °C. A thorough systemic examination was normal, including her cardiovascular system, with no abnormalities detected on electrocardiography. A neurological examination was normal, and she had an MMSE of 30/30. Her blood tests and a CT head were normal, with no history of a head injury.

stem: A 19-year-old woman comes to the psychiatry clinic for initiation of lithium therapy after two episodes of bipolar disorder. Which of the following side effects of lithium is most commonly seen in the short term?
explanation:
Fine tremor
Fine hand tremor is found in approximately 50% of individuals taking lithium during the first month of therapy. This progressively declines over 1-2 years to around 4%.

Hypothyroidism
Hypothyroidism is incorrect. This is seen over the longer term, and occurs in up to 20% of those taking it. The risk of hypothyroidism is increased in patients who have thyroid autoantibodies at the onset of lithium treatment, and antibody assay may be a useful risk predictor for hypothyroidism.

Renal carcinoma
Renal carcinoma is incorrect. Renal carcinoma is seen as a late adverse event associated with lithium therapy, particularly where there is impaired renal function.

Weight gain
Weight gain is incorrect. Weight gain is seen over the longer term in association with lithium therapy. Lithium Lithium has a wide range of pharmacological actions and therefore a wide range of side-effects Up to 20% of people develop hypothyroidism risk of hypothyroidism is increased in patients who have thyroid autoantibodies at the onset of lithium treatment antibody assay may be a useful predictor of risk of hypothyroidism Polyuria and polydipsia occur secondary to nephrogenic diabetes insipidus Neurological side-effects include fine tremor, blurred vision, ataxia and dysarthria Weight gain, electrocardiogram (ECG) changes and leukocytosis may also occur Lithium is not recommended in pregnancy owing to increased risk of Ebstein’s anomaly Risk of relapse is high, particularly in the first 2 weeks of delivery; this is reduced if lithium is re-started in the first 24 h after birth of the child.

Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH)
Syndrome of inappropriate ADH (SIADH) is incorrect. Lithium is a cause of diabetes insipidus and was formerly used as a treatment for SIADH.

stem: A 41-year-old man, a successful graphic designer, has begun to have trouble finding names for people and objects. He has continued to design brochures and logos for small businesses but has had trouble filling out paper orders, making frequent spelling mistakes. Surprisingly, he was caught stealing an item from a client's store. Soon afterward he began to comb the beach, spending many hours looking for seashells. While at home he began to play solitaire compulsively for six hours per day. He developed a new interest in squash, and his game steadily improved. He stopped working as a graphic designer but obtained a courier job and learned and remembered a complex route for delivering packages. There was no family history of dementia. What is the most likely diagnosis in this case?
explanation:
Fronto-temporal dementia
Fronto-temporal dementia is responsible for 2% of all dementias. It is associated with a gradual degeneration of the frontal and/or temporal lobes and is characterised by alteration in character, inappropriate behaviour in social situations and progressive issues with speech and language. It typically presents in middle age, as in this case.

Alzheimer’s dementia
Alzheimer’s dementia is incorrect. This is a slowly progressive disease, but it tends to affect those later in life (peak age 75-80 years) and does not affect personality. It is focused more on deterioration in cognition (which is maintained in the above case). The MMSE is a useful tool to classify the severity of Alzheimer’s. It is the commonest form of dementia, repsonsibile for 50-75% of cases

Dementia with Lewy bodies
Dementia with Lewy Bodies is incorrect. Progressive dementia is the predominant symptom, but it has other characteristic features. Parkinsonism tends to accompany or even precede the dementia, the cognitive function fluctuates throughout the day and there are often complex visual hallucinations. There are none of these characteristic features in the above case.

Parkinson’s disease dementia
Parkinson’s disease dementia is incorrect. This a subcortical form of dementia, which would only occur after several preceeding years of established Parkinson’s disease before any signs of dementia are seen.

Vascular dementia.

stem: A 19-year-old student comes to the clinic for review. She complains that each night just before she falls asleep she has a sensation of not being able to move, and feels that something is touching the skin of her left arm. This is extremely distressing and she wants some medication to prevent it happening again. Physical examination is entirely normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial intervention?
explanation:
Improved sleep hygiene
Improved sleep hygiene is recognised to reduce the incidence of hypnogogic hallucinations, the most likely diagnosis here. It’s likely as a student that consumption of alcohol, late nights and / or early starts drive poor sleep quality. Encouragement to sleep hygiene and reassurance that hypnogogic hallucinations are of no consequence is the most important thing to stress to this patient.

Amitriptyline
Amitriptyline is incorrect. Tricyclic anti-depressants may be of value in treating hypnogogic hallucinations when there is associated narcolepsy.

Fluoxetine
Fluoxetine is incorrect. Fluoxetine is also a potential treatment for hypnogogic hallucinations in the context of narcolepsy.

Modafinil
Modafinil is incorrect. Modafinil is indicated in the treatment of narcolepsy but would not be recommended here ahead of improvements in sleep hygiene.

Venlafexine
Venlafexine is incorrect. Venlafexine is an effective option in treating hypnogogic hallucinations because it suppresses REM sleep.

stem: A 23-year-old woman is admitted after she took a paracetamol overdose. She is given a treatment dose of Nacetylcysteine, and her baseline and repeat biochemical and haematological indices are normal. She does not enjoy her work as a secretary, and she has a regular partner, but they have been arguing recently. She did not intend to kill herself. She denies regularly using alcohol and illicit drugs. Her only past history is of an aspirin ‘overdose’, but you note that at the time the blood level was very low and she was not admitted. There is no other significant past medical history. Her parents are divorced and she lives with her mother. Which of the following from the patient's history is most associated with increased risk of repeated attempts of self harm/suicide?
explanation:
Overdose attempt
Previous episodes of self-harm or suicide attempts are the biggest predictor of future attempts, even if the actual ‘medical’ harm done was minimal. Around 15% of people who commit deliberate self-harm (DSH) will do so again within a year, and 1% will succeed in committing suicide. Other risk factors include: Male gender (three times more likely than women) Concurrent mental disorder or previous psychiatric treatment Alcohol and drug abuse Unemployment and homelessness Physically disabling or painful illness, including chronic pain Low socio-economic status, loss of job Lack of social support and living alone Organic illness – male gender and middle age predict a completed suicide. NICE recommends that people attending hospital or primary care after an episode of self-harm should receive a biopsychosocial assessment. Identifying the level of risk for repeat attempts and completed suicide is key in deciding who can be safely discharged and the level of mental health services they may need in the community. Very high-risk individuals who refuse treatment may need detention under the Mental Health Act.

Arguing with partner
Arguing with partner is incorrect. Arguing with a partner has not been specifically linked to suicide attempts.

Dissatisfaction with work
Dissatisfaction with work is incorrect. Dissatisfaction with work has not been specifically linked to suicide attempts.

Her age
Her age is incorrect. Rates are currently highest in the age group 45–49.

Parental divorce
Parental divorce is incorrect. Parental divorce has not been shown specifically to be a risk factor for suicide. That said, ‘significant life events’ which can include bereavement, witnessing or experiencing abuse or family breakdown are risk factors. Suicide Statistics Report 2016. Including data for 2012-2014; Samaritans Suicide Risk Assessment and Threats of Suicide. Patient.co.uk.

stem: A 71-year-old woman on an orthopaedic ward has become unwell 72 hours after elective surgery. She is agitated, sleepless and exquisitely sensitive to noise. She has a history of anxiety and depression. Her temperature and vital signs are unremarkable, her CRP is 116 and on an arterial blood gas her PaO 2 is 12.0. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Benzodiazepine withdrawal
The benzodiazepine withdrawal syndrome may often be missed and explained in terms of a reappearance of the original anxiety symptoms. It is characterised by anxiety and restlessness, nausea and sweating, with heightened sensitivity to perceptual stimuli in all modalities. Insomnia may also occur. There is a marked increase in rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. The CRP raise in this case is consistent with recent surgery. General notes Withdrawal symptoms are more commonly experienced when drugs with a short half-life are prescribed, such as lorazepam and temazepam. Withdrawal symptoms can be expected to start 2–3 days after abruptly stopping a short-acting benzodiazepine, but may not be observed until 7–10 days after abruptly stopping diazepam. The withdrawal syndrome itself may last 7–10 days, once symptoms occur.

Urinary tract infection
Urinary tract infection is incorrect. Infection, particularly in the elderly, can cause changes in cognition, but would be unlikely in this case in the context of normal observations. Her CRP is appropriately elevated in the context of recent surgery.

Pulmonary embolus
Pulmonary embolus is incorrect. While it is an important consideration following surgery (especially orthopaedic), PE alone would not adequately explain this patient’s presentation, and abnormalities in observations such as tachypnoea, tachycardia and/or decreased oxygen saturation would be likely.

Paroxetine withdrawal
Paroxetine withdrawal is incorrect. Paroxetine is an selective serotonin-reuptake inhibitor (SSRI), with among the highest incidence of adverse effects upon withdrawal of any agent in this class. SSRI withdrawal syndrome typically begins within 24-48 hours after withdrawal, making this a less likely answer here. The main symptoms are dizziness, nausea, headache and flu-like symptoms, though anxiety, insomnia or vivid dreams, and confusion may also be present.

stem: An 18-year-old woman has a history of panic attacks. She notices that during her attacks she feels disconnected from the external world, as if it is unreal. What is the best description of this symptom?
explanation:
Derealisation
Derealisation is the subjective feeling of an altered reality of the environment. A person may complain of the world seeming like a dream or as if it is unreal.

Hallucination
Hallucination is incorrect. A hallucination is a false sensory perception in the absence of a real external stimulus (eg auditory, visual, tactile, gustatory or olfactory hallucinations).

Illusion
Illusion is incorrect. An illusion is a false perception of a real external stimulus (eg thinking a shadow in the dark is a person or a voice in a crowd is talking to them). Illusions are more common where there is a reduced level of consciousness – in delirium or encephalopathy, for example.

Depersonalisation
Depersonalisation is incorrect. Depersonalisation is a subjective feeling of altered reality of the self. A person may feel as if they are not their normal self, that they need to ‘wake up’ from their present state or that they feel ‘unreal’.

Psychomotor retardation.

stem: A 35-year-old man presents to his GP complaining of difficulty in attaining and maintaining an erection with his partner, which he states is exacerbating problems in their relationship. These issues have been problematic for over three months with no response to conservative management. Morning erections are still spontaneously occurring. He has a healthy active lifestyle, is a never-smoker and drinks little alcohol. He has no risk factors for coronary heart disease; serum lipids, fasting glucose and hormonal profile are normal and there is no focal neurology or anatomical variant on examination. What would be the most appropriate first-line treatment?
options: Lifestyle changes and advice to avoid cycling
explanation:
Psychosexual counselling
Erectile dysfunction (ED) is the persistent or recurrent inability to achieve and maintain a penile erection of sufficient rigidity to permit satisfactory intercourse for at least three months. ED can be secondary to vasculogenic causes (therefore it is extremely important to identify cardiovascular risk factors), neurogenic causes (eg degenerative disorders and polyneuropathy), structural causes (eg Peyronie’s disease), hormonal causes (eg thyroid disease and Cushing syndrome), drug-induced causes (eg SSRIs) and psychogenic causes. The cause is often multifactorial. This patient has had many of these causes ruled out in the vignette. Furthermore, the presence of morning erections makes a physical cause much less likely than a psychological cause. Because of this, and given the clear difficulty in managing this conservatively, referral for psychosexual counselling and therapy is the most appropriate treatment at this stage.

Lifestyle changes and advice to avoid cycling
Lifestyle changes and advice to avoid cycling is incorrect. Lifestyle changes and a period avoiding cycling are reasonable first-line measures for a patient who first presents with erectile dysfunction.

Phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE-5) inhibitor
Phosphodiesterase-5 (PDE-5) inhibitor is incorrect. PDE-5 inhibitors, eg sildenafil, are effective, relatively safe and well-tolerated treatments for erectile dysfunction. Although this would be a reasonable adjunctive treatment at this stage, this does not address the likely underlying driving aetiology of his erectile dysfunction – psychological distress.

Referral to urology
Referral to urology is incorrect. Referral to urology is only appropriate for those for whom oral treatment is contraindicated, not tolerated or ineffective. This patient has not yet tried any active treatment options and, as such, should not be referred to urology at this stage. Somatoform DisordersThe risk of successful suicide is higher in which one of the following individuals?

Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI)
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) is incorrect. SSRIs could be a reasonable treatment option for a patient with significant anxiety or depression. There is no clear evidence of this in the stem, and furthermore, SSRIs can in themselves cause or contribute to erectile dysfunction.

stem: An anxious 20-year-old man complains of severe right lower quadrant pain. On examination there is rebound tenderness. Blood testing shows a leukocytosis. A provisional diagnosis of acute appendicitis is made. However, his pain decreases dramatically after the administration of intravenous normal saline, which he thought was to be administered for his pain but was actually given as he was mildly hypotensive. What is the condition here?
explanation:
Placebo response
Patients commonly respond to a placebo in many medical interventions.

Hypovolaemia
Hypovolaemia is incorrect. There is no evidence that the patient, in this case, was hypovolaemic, and this should not cause specific pain as even in a ruptured appendix, which could cause hypovolaemia, the pain would then be generalized.

Psychogenic pain
Psycogenic pain is incorrect. This is a physical pain caused by extended psychological factors and, while this a possibility, the age of the patient, acuteness of pain and improvement following saline administration make this an unlikely answer.

Histrionic personality disorder
Histrionic personality disorder is incorrect. This is a cluster B personality disorder (dramatic) and is characterised by attention seeking, need for approval and often seductive behaviour. None of the symptoms here suggest that. Somatoform DisordersA man with a dubious record of compliance with HMRC regulations faces a tax audit. He begins to speak about welfare-benefit cheats and people who do not pay their share of costs to society. What defence mechanism is being utilised here?

Factitious disorder
Factitious disorder is incorrect. Such responses do not suggest that the pain or discomfort is factitious, psychogenic or exaggerated. Factitious disorder is the feigning of symptoms where there is no apparent secondary gain; the fact that the pain improves after the IV saline means that this is not the correct answer.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department claiming to be hearing voices. She says that the voices tell her that she is worthless and should kill herself. There is a history of three previous drug overdoses and episodes of suicidal ideation. She currently takes sertraline for generalised anxiety disorder. Physical examination is unremarkable. She is withdrawn and refuses to engage with your questions; she does tell you, however, that her boyfriend is controlling her with his mobile phone and that she can tell this by the numbers which appear on it. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Schizoaffective disorder
The auditory hallucinations seen here, particularly involving a commentary on the patient’s actions, along with major depression, are typical of those seen in schizoaffective disorder.

Bipolar disease
Although this patient is exhibiting symptoms of psychosis, in bipolar disease, a history of recurrent episodes of depression and mania (eg flight of ideas, disinhibition and elated mood) would be expected.

Drug-induced psychosis
Drug-induced psychosis is a potential alternative diagnosis, although the prolonged duration of this patient’s disease counts more towards a diagnosis of schizoaffective disorder.

Personality disorder
Personality disorders are not associated with auditory hallucinations providing a commentary or with delusions of thought insertion. Schizophrenia

Severe depression
Although this patient has a history of suicidal ideation and likely depression, the psychotic features of hallucinations and delusions are more commonly associated with schizoaffective disorder.

stem: Which of the features in this scenario is the strongest risk factor for re-feeding syndrome?
explanation:
BMI 15
The risk of developing the refeeding syndrome is directly related to the amount of weight loss during episode of anorexia, and the rapidity of weight regain. As such a BMI of 15 or less predicts higher risk of refeeding syndrome.

BP 100/60
BP 100/60 is incorrect. Borderline hypotension is not unusual in anorexia, and is not a risk factor for re-feeding syndrome.

Glucose 5.9
Glucose 5.9 is incorrect. Although the re-feeding syndrome is related to reactive hyperinsulinaemia and subsequent hypophosphataemia, a glucose of 5.9 isn’t a risk factor for the syndrome.

K 3.8
K 3.8 is incorrect. The potassium is in the normal range, and standard feeding protocols include adequate potassium replacement, meaning significant hypokalemia is unlikely.

PO4 0.9
PO4 0.9 is incorrect. Only hypophosphataemia at baseline is considered a risk factor for re-feeding syndrome.

stem: A 45-year-old man with mild learning difficulties and a known genetic syndrome has been noted by his family to be developing problems with his memory and communication. He is seen in the memory clinic and is diagnosed with Alzheimer’s dementia. What genetic syndrome is most likely to be linked to Alzheimer’s dementia?
explanation:
Down syndrome
Down syndrome is the most common cause of mental disability and affects approximately 1 in 1000 live births. The incidence of giving birth to a child with Down syndrome rises with advancing maternal age at the time of conception. Approximately 94% of cases of Down syndrome are caused by trisomy 21, 3.5% by translocation and 2.5% by mosaicism. Down syndrome is significantly associated with Alzheimer’s disease, both clinically and on neuropathological findings. Autopsy studies have shown neuropathology in virtually all brains of adults over the age of 40 years with Down syndrome, similar to that found in the brains of people who develop Alzheimer’s dementia.

Tuberous sclerosis
Tuberous sclerosis is incorrect. This is a rare multi-system genetic condition resulting in benign tumours but growing in the patient. Around 50% of patients with tuberous sclerosis have a degree of learning disability, the condition is not linked to Alzheimer’s dementia.

Prader–Willi syndrome
Prader-Willi syndrome is incorrect. This is a genetic condition resulting from the deletion/lack of function of genes on chromosome 15, and causes symptoms including constant hunger, restricted growth and learning difficulties. Prader-Willi syndrome is not associated with Alzheimer’s dementia.

Lesch–Nyhan syndrome
Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is incorrect. This is an X-linked recessive condition, caused by an inborn error of purine metabolism, resulting in abnormally high levels of xanthine and uric acid in the blood of the affected person. A deficient production of hypoxanthine phosphoribosyltransferase is responsible for the abnormality in purine metabolism. This results in gout, renal problems, poor muscle control and learning disability, and is characterised by self-injurious behaviour in the majority of affected patients. It is not linked to Alzheimer’s dementia. Genetic Counselling Including Patterns of InheritanceFragile-X syndrome
Fragile X syndrome is incorrect. It is the most common inherited cause of mental disability, but second to Down syndrome in terms of all genetic causes (Down syndrome being caused by trisomy 21 and not an inherited defect). Fragile X syndrome is not linked to Alzheimer’s dementia.

stem: An 18-year-old man comes to the psychiatry clinic for assessment. Although he has found it easy to form relationships at school, and has excelled at speaking and presentation tests, he has always struggled with written work. This precipitated him leaving school with no formal qualifications. He is working well in his new role as an apprentice car mechanic. Assessment in the clinic reveals normal eyesight and hearing. A writing test reveals difficulties in sentence construction and in spelling. Neurological assessment reveals dyspraxia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Dyslexia
Reading and writing difficulties in an otherwise intelligent individual, accompanied by symptoms of dyspraxia, is most likely to be due to dyslexia. It is more common in males than females and a number of interventions are available to help individuals their written language skills.

Autism spectrum disorder
Autism spectrum disorder is incorrect. This is a developmental disorder characterised by significant difficulties in social interaction and nonverbal communication, along with restricted and repetitive patterns of behaviour and interests.

ADHD
ADHD is incorrect. ADHD is characterised by inattention and an inability to complete tasks, which wouldn’t fit with the picture of high attainment in his apprenticeship described here.

Low intelligence
Low intelligence is incorrect. The fact that he has a good level of attainment in presentation tasks at school, and in his work as an apprentice mechanic, counts against low intelligence.

Cataplexy
Cataplexy is incorrect. Cataplexy is sudden onset muscular weakness and collapse triggered by emotional events.

stem: A 22-year-old man is found in the street by the police and brought to the Emergency Department. He is seminaked and has been approaching passers-by in an agitated fashion. Which one of the following statements by the patient most strongly suggests the presence of schizophrenia?
options: ‘All the police in this town have been spying on me’
‘I have been given special powers by God to eliminate the Antichrist’
‘If you don’t let me go I’ll kill myself’
‘The salaam transputer has degenerated my brain’
‘The voices control me; they made me take my clothes off’
explanation:
‘The voices control me; they made me take my clothes off’
In this statement he is displaying two first-rank symptoms of schizophrenia: first, auditory hallucinations; second, exhibiting the ‘made’ or ‘passivity’ phenomenon, whereby he believes his actions are controlled by an external force.

‘All the police in this town have been spying on me’
‘All the police in this town have been spying on me’ 'All the police in this town have been spying on me' is incorrect. Although this is a paranoid delusion, it is not as strong evidence as ‘The voices control me; they made me take my clothes off’, where hallucinations are also present. This statement could represent other conditions such as a paranoid personality disorder.

‘I have been given special powers by God to eliminate the Antichrist’
‘I have been given special powers by God to eliminate the Antichrist’ 'I have been given special powers by God to eliminate the Antichrist' is incorrect. Once again it is a grandiose delusion but without hallucinations, so is not as strong a marker for schizophrenia as ‘The voices control me; they made me take my clothes off’. This statement could represent evidence of other conditions such as a manic bipolar episode or psychosis secondary to drugs (eg amphetamines).

‘If you don’t let me go I’ll kill myself’
‘If you don’t let me go I’ll kill myself’ 'If you don't let me go I'll kill myself' is incorrect. This statement is not suggestive of any of the symptoms of schizophrenia.

‘The salaam transputer has degenerated my brain’
‘The salaam transputer has degenerated my brain’ 'The salaam transputer has degenerated my brain' is incorrect. It is also a delusion but without a suggestion of hallucinations, which makes E a better choice.

stem: A 70-year-old man is referred by his General Practitioner with a Montreal Cognitive Assessment score of 22/30 in the context of a 14-month history of insidious onset, but progressive memory loss and behavioural change. His son, who accompanies him, states that he is very changeable even on a day-to-day basis, with some days being relatively coherent and able to converse and others being extremely drowsy and mute. Over the last three weeks he has started to have multiple falls. On examination you note hypomimia, bradykinesia and some axial rigidity. Which one of the following is the most likely primary brain pathology or histopathology?
explanation:
Lewy bodies
This patient has dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB), demonstrating progressive dementia, fluctuating cognition with pronounced variations in attention and alertness, and spontaneous features of parkinsonism. Additional core features of DLB (which are not present in this case) include recurrent complex visual hallucinations and severe sensitivity to neuroleptics. Lewy bodies are eosinophilic inclusions found diffusely in both subcortical and cortical areas of the brain in DLB. They are also present in Parkinson’s disease, but are restricted to subcortical areas. Clinically DLB can be differentiated from Parkinson’s disease dementia by the timing of the cognitive dysfunction vs the movement disorder: in DLB, the onset of movement disorder occurs at least 1 year after the onset of cognitive symptoms, as in this case.

Beta-amyloid protein
Beta-amyloid protein is incorrect. This patient exhibits marked fluctuation in alertness along with parkinsonism, and as such the diagnosis is more likely to be DLB than Alzheimer’s disease (AD). AD is characterised histopathologically by the presence of extacellular clumps of beta-amyloid protein (and neurofibrillary tangles).

Micro-infarcts
Micro-infarcts is incorrect. The diagnosis in this case is most likely to be DLB. Vascular dementia, another common cause of dementia, does not have pathognomonic histopathology; however, micro-infarcts would likely be seen. Features supporting a diagnosis of vascular dementia would be: acute onset of symptoms, step-wise progression, underlying vascular risk factors and lower limb gait disorder – typically shuffling small steps, known as ‘marche à petits pas’.

Pick bodies
Pick bodies is incorrect. Pick bodies are argyrophilic inclusions within neurons seen in the frontotemporal dementias (FTD). The stem here is typical for a diagnosis of DLB. Features typical of FTD would include: relative preservation of memory, prominent behavioural and personality change, with early and significant disinhibition.

Tau protein
Tau protein is incorrect. Tau protein is abnormally hyperphosphorylated and aggregated into bundles to form intraneuronal neurofibrillary tangles characteristic of AD. AD is the most common cause of dementia, but it is not associated with pronounced fluctuations in attention and alertness or parkinsonism as described in this case. The diagnosis here is DLB.

stem: A 34-year-old man with a long history of a major depressive disorder phones the Emergency Department asking for advice. His mood has been lower than usual and his psychiatrist recently changed his antidepressant from sertraline to low-dose imipramine. He freely admits that when he is low in mood he tends to develop physical symptoms, but he's particularly worried about a pain in his right eye. This started rapidly about 2 hours ago and is becoming more intense. How should this patient be managed?
options: Advise him to increase the dose of imipramine
Advise him to take simple analgesia
Reassure and advise him to think of the pain in psychological terms
explanation:
Urgent ophthalmology review
This patient describes a probable case of acute glaucoma arising from the anticholinergic side effects of the tricyclic drug imipramine. The side effects of the tricyclics can be predicted from a consideration of their mode of action: Neurotransmitter system Side effect Anticholinergic: muscarinic Dry mouth Constipation Urinary retention Blurred vision Acute glaucoma Anti-alpha-adrenergic Postural hypotension Tachycardia Anti-histaminergic Sedation Weight gain Quinidine-like action Flattened t-waves, prolonged QT, negatively ionotropic In contrast, for the selective serotonin-reuptake inhibitors the side effects can be predicted by imagining a sudden influx of serotonin into the circulation. Thus there is nausea, diarrhoea, insomnia, agitation and sexual dysfunction.

Advise him to increase the dose of imipramine
Advise him to increase the dose of imipramine is incorrect. This patient's symptoms are probably secondary to his imipramine, and increasing the dose may potentially exacerbate matters.

Advise him to take simple analgesia
Advise him to take simple analgesia is incorrect. This patient describes symptoms of a potentially sightthreatening condition and requires urgent ophthalmology review.

Reassure and advise him to think of the pain in psychological terms
Reassure and advise him to think of the pain in psychological terms is incorrect. This patient describes symptoms of a potentially sight-threatening condition and requires urgent ophthalmology review.

Urgent psychiatric review.

stem: A 27-year-old woman attends cardiology outpatients with a four-month history of attacks of palpitations, associated with sweating and dyspnoea. During these episodes she feels strange and unreal, and is frightened that she is having a heart attack. On one occasion she woke up with the symptoms and attended the Emergency Department in the middle of the night. An ECG was found to be normal and she was sent home when the symptoms resolved. Following a recent attack on a bus on the way to work, she has been reluctant to go out unless a relative is with her. On examination resting blood pressure is 145/100 mmHg, pulse 72 bpm and regular, and the rest of the cardiovascular examination is normal. You are reviewing her with the results of ambulatory cardiac monitoring, which show no evidence of arrhythmia. Which of the following is the most suitable long-term treatment option?
explanation:
Citalopram
The patient has panic disorder with agoraphobia. Agoraphobia is a fear or avoidance of situations in which a panic attack would be particularly unpleasant. The diagnosis is made by the presence of the following: recurrent panic attacks (palpitations, sweating, dyspnoea, de-realisation, fear of having a heart attack), some of which are spontaneous fear of having further attacks. Panic disorder can be successfully treated with a psychological therapy, either alone or in combination with medication. SSRIs are the usual first-line medications (paroxetine and citalopram have a UK licence), although some tricyclic antidepressants (clomipramine and imipramine) and monoamine oxidase inhibitors (phenelzine and moclobemide) are also effective.

Propranolol
Propranolol is incorrect. Propranolol may reduce palpitations but does not prevent panic attacks.

Diazepam
Diazepam is incorrect. Benzodiazepines may be used as an adjunct to selective serotonin-reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) therapy during the initial phases of treatment, or as second-line therapy.

Thioridazine
Thioridazine is incorrect. This is a neuroleptic reserved for second-line treatment of psychotic disorders. Panic DisorderCounselling
Counselling is incorrect. Counselling has no role in the management of panic attacks. A program of targeted cognitive behavioural therapy is much more appropriate.

stem: A 17-year-old woman is reviewed in the psychiatric clinic. Her expected weight is 55 kg and since follow-up began, her lowest weight has been 49.5 kg. She goes through episodes of binge-eating and vomiting and also reports prolonged fasts; her BMI is 19 kg/m2. She is scared of putting on weight and has missed her last two periods. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Bulimia nervosa
Bulimia nervosa is characterised by: Binge-eating with associated feelings of loss of control and intense guilt Periods of dietary restraint that can include episodes of fasting, vomiting, laxative abuse or excessive exercise. Bulimia is not usually associated with severe weight loss; this woman has not lost much weight and a BMI of 19 kg/m2 is still within the normal range (18.5–24.9).

Anorexia nervosa – restricting type
Anorexia nervosa – restricting type is incorrect. The DSM V definition of anorexia mandates: limited energy intake relative to needs causing a significantly low body weight in the context of the patient’s demographics and physical health intense fear of gaining weight or of becoming fat disturbance in the way in which one’s body weight or shape is experienced or persistent lack of recognition of the seriousness of the current low body weight. The restricting type requires that during the last three months, the individual has not engaged in recurrent episodes of binge eating or purging behaviour. This patient has had episodes of binge-eating and purging and they do not have a significantly low body weight. DSM V criteria describes significantly low body weight as “a weight that is less than minimally normal.”.

Anorexia nervosa – binge-eating/purging type
Anorexia nervosa – binge-eating/purging type is incorrect. Once again this woman does not fulfil the diagnostic criteria for anorexia nervosa. The DSM V definition of anorexia mandates: limited energy intake relative to needs causing a significantly low body weight in the context of the patient’s demographics and physical health intense fear of gaining weight or of becoming fat disturbance in the way in which one’s body weight or shape is experienced or persistent lack of recognition of the seriousness of the current low body weight. The binge-eating/purging type requires that during the last three months, the individual has engaged in recurrent episodes of binge eating or purging behaviour. Whilst this patient has had episodes of binge-eating and purging they do not have a significantly low body weight. DSM V criteria describes significantly low body weight as “a weight that is less than minimally normal.”.

Depression
Depression is incorrect. There are no core features of depression.

Personality disorder
Personality disorder is incorrect. There is no suggestion of a personality disorder. The main differential diagnoses of eating disorders are anorexia and bulimia. Depression and obsessive–compulsive disorder are frequently associated with anorexia, which has a high long-term mortality of 18–20%. Anorexia can be divided into two subtypes based on symptoms during the last 3 months: - restricting subtype: characterised by dieting, fasting or excessive exercise - binge-eating/purging subtype: characterised by recurrent episodes of binge-eating or purging Binge episodes and fasting episodes can be seen in both anorexia and bulimia, but purging behaviours (eg laxatives and diuretic abuse) are more characteristic of bulimia. Bulimia Nervosa A 17 year old woman comes to the clinic for review. She is some 3 months away from her A-levels and is depressed and anxious about her potential grades. She is currently waking at 4:30am, and is findng it difficult to eat. She has thought that it might be easier to just take an overdose of paracetamol, and end it all, but has so far resisted the urge to do so. She has no physical health problems and is predicted to achieve 4 A grades.

stem: A 52-year-old man with a history of bipolar mood disorder presents to the emergency department with agitation, insomnia and bizarre ideas. He is usually managed with long term lithium, but compliance is variable and abuse of recreational drugs has been previously reported. Which of the following symptoms would lead you to doubt the diagnosis of a manic episode?
explanation:
Visual hallucinations
Visual hallucinations are not normally seen in association with mania, and are more likely to be seen in association with an underlying organic disorder.

Distractibility
Distractibility is incorrect. Distractibility and loss of concentration is a common feature of mania.

Flight of ideas
Flight of ideas is incorrect. Flight of ideas is a classical feature of mania.

Tearfulness
Tearfulness is incorrect. Although tearfulness might seem incongruent, rapid fluctuation in mood is very common in episodes of mania.

Delusional ideas
Delusional ideas is incorrect. Delusions are seen in patients with mania. These more normally take the form of grandiose delusions rather than paranoid ideas.

stem: A 21-year-old man describes episodes of drowsiness during the day that can come on suddenly and at any time. He also tells you that, on a number of occasions, he has awoken early in the morning with the feeling that he cannot move his arms and legs, which he finds very frightening. On examination there are no neurological abnormalities. Which investigation would be most useful in arriving at a diagnosis?
explanation:
Multiple sleep latency test
The case describes a patient with narcolepsy. The classical features are an intense desire to go to sleep and associated sleep paralysis, as described here. Up to 70% of patients with narcolepsy also have cataplexy. About one-third of all patients have a family history of the disorder. There is a strong HLA association; about 95% of white people with narcolepsy are positive for the DRw16 subtype of DR2. The MSLT will demonstrate rapid eye movement (REM) sleep at sleep onset, or shortly after the onset of sleep, in those with narcolepsy.

EEG with photic stimulation
EEG with photic stimulation is incorrect. This test might be used in the evaluation of a patient with symptoms suggestive of photosensitive epilepsy.

HLA typing
HLA typing is incorrect. Despite the strong HLA association, HLA typing is very unlikely to help you reach a specific diagnosis in this setting.

MRI of the brain
MRI of the brain is incorrect. In this setting, the brain scan is likely to be normal and therefore will not help you to arrive at a diagnosis. NarcolepsySingle photon emission CT
Single photon emission CT (SPECT) is incorrect. SPECT scans are occasionally used in the investigation of patients with neurological disease. One example is the dopamine active transporter (DAT) SPECT scan, used in some circumstances to help with the evaluation of patients with parkinsonism.

stem: A 35-year-old man complains of chest pain. When the doctor asks questions he replies, ‘You are the doctor, you tell me’. He is also unhappy with the doctor’s attitude and states that if he is not treated properly he will sue the hospital. What is this patient’s personality trait?
explanation:
Passive–aggressive
Passive–aggressiveness is described as covert aggression expressed through passivity, masochism and selfdefeating behaviour. Such an individual is often angry and often angers others. The usual result is further deterioration of the interaction, with even greater anger and passive–aggressiveness.

Antisocial
Anti-social is incorrect. Anti-social personality disorder is characterised by impulsive, irresponsible and often criminal behaviour with a blatant disregard for the feelings or rights of others.

Passive–dependent
Passive-dependent is incorrect. Passive-dependent personality disorder involves difficulty making everyday decisions without an excessive amount of input and advice from others.

Avoidant
Avoidant is incorrect. Avoidant personality traits are defined by shyness and withdrawn behaviour.

Narcissistic
Narcissistic is incorrect. Patients with narcissistic personality disorder have an inflated sense of their own importance, a deep need for admiration and a lack of empathy for others. This is also associated with very limited self-esteem.

stem: You see a woman who tells you she has felt empty and low in mood for a long time. She tells you that she has no friends, prefers to stay at home but hates being alone, uses cannabis, has a history of alcohol use and history of self-harm with threatening suicide. On examination of her Emergency Department records it transpires she has self-harmed on around six occasions over the past year. She denies early morning wakening or lack of appetite. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Borderline personality disorder
Borderline personality disorder is characterised by instability of mood, self-image and interpersonal relationships. Frequently patients complain and worry about being left alone, but are unstable with respect to interpersonal relationships. They have a problem with self-harming and feelings of emptiness. Management of personality disorder is generally to avoid medication, and counsel patients with strategies to avoid this type of behaviour if possible.

Depressive disorder
Depressive disorder is incorrect. This patient has no appetite loss or early morning wakening, which are normally associated with endogenous depression, the chronic repeated cycles of her abnormal behaviour make personality disorder more likely than a depressive illness.

Schizoid personality disorder
Schizoid personality disorder is incorrect. Schizoid personality disorder is characterised by a lack of interest in social relationships, a tendency towards a solitary or sheltered lifestyle, secretiveness, emotional coldness and apathy rather than the impulsive behaviour seen here.

Histrionic personality disorder
Histrionic personality disorder is incorrect. Histrionic personality disorder is characterised by a pattern of excessive attention-seeking emotions, usually beginning in early adulthood, including inappropriately seductive behaviour and an excessive need for approval. Personality Disorders

Narcissistic personality disorder
Narcissistic personality disorder is incorrect. Narcissistic personality disorder is characterised by individuals who have an inflated sense of their own importance, a deep need for admiration and a lack of empathy for others.

stem: A 52-year-old woman is reviewed on the ward before discharge after a 3-day admission for alcohol detoxification. She is requesting to be discharged. This is her third admission over the past 2 years, and she would like some medication to reduce any alcohol cravings that she has. Which of the following is a potential option in this regard?
explanation:
Naltrexone
Naltrexone is a partial opioid antagonist and does have value in reducing alcohol cravings in patients with alcohol dependence syndrome. It is however no substitute to CBT / alcoholics anonymous, and must be used in combination with these interventions, under the supervision of a psychiatrist.

Buproprion
Buproprion is incorrect. Buproprion is an anti-depressant which is used as an agent for smoking cessation.

Chlordiazepoxide
Chlordiazepoxide is incorrect. This is a benzodiazepine used in the management of short term alcohol withdrawal, but long term use is not advised.

Disulfiram
Disulfiram is incorrect. This isn’t an agent which blocks alcohol cravings, but is an aldehyde dehydrogenase inhibitor, which drives accumulation of acetaldehyde leading to significant adverse effects of alcohol consumption including vomiting. Alcohol Misuse and DependenceA 50-year-old woman who is admitted on the liver ward with decompensated alcoholic liver disease becomes very anxious and agitated, as she tells you there are snakes on the wall. The only thing you see on the wall is a retaining bracket. What is this symptom called?

Thiamine
Thiamine is incorrect. This is important as prophylaxis against thiamine deficiency, but doesn’t have a role in reducing alcohol cravings.

stem: A 33-year-old housewife comes to the clinic. She has been extremely troubled by episodes of repetitive behaviour since the birth of her last child. After changing the child’s nappy she finds she has to wash her hands at least eight times. She is the same with preparing food, and will only touch public toilets with her foot to avoid catching a bacterial infection. Clinical examination and basic haematology and biochemistry investigations are entirely normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate way to manage her?
options: Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) and exposure response prevention (ERP)
explanation:
Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) and exposure response prevention (ERP)
This woman has symptoms consistent with obsessive-compulsive disorder, and a combination of CBT and ERP, which can be conducted by telephone in many cases. Although pharmacotherapy may shorten to the time before which a response to treatment is seen, psychological intervention is preferred in the first instance.

Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) and sertraline
Cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) and sertraline is incorrect. CBT without ERP is considered less effective than the two in combination, and selective serotonin-reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are considered a secondary intervention.

Exposure response prevention (ERP) and sertraline
Exposure response prevention (ERP) and sertraline is incorrect. ERP without CBT is considered less effective than the two in combination, and according to guidance, psychological therapies are preferred in the first instance.

Amitriptyline
Amitriptyline is incorrect. Tricyclic anti-depressants don’t have a role in the management of OCD, with SSRIs the preferred option in resistant patients.

Diazepam
Diazepam is incorrect. Benzodiazepines are not considered an option because they are addictive and mask symptoms rather than resolving the underlying problem.

stem: A 22-year-old man is admitted for assessment after being found wandering the streets saying that he is being controlled by radio waves from a mobile-phone tower. He hears voices being critical about him. After talking to his family it is clear he has had these symptoms for 6 weeks. Which treatment is most appropriate to control his symptoms?
explanation:
Risperidone
This man has characteristic symptoms of schizophrenia (auditory hallucinations and delusions of control). Antipsychotics are first-line treatment for schizophrenia. Antipsychotics are commonly divided into ‘typical’ antipsychotics, which are the older drugs, and ‘atypical’, which are newer second-generation drugs. 2002 NICE guidelines used to recommend atypical antipsychotics in preference due to fewer side-effects, particularly extrapyramidal side-effects and tardive dyskinesia. However, the more recent 2014 guidelines no longer explicitly recommend atypical antipsychotics, and instead state the choice should be based on the views of the patient and healthcare professional after considering the likely benefits and possible side-effects of each drug. In practice, atypical drugs are often still first-choice, which is why risperidone is correct as the only atypical antipsychotic among the possible answers.

Chlorpromazine
Chlorpromazine is incorrect as chlorpromazine is a typical antipsychotic and its common side-effects include extrapyramidal symptoms, tardive dyskinesia, weight gain and glucose intolerance.

Cognitive behavioural therapy
Cognitive behavioural therapy is incorrect as cognitive behavioural therapy alone is unlikely to be the most appropriate initial treatment in a new presentation of schizophrenia, although it may have a role in long-term management and prevention of relapse

Fluoxetine
Fluoxetine is incorrect as fluoxetine is an antidepressant not an antipsychotic. Schizophrenia A previously convicted criminal now spends time working in a local nursing home and has recently joined the fire-fighting service. What defence mechanism is most strongly suggested by this behaviour?

Haloperidol
Haloperidol is incorrect as haloperidol is also a typical antipsychotic and has a particularly high incidence of extrapyramidal side-effects.

stem: A 39-year-old man is an inpatient on the Psychiatric Ward. He was treated with electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) alongside antidepressants for treatment-resistant depression, and reports that his mood is improving. However, he refuses to eat if there is no provision for a stroll in the garden in the afternoon. Which learning principle would you apply to explain this patient’s behaviour?
explanation:
Premack principle
This patient is exhibiting learned behaviour according to a reinforcement hierarchy. A patient’s less preferred behaviour can be treated with the use of a desired reward. In this instance, the patient’s eating problems associated with his depression can be treated if the eating problem is considered for treatment before that of his depression, and if the desired eating behaviour is rewarded to ensure its recurrence. The major elements in the Premack principle are: More preferred activities reinforce less preferred activities. The specific degree of preference is determined by the individual who holds the preference. Recognition of the most preferred activity must take place before the reinforcement can be given. Patients with eating disorders can be treated by the application of this principle.

Classical conditioning
Classical conditioning is incorrect. Classical conditioning refers to learning a new behaviour in association with a stimulus, where the behaviour and the stimulus are linked together to produce a new learned response: for example, feeling of excitement about Christmas when you smell a real Christmas tree.

Extinction
Extinction is incorrect. Extinction is when a conditioned learned behaviour disappears over time if it is not reinforced.

Operant conditioning
Operant conditioning is incorrect. Operant conditioning refers to a type of learning in which a behaviour is changed by the behaviour’s consequences, such as reward or punishment. Depression

Incidental learning
Incidental learning is incorrect. Incidental learning is where learning occurs without any intention to learn: for example, learning how to use extra features in a computer programme while using it for a task at work.

stem: A 74-year-old woman is noted to have poor self care with symptoms of early morning wakening and decreased appetite. She gets agitated easily. There is a history of recent death in the family. She also recently lost her job. She has difficulty in answering short-term recall questions. Routine physical examination is unremarkable, apart from the fact that her BMI is significantly reduced at 19. What is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Depressive pseudodementia
Early morning wakening and decreased appetite are symptoms of depression, and there have clearly been life events that may have precipitated that illness. Short-term memory loss may occur in conjunction with depression (depressive pseudodementia) as well as being seen in dementia. The memory loss improves with treatment of the depression. Other physical signs of depression include weight loss, constipation, loss of libido, impotence in men, fatigue and generalised body aches and pains. Physchomotor retardation or agitation of behaviour may occur.

Pathological grief
Pathological grief is incorrect. Pathological grief disorder is associated with a prolongation of the normal grief response and a degree of grief response where patients cannot continue with activities of daily living. What marks this scenario out as depression is the early morning wakening and decreased appetite.

Dementia
Dementia is incorrect. Although dementia is the main differential here, depression should be ruled out first, particularly with the proximity to recent bereavement.

Personality disorder
Personality disorder is incorrect. The features of depression including poor self care, early morning wakening and decreased appetite point us towards this as the underlying diagnosis, rather than for instance withdrawal from society associated with schizoid personality disorder. Depression A 49 year old woman presents to the psychiatry clinic for review. She has severe anxiety and has failed to respond to an SSRI. A decision is made to start buspirone therapy. Which one of the following should you warn her she is most likely to suffer from?

Delirium
Delirium is incorrect. The chronic course of her symptoms, associated with significant life events, (bereavement and job loss) count against delirium as the cause.

stem: Following a severe stroke, a 52-year-old man complains of difficulty in remembering events, people’s names and daily activities. He can remember events that occurred prior to his stroke, but appears unable to form new, long-term memories. On neuropsychological testing, he is able to perform tasks such as solving puzzles, visual discriminations and skilled eye–hand coordination movements. However, he is unable to consolidate any new information for immediate explicit recall. What would be the most appropriate description of his present condition?
explanation:
Anterograde amnesia
Failure to acquire and consolidate new information after trauma, e.g. severe disease, injury, surgery or malnutrition, is called ‘anterograde amnesia’. Although other cognitive abilities remain intact, the patient cannot cope with daily life without help: this is owing to a major cognitive failure to store immediate learning experiences for long-term memory. This patient’s language skills do not seem to be affected since he can carry on a conversation about general events, although he cannot recall them afterwards. The patient can also count backwards and forwards. Such patients tend to require constant care and supervision.

Retrograde amnesia
Retrograde amnesia is incorrect. This refers to the failure to recall events or information that was learned before the trauma/injury/disease.

Simple amnesia
Simple amnesia is incorrect. This describes the loss of information from the memory as a result of disease or injury to the brain.

Lacunar amnesia
Lacunar amnesia is incorrect. This is the loss of a memory about a specific event.

Dissociative amnesia
Dissociative amnesia is incorrect. This describes difficult recalling information from the memory, and is often the result of severe psychological stress or trauma.

stem: A 25-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner with feelings of low mood and lethargy, particularly during the colder months. Her symptoms have been associated with a craving for carbohydrates, resulting in a 5 kg weight gain. She reports having felt better in herself a few months earlier, with a positive mindset and a more active lifestyle. Most of her day is spent working in a small office for a local accountancy firm. Her medical history reveals no other mental illnesses or physical complaints. Physical examination is normal. What is the recommended initial management for this patient?
explanation:
Cognitive behavioural therapy
This patient has a diagnosis of seasonal affective disorder (SAD). In people with SAD, there is a regular temporal relationship between the onset of depressive symptoms and a particular time of the year. Typically, episodes of depression begin in autumn or winter and end in spring or summer as the number of hours of daylight increases. Symptoms of hyperphagia, hypersomnia and weight gain are more typical in SAD, compared with matched non-seasonal controls. The aetiology of SAD is thought to be related to melatonin metabolism and changes during winter, although it is unclear whether light therapy has any effect on symptoms. Guidelines now recommend that SAD should be treated like other subtypes of depression with the use of cognitive behavioural therapy and access to antidepressants for appropriate patients.

Lithium
Lithium is used in the treatment of bipolar affective disorder. Although bipolar disorder may follow a seasonal pattern, it is less likely, compared to a diagnosis of SAD, and episodes of frank mania are absent in the scenario.

Low-dose clonazepam
It is important to avoid sedatives such as benzodiazepines in SAD, as these can exacerbate symptoms.

Melatonin
Melatonin is a naturally occurring hormone produced by the pineal gland that is involved in the circadian rhythm. One of the theories underlying SAD is that lack of sunlight predisposes to hypothalamic dysfunction and increased melatonin production. Prescribing melatonin would exacerbate the symptoms. Depression

Sertraline
Sertraline is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor used in the management of depression and anxiety. Although it can be used in SAD, the first line of management would be to begin with cognitive behavioural therapy.

stem: A 25-year-old man presents to the General Practitioner with involuntary movements and vocalisations that he has been experiencing since childhood. These symptoms have become more frequent and disruptive in recent months, affecting his work and social life. He also reports episodes of repetitive blinking, shoulder shrugging, and throat clearing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Tourette syndrome
Tourette syndrome is characterised by multiple motor tics, such as shoulder shrugging or blinking, alongside at least one vocal tic, such as throat clearing every day or intermittently over a year beginning before age 18 years old which fits perfectly with this patient’s long-standing history starting from childhood into adulthood now impacting daily functioning significantly

Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
While attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) can be associated with Tourette syndrome, it primarily involves symptoms of difficulty sustaining attention on tasks or play activities, hyperactivity, and impulsivity rather than the motor and vocal tics described in this patient.

Huntington’s disease
Huntington's disease usually presents later in life with a combination of motor dysfunction (chorea), cognitive decline, and psychiatric issues like depression or irritability. The onset typically occurs between 30 to 50 years old which does not align with this patient's history starting from childhood.

Obsessive-compulsive disorder
Although obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) can co-occur with Tourette syndrome, it predominantly involves intrusive thoughts (obsessions) and repetitive behaviours aimed at reducing anxiety (compulsions). The description of involuntary movements such as repetitive blinking and shoulder shrugging is more characteristic of tics seen in Tourette syndrome rather than compulsions seen in OCD.

Schizophrenia
Schizophrenia commonly includes symptoms like hallucinations, delusions, and disorganised speech or behaviour but does not typically present with motor or vocal tics as described here. Onset generally occurs in late adolescence to early adulthood but would include psychotic features which are not mentioned by this patient. Tourette SyndromeA 41-year-old man, a successful graphic designer, has begun to have trouble finding names for people and objects. He has continued to design brochures and logos for small businesses but has had trouble filling out paper orders, making frequent spelling mistakes. Surprisingly, he was caught stealing an item from a client's store. Soon afterward he began to comb the beach, spending many hours looking for seashells. While at home he began to play solitaire compulsively for six hours per day. He developed a new interest in squash, and his game steadily improved. He stopped working as a graphic designer but obtained a courier job and learned and remembered a complex route for delivering packages. There was no family history of dementia.

stem: A 30-year-old man presents complaining about becoming blind. He has no other past medical history other than episodes of breathlessness when he was a teenager. He has recently been made redundant from his job and it appears that he is also in the midst of a custody dispute for his children. Medical and neurological examinations are normal. He has no obvious evidence of mental illness. His pupils react normally to light and accommodation. What psychiatric diagnosis is most likely in view of his current symptoms?
explanation:
Conversion disorder
This mental disorder has no known physiological causes, although the symptoms resemble neurological disorder. The symptoms include blindness, deafness, loss of feeling and loss of muscle power. Possible psychological explanations for presentation with conversion disorder include conflicting views, avoiding unpleasant activities and seeking sympathy and support. The symptoms are real organic illnesses and appear not to be a temporary state of illness. In many cases, the symptoms may reappear even after proper medical intervention if the environmental factors causing the illness are not eliminated. Behavioural therapy is recommended in most cases.

Somatisation disorder
Somatisation disorder is incorrect. Somatisation disorder presents with multiple physical illnesses affecting different body systems, spanning a period of 2 years or more. No physical cause for the illnesses is discovered.

Hypochondriacal disorder
Hypochondriacal disorder is incorrect. Hypochondriasis is a persistent belief in an underlying physical illness despite multiple episodes of reassurance from medical services.

Depersonalisation
Depersonalisation is incorrect. Depersonalisation is characterised by detachment from reality or from oneself in response to an episode of psychological stress.

Delusion
Delusion is incorrect. A delusion is a belief which is held without basis in fact. It occurs against the background of psychotic depression, bipolar disorder, or schizophrenia. Conversion Disorder You are referred a 48-year-old man who has been arrested by the police on suspicion of committing a number of aggravated robberies in the past few weeks. He is acting rather strangely, staring intently at you when you interview him, and the police feel he may be psychotic. You suspect he has Ganser syndrome.

stem: An 89-year-old woman presents with disorientation and restlessness. She lives independently and is usually mentally alert, but has been increasingly unwell for the past week; apparently she saw her GP for a medication change a short time before. She has long-standing hypertension, atrial fibrillation, osteoarthritis and a hiatus hernia. Physical examination and blood tests are unremarkable; urine examination is also normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Polypharmacy
This lady has delirium and multiple medications are one of the most common causes in the elderly. Patients with early cognitive impairment are particularly vulnerable to the effects of polypharmacy.

Accidental poisoning
Accidental poisoning is incorrect. Given her usual normal cognition, physical examination and blood tests.

Alcohol withdrawal
Alcohol withdrawal is incorrect. There is no history of alcohol use and this lady has a normal physical examination with none of the symptoms of alcohol withdrawal described (eg tremor, nausea, irritability, tachycardia, etc).

Alzheimer’s disease
Alzheimer’s disease is incorrect. 1 week is too short a history for Alzheimer’s disease.

Chest infection
Chest infection is incorrect. Given the normal physical examination and blood tests. DeliriumAn elderly man complains of increasing sadness and an inability to find pleasure in anything. He has recently been forced to retire from his job and has several chronic medical problems.

stem: A 54-year-old man presents to the surgical on call service with acute pancreatitis for the third time over the past 18 months. You are asked to review him some 3 days after his admission with respect to long term drug therapy for possible cirrhosis. Which of the following features in his history would most strongly suggest a diagnosis of alcohol dependence syndrome?
options: Continued drinking despite persistent abdominal pain
Denying recent alcohol use despite evidence to the contrary
Two previous convictions for driving while intoxicated
explanation:
Continued drinking despite persistent abdominal pain
In this case the patient has had 3 significant episodes of pancreatitis, and persistent drinking despite clear evidence of harmful effects would indicate alcohol dependence syndrome.

Denying recent alcohol use despite evidence to the contrary
Denying recent alcohol use despite evidence to the contrary is incorrect. This is a common feature of patients who present with alcohol related problems and may just be linked to embarrassment about their situation.

Multiple old rib fractures
Multiple old rib fractures is incorrect. Although multiple old rib fractures are linked to binge drinking and may indicate alcohol related osteoporosis or osteomalacia, they may not necessarily be linked to alcohol dependence.

Pathological jealousy
Pathological jealousy is incorrect. Pathological jealousy would be considered a personality trait / disorder, rather than being linked to alcohol dependence.

Two previous convictions for driving while intoxicated.

stem: A 75-year-old woman presents to her GP due to a 6-month history of cognitive decline. On examination the GP notices she has a resting tremor and shuffling gait. What is the the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Lewy body dementia (LBD)
This patient has clinical signs of Parkinson’s. Lewy body dementia (LBD) is diagnosed when a patient develops symptoms of dementia either before or at the same time as Parkinsonian symptoms. Other characteristic features of LBD include fluctuations in cognition and alertness, visual hallucinations, hypersensitivity to neuroleptic medication and repeated falls.

Alzheimer’s disease
Alzheimer’s disease is incorrect. Alzheimer’s disease would not give you Parkinsonian symptoms.

Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease
Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease is incorrect. Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (CJD) is a rapidly progressing physical and cognitive decline. Early in the disease it can present with non-specific symptoms, including anxiety, personality change, depression and forgetfulness. As the disease progresses, patients develop dementia, ataxia, and myoclonus. Patients can go from normality to death within months and you would not expect Parkinsonian symptoms.

Frontotemporal dementia
Frontotemporal dementia is incorrect. Frontotemporal dementia would not give you Parkinsonian symptoms. Typical features include prominent changes in personality and social behaviour, apathy and compulsive behaviours; Parkinsonism can occur, but in advanced stages of the disease.

Huntington’s disease
Huntington’s disease is incorrect. Huntington’s disease is an autosomal dominant condition that initially presents with chorea, personality changes and neuropsychiatric symptoms, followed later by dementia; it does not feature Parkinsonian symptoms.

stem: You review a 78-year-old woman who is deeply withdrawn owing to severe depression. You are considering electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). Which of the following factors absolutely precludes the use of ECT?
explanation:
Raised intracranial pressure
Raised intracranial pressure is the only absolute contraindication to electroconvulsive therapy (ECT).

An indwelling cardiac pacemaker
An indwelling cardiac pacemaker is incorrect. Although experience of ECT in patients with cardiac pacemakers is limited, evidence suggests as long as pacemaker function is adequately assessed before the event, it is considered appropriate with respect to benefit risk.

Patient’s age >60 years
Patient’s age>60 years is incorrect. The greatest need and potential impact of ECT is often seen in the elderly population.

Pregnancy
Pregnancy is incorrect. In severe depression during pregnancy, especially in cases of psychosis, agitation or severe psychomotor retardation, ECT can be the safest and quickest treatment option.

Hypochondriasis in younger age groups
Hypochondriasis in younger age groups is incorrect. Hypochondriasis is considered a relative contraindication because of unfavourable outcomes in younger patients, but failure to respond to tricyclic antidepressants or other antidepressive drug combinations may lead to ECT.

stem: A 19-year-old lady is being investigated for excessive daytime sleepiness, including on one occasion falling asleep at the wheel. As part of her investigations she has a multiple sleep latency test (MSLT), which includes electroencephalography (EEG) monitoring. What feature is characteristically seen on EEG in narcolepsy?
options: Late onset of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep
Rapid onset of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep
explanation:
Rapid onset of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep
The MSLT involves a patient being placed in a sleep-inducing environment and instructed to try and sleep. Monitoring includes EEG, electrooculography (EOG) and electrocardiography (ECG). On average, normal subjects fall asleep in 10–15 minutes, whereas people with narcolepsy fall asleep in less than 8 minutes. The naps of patients with narcolepsy often include REM sleep, and the presence of two or more naps containing REM sleep is virtually diagnostic of narcolepsy.

Late onset of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep
Late onset of rapid eye movement (REM) sleep is incorrect. Patients with narcolepsy display early-onset REM sleep.

Prolonged stage 1 sleep
Prolonged stage 1 sleep is incorrect. There are five stages of sleep: 1 (light sleep); 2, 3 and 4 (deepest sleep); and REM stage. In normal people during sleep, they progress cyclically from 1 through to REM at an average of 90–110-minute cycles. The earlier sleep cycles have relatively short REM sleep and long periods of deep sleep, but later in the night REM periods lengthen and deep sleep time decreases. In narcolepsy it is the REM stage that is early and prolonged, meaning less deep sleep.

Prolonged stage 2 sleep
Prolonged stage 2 sleep is incorrect. There are five stages of sleep: 1 (light sleep); 2, 3 and 4 (deepest sleep); and REM stage. In normal people during sleep, they progress cyclically from 1 through to REM at an average of 90–110-minute cycles. The earlier sleep cycles have relatively short REM sleep and long periods of deep sleep, but later in the night REM periods lengthen and deep sleep time decreases. In narcolepsy it is the REM stage that is early and prolonged, meaning less deep sleep.

Prolonged stage 3 sleep
Prolonged stage 3 sleep is incorrect. There are five stages of sleep: 1 (light sleep); 2, 3 and 4 (deepest sleep); and REM stage. In normal people during sleep, they progress cyclically from 1 through to REM at an average of 90–110-minute cycles. The earlier sleep cycles have relatively short REM sleep and long periods of deep sleep, but later in the night REM periods lengthen and deep sleep time decreases. In narcolepsy it is the REM stage that is early and prolonged, meaning less deep sleep.

stem: A 58-year-old publican attends the clinic with confusion; short term memory loss and ophthalmoplegia. You suspect he has thiamine deficiency resulting in Wenicke-Korsakoff syndrome. Which one of the following pathological changes is a characteristic feature of the Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome?
options: Neuronal loss in the mammillary bodies
explanation:
Neuronal loss in the mammillary bodies
The hallmark pathological feature of Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome is neuronal loss and gliosis in the mammillary bodies. These structures are vital for memory processing and are particularly vulnerable to thiamine deficiency, which impairs energy metabolism and neuronal survival. The lesions are symmetrical and also involve adjacent structures like the periaqueductal grey matter and thalamus. This neuronal damage leads to the characteristic confusion, memory impairment, and ophthalmoplegia seen in Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome, especially in individuals with chronic alcohol use.

Cerebellar atrophy
Cerebellar atrophy is commonly associated with chronic alcohol abuse rather than being a specific consequence of thiamine deficiency. Alcohol has a direct toxic effect on the Purkinje cells in the cerebellum, leading to ataxia and incoordination. While cerebellar changes may coexist with Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome, they are not a defining feature of the condition. Furthermore, cerebellar atrophy develops over a longer period, whereas Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome can occur acutely with thiamine deficiency.

Dilatation of the IIIrd ventricle
