Dilatation of the third ventricle is typically associated with increased intracranial pressure or obstructive hydrocephalus rather than nutritional deficiencies. While chronic alcohol use may cause brain atrophy and ventricular enlargement, this is unrelated to the specific pathology of thiamine deficiency. The lesions of Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome are concentrated in the mammillary bodies, periaqueductal grey matter, and thalamus, not in structures leading to ventricular dilation. This option confuses a generalised effect of alcohol abuse with the specific findings of thiamine deficiency.

Demyelination in the pons medulla
Demyelination in the pons and medulla is a characteristic feature of central pontine myelinolysis (CPM), not Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome. CPM is caused by rapid correction of hyponatraemia, leading to osmotic injury to myelin sheaths. In contrast, Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome involves metabolic and neuronal damage due to thiamine deficiency. While both conditions can occur in individuals with chronic alcohol use, the pathological mechanisms and affected regions are distinct.

Microvascular lesions in the cortex
Microvascular lesions in the cortex are associated with conditions like diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and cerebral amyloid angiopathy rather than thiamine deficiency. These lesions result from chronic damage to the small cerebral vessels, leading to cognitive decline or vascular dementia. Wernicke–Korsakoff syndrome primarily involves neuronal damage in subcortical structures such as the mammillary bodies and periventricular regions. Thus, cortical microvascular lesions are not characteristic of this syndrome and indicate a different pathological process.

stem: A 28-year-old woman who has recently given birth to a healthy child presents with symptoms of emotional lability. Which of the following would make you most suspicious that she has a postnatal depressive disorder?
options: Onset of symptoms at four days post-delivery
A low score on the Edinburgh Post-Natal Depression Scale
explanation:
Presence of guilty thoughts
The presence of guilty thoughts is a marker of more serious depression. Other factors that help to discriminate a post-partum depression include: irritability and inability to sleep (especially when the baby is asleep) thoughts of worthlessness and inability to cope not enjoying the baby suicidal ideation

Onset of symptoms at four days post-delivery
Onset of symptoms at four days post-delivery is incorrect. Onset of symptoms at four days post-delivery is more suggestive of post-partum blues, which typically occurs between the 3rd and 6th day after delivery. Typical symptoms of post-partum blues include crying, fatigue, sensitivity to criticism, anxiety, irritability, helplessness and labile mood. Reassurance and explanation are usually all that is needed. Depressive illnesses usually begin after the first two weeks from delivery.

A low score on the Edinburgh Post-Natal Depression Scale
A low score on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale is incorrect. A high score on the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale would be suggestive of postnatal depression.

Anxiety about the baby
Anxiety about the baby is incorrect. Anxiety about the baby is very common and very normal in new mothers. It is also common in post-partum blues, which is a mild, transient disturbance in mood typically occurring in the first week after delivery. It is estimated 50–60% of women experience what is also known as ‘baby blues’. 637

Irregular sleep pattern
Irregular sleep pattern is incorrect. Inability to sleep is a common occurrence after the birth of a baby, given a baby’s irregular feeding and sleeping times. It does also occur in post-partum depression.

stem: A 17-year-old man is brought to the Emergency Department by the police. He has been arrested for assault and claims that he ‘was told to do it’. Which of the following clinical features in the psychiatric history is most strongly associated with schizophrenia?
explanation:
Lack of insight
Ninety-seven per cent of patients with schizophrenia are not aware that they are unwell at presentation. Lack of insight is extremely common.

Restlessness
Restlessness is incorrect. While insomnia and restlessness may be seen in the highly aroused patient with acute schizophrenia, they are also associated with affective disorders and may be side effects of antipsychotic treatment.

Withdrawal from social contacts
Withdrawal from social contacts is incorrect. While negative symptoms such as lack of interaction may be seen in schizophrenia, this is not as commonly associated with the condition as lack of insight.

Insomnia
Insomnia is incorrect. While insomnia and restlessness may be seen in the highly aroused patient with acute schizophrenia, they are also associated with affective disorders and may be side effects of antipsychotic treatment. Schizophrenia You see a woman who tells you she has felt empty and low in mood for a long time. She tells you that she has no friends, prefers to stay at home but hates being alone, uses cannabis, has a history of alcohol use and history of self-harm with threatening suicide. On examination of her Emergency Department records it transpires she has self-harmed on around six occasions over the past year. She denies early morning wakening or lack of appetite.

Panic attacks during social interaction
Panic attacks during social interaction is incorrect. They may show signs of autonomic arousal with associated anxiety, but panic attacks are rare and are not situation specific, being more likely to occur in relation to abnormal thoughts or experiences.

stem: A 45-year-old woman attends her GP surgery complaining of poor sleep. On closer questioning she says she avoids leaving the house because she is scared of people looking at her, and 2 weeks ago at a restaurant she had an episode of tachycardia and breathlessness with intense fear. What is the likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Social phobia
Patients with social phobia have a particular anxiety about public places or situations as they feel they are being scrutinised, ridiculed or humiliated by other people (eg eating in front of others at a restaurant). They may experience episodes of intense fear, anxiety or panic attacks and avoid these situations.

Agoraphobia
Agoraphobia is incorrect. Agoraphobia tends be fear of being in a situation where a person cannot freely escape or where help may not be available if something goes wrong. It does not necessarily have to be with regards to enclosed spaces (eg being in a lift or train), it can also be a fear of open spaces.

Depression
Depression is incorrect. Although poor sleep can be one of the symptoms of depression, this patient does not display any of the other characteristic symptoms of depression such as: low mood, tearfulness, loss of interest in activities, thoughts of worthlessness, guilt or suicidal ideations. Her predominant symptom is a fear of people looking at her. The classical sleep disturbance in depression is early morning waking.

Generalised anxiety disorder
Generalised anxiety disorder is incorrect. A central feature of generalised anxiety disorder is excessive worry or anxiety about a wide range of issues and situations, along with other physical symptoms such as restlessness, difficulty concentrating, irritability or sleep disturbance. This lady’s symptoms are more in keeping with a specific phobia rather than anxiety about multiple things. Phobic Disorders A 39-year-old man with a 10-year history of alcoholism presents to his General Practitioner after successfully completing an inpatient drug rehabilitation programme. He is seeking advice on how to maintain his sobriety.

Panic disorder
Panic disorder is incorrect. Panic disorder is diagnosed when a person has regular panic attacks without an obvious precipitant. If a person’s panic attacks are consistently associated with a specific trigger, (eg a fear of being scrutinised in public places), then a diagnosis of panic disorder is excluded and this would be better classified as a type of phobia.

stem: A 75-year-old lady admitted with confusion and urinary tract infection is commenced on appropriate antibiotics. You are called to see her during the night because of severe agitation. She is trying to get out of bed and is at significant risk of falling. You review her notes and find she has a history of Parkinson’s disease and hypertension. Her BP is 122/82, with pulse 88 and regular. Her temperature is 38.8°C. She refuses further examination. What treatment would you prescribe?
explanation:
Lorazepam
In the context of Parkinson’s, haloperidol is not advised but lorazepam is endorsed by NICE guidelines as an alternative. It should be used at the lowest dose possible, with a dose of 0.5 mg the suggested starting level.

Temazepam
Temazepam is incorrect. This is a long-acting benzodiazepine not recommended in this situation, because its effects may persist long after sepsis-related delirium has begun to resolve.

Haloperidol
Haloperidol is incorrect. Given the history of Parkinson’s disease, neuroleptics are best avoided because of their potential negative impact on movement.

Trazodone
Trazodone is incorrect. Trazodone is a tricyclic antidepressant used over the longer term as a treatment for depression, not for delirium.

Tramadol
Tramadol is incorrect. This an opiate-based analgesic that does not have a role in the treatment of delirium and may indeed worsen confusion. DeliriumA 23-year-old female nurse is caught stealing diuretics from the ward. On further questioning she has concerns about her weight and is scared of being fat. She feels she is always thinking about eating and often eats large amounts of food, and then makes herself sick and uses diuretics from the ward to try and lose weight. On examination she has a BMI of 23 and you noticed thickened skin on her knuckles.

stem: A 45-year-old man attends for cognitive behavioural therapy for his depression. The therapist notices after a few sessions that he is becoming annoyed about some of the situations the patient is describing, as it reminds him of situations he has experienced in the past. What is the term that best describes the therapist’s own feelings, emotions and attitudes to his patient?
explanation:
Countertransference
Transference, countertransference, resistance, transitional object and acting out are all terms used in psychotherapy. Countertransference describes the therapist’s own feelings, emotions and attitudes towards their patient. The therapist needs to be aware of these feelings and to screen out those that are stemming only from him/her and to take note of those generated by contact with the patient. The latter can be due to an interesting aspect of the patient.

Transference
Transference is incorrect. This is an unconscious process in which the patient transfers to the therapist feelings and emotions that were experienced in another part of the patient’s life, e.g. in relation to his/her parents.

Resistance
Resistance is incorrect. This relates to the words and actions of a patient that act to obstruct them from gaining access to their unconscious - for example, refusing to talk about a certain problem.

Transitional object
Transitional object is incorrect. This is something selected by an infant for self-soothing, e.g. a blanket or toy; its role is to help with the separation-individuation process. Depression A 33-year-old primiparous woman is 2 days post-partum, having delivered a normal baby boy. She has become increasingly anxious and has told the midwife she thinks the baby is ‘a changeling’. Careful evaluation fails to identify other bizarre beliefs, and she is continuing to care for the baby. Which one of the features below is most likely to reassure you that the patient is not psychotic?

Acting out
Acting out is incorrect. This is the expression of unconscious emotional conflicts directly into actions without the patient being consciously aware of their meaning, e.g. a young child throwing a temper tantrum when they do not yet have the ability to express their emotions.

stem: When seen in the Outpatient Clinic a 35-year-old woman tells you she is currently taking St John’s wort, which she buys from her local health food shop. For which condition is this remedy taken?
explanation:
Depression
St John’s wort, also known as Hypericum perforatum, is a popular herbal remedy for treating mild depression. Its mechanism of action is thought to be via the up-regulation of serotonin and dopamine. It is worth noting that St John’s wort also up-regulates cytochrome P450 CYP3A4 and therefore has a number of important interactions with other medications, e.g. antibiotics, anticoagulants, anti-epileptics and statins. Antidepressants should not be used with St John’s wort owing to the potential for interaction. In addition, when a patient stops taking St John’s wort, concentrations of interacting drugs may increase, causing toxicity. A meta-analysis in 2015 concluded that hypericum extracts were superior to placebo and there was no statistically significant difference in superiority compared with the other antidepressant drug classes included in the analysis (tricyclics (TCAs), selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs), serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) and serotonin antagonist and reuptake inhibitors (SARIs). However, due to the limitations in current evidence surrounding St John’s wort, recommendations in clinical practice are difficult.

Osteoarthritis
Osteoarthritis is incorrect. One commonly used alternative therapy or supplement used by patients with osteoarthritis is glucosamine. Animal studies have found that glucosamine can delay the breakdown of cartilage and aid the repair of damaged cartilage, However, there is little evidence to support its use in humans.

Back pain
Back pain is incorrect. A commonly used alternative therapy for back pain is acupuncture. NICE guidelines currently recommend acupuncture for persistent lower back pain.

Bruising
Bruising is incorrect. One alternative therapy used for bruising is arnica; however, this has not been demonstrated to be any more effective than placebo. Depression A 34-year-old man seeks treatment for depression. He has recently lost his job and is awaiting a divorce hearing. There is no past medical history of note, he drinks three bottles of wine per week. He feels hopelessness and despair with lethargy. He denies suicide plans, stating there is no point in suicide. At which time is the patient most likely to commit suicide?

Migraines
Migraines is incorrect. Acupuncture is also recommended by NICE guidelines in the treatment of migraines.

stem: A 30-year-old man with schizophrenia has been walking around wearing a metal helmet and has covered all his windows with tin foil. He reports this is to stop his thoughts leaking out of his head and being read by others around him. What is this symptom called?
explanation:
Thought broadcast
Thought broadcast is the belief that others can read or hear the individuals’ thoughts as they are ‘broadcast’ from them by external forces.

Auditory hallucination
Auditory hallucination is incorrect. An auditory hallucination is the false perception of hearing a sound or voice in the absence of a stimulus.

Thought blocking
Thought blocking is incorrect. In thought blocking, patients may complain that their minds have ‘gone blank’ and will lead to a sudden cessation of speech mid-sentence.

Thought echo
Thought echo is incorrect. Thought echo is a form of auditory hallucination in which a person can hear their own thoughts being spoken aloud. Schizophrenia A 23-year-old lady on antipsychotic medication for schizophrenia is referred to the Endocrine Clinic by her GP. She complains of significant galactorrhoea, particularly when her breasts are stimulated during sexual intercourse with her boyfriend. Since starting medication she has been able to hold down a job and form a stable relationship, and she is reluctant to discontinue it. On examination her BP is 125/80 mmHg, physical examination including visual field testing is unremarkable, but in the presence of a chaperone she demonstrates that her breasts express milk. Investigations:

Thought withdrawal
Thought withdrawal is incorrect. Thought withdrawal or insertion is the belief that thoughts are being removed or put into one’s mind by some external agency or force.

stem: What treatment should be administered?
explanation:
Dantrolene
The most likely diagnosis is neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS). It is a known complication of neuroleptic treatment. It presents with an altered mental state, pyrexial, rigidity and autonomic dysfunction. Leukocytosis, elevated CK and hypocalcaemia are common features. Management consists of muscle relaxants, such as dantrolene, dopamine agonists such as bromocriptine, and intravenous fluids.

Aciclovir
Aciclovir is incorrect. Although this patient is pyrexial, the recent prescription of haloperidol, rigidity and marked hypertension, fit better with NMS.

Cefuroxime
Cefuroxime is incorrect. The muscle rigidity and elevated CK is more consistent with NMS than with other causes of decreased consciousness such as meningitis.

Nifedipine
Nifedipine is incorrect. Although there is marked hypertension, calcium channel antagonists are unlikely to significantly impact on the underlying pathophysiology versus other options such as dantrolene.

Propranolol
Propranolol is incorrect. Similar to nifedipine, although propranolol may reduce blood pressure and tachycardia, it won’t significantly reduce underlying muscle rigidity and necrosis.

stem: A 56-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner with low mood, decreased concentration, reduced libido and a lack of interest in his usual hobbies for the past six weeks. The only significant life event of note is that he has recently been started on atenolol for hypertension two months ago. He has no other physical or psychiatric history. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Drug-induced mood disorder
This man has a very short history of depressive symptoms and has recently begun taking a beta blocker, which is known to cause a number of side-effects, including: depression, erectile dysfunction, fatigue, headache and nightmares. Given the associated symptoms and initiation of medication, without any other significant life changes or stressors, the patient should be switched to an alternative antihypertensive.

Bipolar disorder
Bipolar disorder is incorrect. The typical features of bipolar disorder are not described here, with episodes of mania, mixed mania, or hypomania, as well as episodes of depression. The patient has a short Chathistory with AI of Tutor depressive symptoms, without evidence or history of periods of elated mood. However, a patient may develop symptoms of mania in the future, which would require a revision of the initial diagnosis.

Dysthymia
Dysthymia is incorrect. This patient’s symptoms only started six weeks ago. Dysthymia is a diagnosis when an individual experiences persistent (over more than two years) depressive mood, lasting most of the day and occurring on most days. Treatment is the same as that for endogenous depression. During the first two years of dysthymic disorder, the patient never reaches the criteria to be diagnosed with depression, nor any previous history of mania, mixed mania or hypomanic symptoms.

Endogenous depression
Endogenous depression is incorrect. As per the International Classification of Diseases, 11th revision (ICD-11 ) a single depressive episode lasts at least two weeks with depressed mood and loss of interest in normal activities that lasts most of the day. It can be accompanied by loss of concentration, hopelessness, loss of appetite and thoughts of death and suicide. However, the recent initiation of a known pharmacological trigger needs to be investigated, before a diagnosis of endogenous depression is made.

Personality disorder
Personality disorder is incorrect. This patient has a single episode of low mood, with no features of a personality disorder. There are several subtypes of personality disorder. Their overarching features include maladaptive behaviours, which typically are developed early in life. Therefore, symptoms of a personality disorder usually manifest in late adolescence or early adulthood, rather than in this age group.

stem: A 24-year-old man who recently started on haloperidol is transferred from the local psychiatric unit with pyrexia, fluctuating consciousness, muscular rigidity and autonomic instability. What is your working diagnosis?
explanation:
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is a serious, rare idiosyncratic reaction occurring in response to neuroleptic therapy. It is characterised by fever, fluctuating conscious level, muscular rigidity, autonomic dysfunction, tachycardia, labile blood pressure and urinary incontinence. Blood tests can show elevated creatinine kinase, raised white cell count and deranged liver function tests. It is thought to be caused by sympathetic overactivity occurring as a result of dopaminergic antagonism. It can be potentially fatal. Treatment includes stopping the causative drug, dantrolene and supportive care, usually in an intensive therapy unit setting, with rehydration therapy and blood pressure management.

Acute dystonia
Acute dystonia is incorrect. Dystonias are the sustained involuntary contractions of major muscle groups (eg eye muscles, leading to oculogyric crisis; neck muscles, leading to torticollis; etc).

Cerebral event
Cerebral event is incorrect. A cerebral event or stroke is very unlikely to give this combination of symptoms, in particular pyrexia, muscular rigidity and autonomic instability. It is also rare in this age group.

Meningitis
Meningitis is incorrect. Although both meningitis and encephalitis would be a differential given his pyrexia and fluctuating consciousness, when combined with the other symptoms and history of recently starting haloperidol, NMS is a much more likely diagnosis.

Serotonin syndrome.

stem: A 28-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner feeling extremely angry with his co-workers. He believes they laugh at his lack of skill and experience and admits to fantasising about taking a gun to work and shooting everyone in the office. During the consultation, he shows no anxiety or remorse when discussing his violent thoughts. Which of the following factors would be the most appropriate indicator of his risk of acting on these fantasies?
options: A history of violence towards others
A lack of anxiety associated with his statements
The presence of temporal lobe epilepsy
explanation:
A history of violence towards others
This is the strongest predictor of future violent behaviour, as past actions are a significant indicator of future risk. Individuals who have previously exhibited violent behaviour are more likely to repeat these actions, particularly if they struggle with anger management and interpersonal conflicts. In this patient, his lack of anxiety or remorse, coupled with violent fantasies, raises concern. A history of violence would significantly heighten the risk of him acting on his thoughts.

The presence of persecutory delusions
Persecutory delusions are typically linked to psychiatric conditions such as psychotic disorders or severe depression. These conditions can contribute to aggression, but appropriate treatment of the underlying mental health issue often reduces the risk of violence. In contrast, this patient's anger and violent fantasies are more consistent with personality issues rather than a primary psychotic disorder.

A history of alcohol abuse
Although alcohol abuse is a known risk factor for violence due to impaired judgement and reduced inhibition, it is not the strongest predictor of future violence. Alcohol use may exacerbate aggressive tendencies but does not independently predict violent behaviour as reliably as a history of violence. Additionally, there is no indication that this patient is currently under the influence of alcohol or has an active substance use disorder.

A lack of anxiety associated with his statements
While this may suggest impaired empathy or increased impulsivity, it is not the most reliable predictor of violent behaviour. The absence of anxiety can be seen in personality disorders such as antisocial personality disorder but does not necessarily indicate an intention to act on violent fantasies. In this case, it suggests emotional detachment but lacks the predictive power of a history of violence.

The presence of temporal lobe epilepsy
Temporal lobe epilepsy is associated with neurological symptoms such as automatisms, déjà vu, and altered consciousness but is not linked to premeditated violence. Individuals with temporal lobe epilepsy may experience emotional disturbances, but these are usually transient and unrelated to antisocial behaviour. There is no evidence in this case to suggest neurological impairment or seizure activity.

stem: A 23-year-old woman who presented with an acute psychotic episode has been started on Risperidone. She has a significant improvement in her mental state, but asks on discharge about long term physiological effects of her treatment. She has no significant past medical history and takes only the oral contraceptive pill. Her BP is 115/72 mmHg, BMI is 23 and there are no abnormal findings on physical examination. Which of the following is most frequently seen with Risperidone therapy?
explanation:
Hyperprolactinaemia
Hyperprolactinaemia is a common occurence in patients prescribed Risperidone therapy, and can in in some cases lead to gynaecomastia in men, menstrual disturbances or amenorrhoea in women, and galactorrhea in both women and men.

Diabetes mellitus
Diabetes mellitus is incorrect. Diabetes mellitus is another concern with respect to atypical antipsychotic therapy. In the Risperidone program however, the risk of diabetes was not increased vs placebo, (diabetes mellitus was reported in 0.18% in Risperidone-treated subjects compared to a rate of 0.11% in placebo group. Overall incidence from all clinical trials was 0.43% in all Risperidone-treated subjects).

Jaundice
Jaundice is incorrect. Elevations in transaminases are relatively common, although jaundice is only rarely associated with Risperidone treatment.

Orthostatic hypotension
Orthostatic hypotension is incorrect. This is uncommonly seen in risperidone treatment.

Vertigo
Vertigo is incorrect. Like orthostatic hypotension, vertigo is uncommonly seen.

stem: A 35-year-old man is referred to the Gastroenterology Clinic with a 12-month history of intermittent abdominal pain, flatulence and alternating diarrhoea and constipation. He has also complained of fatigue, restlessness, intermittent headaches and general muscle weakness since his father passed away 15 months ago from colorectal cancer aged 59. Abdominal examination is unremarkable. A colonoscopy nine months ago was normal and recent full blood count and renal and liver profiles are all normal. Which one of the following options is the most appropriate next step?
options: Enquire regarding concurrent anxiety or low mood
Small bowel biopsy with periodic acid–Schiff staining
explanation:
Enquire regarding concurrent anxiety or low mood
The lack of significant findings on clinical examination and presenting for a second opinion, along with normal blood tests and colonoscopy, count against an organic disorder. Irritable bowel syndrome seems unlikely, given the proximity to the death of the patient’s father and the additional headache, fatigue and muscle weakness. Somatoform disorders are commonly seen in conjunction with anxiety and depression, but this is not a strict rule. Patients should be reassured that sinister medical diseases have been ruled out, and an explanation that the body/mind can generate symptoms in the absence of disease provided. The recent death of his father is likely to be a trigger/stress for the symptoms experienced. Ideally, care should be led by one clinician, with the aim of limiting further unnecessary investigations, referrals and additional treatments. Co-morbid psychiatric disorders, like anxiety and depression, should be treated to the chance of recovery.

CT scan of the abdomen
There is unlikely to be any benefit to the patient from a CT scan of the abdomen. Given the constellation of symptoms, lower gastrointestinal diseases seem most likely and they have been ruled out by direct visualisation. Further investigations at this stage would only prompt further anxiety.

Faecal occult stool testing
Faecal occult stool testing is a screening test used in patients over 50 years old to investigate for potential colorectal cancer. It would be inappropriate to use it as a screening test in patients with a positive family history who are outside this age range, due to the risk of false results. If a genetic colorectal cancer syndrome was expected, a colonoscopy, as has already been performed, would be more appropriate.

Repeat colonoscopy
A repeat colonoscopy is unlikely to be of any benefit to the patient, even if performed ‘for reassurance sake’. In somatoform disorders, testing and referrals to specialists, where there is a low pretest probability of serious disease, are unlikely to resolve somatic symptoms and ease health anxiety.

Small bowel biopsy with periodic acid–Schiff staining.

stem: A 40-year-old man presents to his GP with a feeling of low mood and a lack of enjoyment in life for the past four months. He has no history of previous low mood. When asked about recent life events, he describes in great detail the failure of a project at work. Despite this setback, he has recently been promoted and had a successful annual appraisal. What form of psychological therapy may be beneficial for this patient?
explanation:
Cognitive-behavioral therapy
The vignette describes a form of >cognitive distortion called ‘selective attention’, which is common in depression. Patients attend to negative events much more than other positive or neutral events and, within the CBT model of depression, this contributes to low mood. CBT focuses on addressing cognitive distortions alongside behavioural therapy. There is a strong evidence base supporting CBT, it is recommended by NICE and access to CBT has been widened by the national IAPT service.

Interpersonal therapy
Interpersonal therapy is incorrect. This is also a time-limited focused treatment modality for depression that focuses on helping patients deal with difficulties in their interpersonal environment. These difficulties include complicated bereavements, difficulties defining roles in relationships or recent role transitions. In this scenario there is less evidence that this patient’s depression is the result of change in role as compared to cognitive factors.

Psychodynamic psychotherapy
Psychodynamic psychotherapy is incorrect. This is not indicated for depression as a first-line psychological treatment unless the patient expresses a strong preference. It is not as structured or time-limited as CBT, and in this scenario there is clear evidence of a cognitive distortion that may be treatable with a focused cognitive therapy. Psychodynamic therapy may be helpful in more complex cases where childhood relationships are felt to play an important role in the generation of depression, or when there is comorbid personality disorder.

Cognitive-analytical therapy
Cognitive-analytic therapy is incorrect. Compared to cognitive-behavioral therapy, this is not first-line psychological treatment for depression and the vignette does not highlight patterns of negative behaviour. Therapists and patients work towards understanding problems with detailed reformulations and by understanding patterns of negative behaviours described as snags, traps and dilemmas. These are then used to tailor the rest of the therapy to shifting away from behaviour believed to be contributing to low mood.

Dialectic-behavioural therapy
Dialectical-behavioural therapy is incorrect. This is an intensive form of psychotherapy used to manage patients with borderline personality disorder and chronic suicidal or self-harm behaviour, and is, therefore, not indicated in this case. Depression A 71-year-old woman on an orthopaedic ward has become unwell 72 hours after elective surgery. She is agitated, sleepless and exquisitely sensitive to noise. She has a history of anxiety and depression. Her temperature and vital signs are unremarkable, her CRP is 116 and on an arterial blood gas her PaO 2 is 12.0.

stem: Which one of the following is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
explanation:
Risperidone
Risperidone is associated with significant hyperprolactinaemia, and hence suppression of both folliclestimulating hormone and luteinising hormone. It is quite possible at a prolactin level of around 900 mU/l with risperidone, which results in galactorrhoea. Other atypical antipsychotics such as olanzapine, clozapine and quetiapine are not associated with significant increases in prolactin. If her psychiatric condition is stable then discussion could take place with her psychiatrist to broach the possibility of changing to one of these alternative medications.

Microprolactinoma
Microprolactinoma is incorrect. Microprolactinomas are associated with much greater elevation in prolactin to the 3000 or greater level.

Macroprolactinoma
Macroprolactinoma is incorrect. Macroprolactinomas are associated with elevation in prolactin to 5000 or greater, and visual field defects due to optic chiasm compression are a prominent feature.

Olanzapine
Olanzapine is incorrect. Olanzapine is considered a relative prolactin-sparing anti-psychotic, hence a much lower level than 900 would be expected here.

Clozapine
Clozapine is incorrect. Like olanzapine, there is not thought to be significant risk of hyperprolactinaemia in association with therapy.

stem: A 54-year-old woman presents with major depression, suffering a significant reduction in her appetite, activity and severe sleep disturbance. She has no past medical history of note and takes no regular medication, she has unfortunately been forced to quit her job as a legal researcher. Physical examination is unremarkable apart from a reduced BMI at 19. She has been tried on a course of citalopram with limited effect, and a decision is made to switch her to venlafaxine. Which of the following represents the mode of action of venlafaxine?
explanation:
SNRI
The main mode of action of venlafaxine is as a selective reuptake inhibitor of serotonin, noradrenaline, (and to a lesser extent dopamine), It may be of value in patients who don’t respond adequately to an SSRI.

Monoamine oxidase inhibitor
Monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) is incorrect. MAOIs used to be a mainstay of treatment for depression but are now used mostly for patients with resistant symptoms. Phenelzine is an example of a MAOI.

Partial serotonin receptor agonist
Partial serotonin receptor agonist is incorrect. Buspirone is an example of a partial serotonin receptor agonist, used in the treatment of depression and generalized anxiety disorder.

SSRI
SSRI is incorrect. Citalopram is an example of an SSRI, where only serotonin reuptake is inhibited significantly, rather than other neurotransmitters. Depression

Tricyclic anti-depressant
Tricyclic anti-depressant is incorrect. The exact mode of action of tricyclic anti-depressants is unclear, but it is thought they too have an SNRI like action.

stem: A 28-year-old male has attended for smoking cessation advice. He is keen to stop as soon as possible and decides, along with attending a smoking cessation group, that he would like to use bupropion (Zyban). What is the mechanism of action of bupropion?
explanation:
Noradrenaline-dopamine reuptake inhibitor
Bupropion (Zyban) is a noradrenaline-dopamine reuptake inhibitor used as a treatment adjunct, in combination with motivational support, for smoking cessation. NICE recommended that nicotine replacement therapy or bupropion should be prescribed only for a smoker who commits to a target stop date. The smoker should also be offered advice and encouragement to stop smoking. Therapy to aid smoking cessation is chosen according to the smoker’s likely compliance, availability of counselling and support, previous experience of smoking cessation aids, contraindications and the smoker’s preference. Bupropion is contraindicated in patients with a history of seizures, eating disorders, CNS tumour or those experiencing the acute symptoms of alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal.

Acetaldehyde dehydrogenase inhibitor
Acetaldehyde dehydrogenase inhibitor is incorrect. Disulfiram (Antabuse) is an example of a drug used in the treatment of alcohol, which acts by blocking the enzyme acetaldehyde dehydrogenase, which is involved in the normal metabolism of alcohol.

Monoamine oxidase inhibitor
Monoamine oxidase inhibitor is incorrect. Phenelzine is an example of a monoamine oxidase inhibitor that can be used as an antidepressant.

Dopamine agonist
Dopamine agonist is incorrect. Ropinirole is an example of a dopamine agonist that is used in the treatment of Parkinson’s disease. You are asked for advice in the management of an 84-year-old woman who is currently an inpatient on the oldage psychiatry ward. She was admitted a few days earlier following a period of low mood, self-neglect, poor sleep and poor appetite. She is started on treatment for depression with a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI). A few days later is it noted that she has become drowsy, confused and has had a seizure. None of these symptoms were present on her admission. On examination there is no evidence of infection, she does not appear dehydrated and has no focal neurological signs, but she does have a reduced GCS as she is responding to pain, is confused and disorientated and localising to painful stimuli. What would be the most important blood test to carry out to establish the most likely diagnosis?

Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor is incorrect. Citalopram, fluoxetine and sertraline are all examples of selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor-type antidepressants.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with depression is currently taking selegiline. Her psychiatrist has recommended that she starts paroxetine. What would be the most appropriate prescription?
options: Start paroxetine and slowly wean selegiline
Stop selegiline and start paroxetine straight away
Stop selegiline, wait 14 days, then start paroxetine
Stop selegiline, wait 6 weeks, then start paroxetine
explanation:
Stop selegiline, wait 14 days, then start paroxetine
Both selegiline (a monoamine oxidase inhibitor) and paroxetine (a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor) increase serotonin levels in the brain, and therefore increase the risk of serotonin syndrome. Monoamine oxidase inhibitors cause irreversible inhibition of monoamine oxidase, and therefore even though the half-life of these drugs is 1.5-4 hours, a washout period of two weeks is necessary.

Continue selegiline and start paroxetine
Continue selegiline and start paroxetine is incorrect. Selegiline (a monoamine oxidase inhibitor) and paroxetine (a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor) should not be given together, as they both increase serotonin levels which can lead to serotonin syndrome. Selegiline should be stopped, and after a washout period of 14 days, paroxetine can be started.

Start paroxetine and slowly wean selegiline
Start paroxetine and slowly wean selegiline is incorrect. Both paroxetine (a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor) and selegiline (a monoamine oxidase inhibitor) increase serotonin levels. Taking both together increases the risk of serotonin syndrome. Instead selegiline should be stopped, and after a washout period of 14 days, paroxetine can be started.

Stop selegiline and start paroxetine straight away
Stop selegiline and start paroxetine straight away is incorrect. Selegine is a monoamine oxidase inhibitor, and paroxetine is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor. Both of these raise serotonin levels in the brain, and taking both together increases the risk of serotonin syndrome. After stopping selegiline, a washout period of 14 days is needed before paroxetine can be started, otherwise there is still a risk of serotonin syndrome.

Stop selegiline, wait 6 weeks, then start paroxetine.

stem: A 47-year-old female attends a substance misuse clinic for ongoing support following successfully completing a detoxification programme, and is noted to be prescribed naltrexone. Naltrexone can be used to help prevent relapse in the treatment of which drug dependency?
explanation:
Opioids
Naltrexone is a long-acting opioid antagonist. It can be used as an adjunct to psychosocial treatments to prevent relapse in detoxified patients who were formerly dependent on opioids. Naltrexone should only be initiated in specialist clinics. Patients should have remained opioid-free for at least 7–10 days before naltrexone is started. Naltrexone has also been shown to be useful for relapse prevention in those who misuse alcohol. Psychosocial treatments used in opioid dependence include: couple and family interventions motivational interviewing cognitive–behavioural therapy relapse prevention self-help groups psychotherapy.

Hallucinogens
Hallucinogens is incorrect. There is currently no prescribed medication recommended to prevent relapse in the treatment of dependency on hallucinogens.

Cocaine
Cocaine is incorrect. There is currently no prescribed medication recommended to prevent relapse in the treatment of cocaine dependence.

Cannabis
Cannabis is incorrect. There is currently no prescribed medication recommended to prevent relapse in the treatment of cannabis dependence.

Nicotine
Nicotine is incorrect. Nicotine replacement therapy and bupropion are used in the management of smoking cessation.

stem: A 25-year-old woman shows signs of extreme distress, sweating and palpitations as soon as she enters her former workplace. After consulting her past records, you find that she was seriously abused there. What would be the best description of a person’s reaction to a particular situation, in this case her former workplace?
explanation:
Conditioned response
This scenario is an example of a learned/conditioned response, whereby a neutral stimulus elicits a positive or negative emotional/physiological response, in the absence of the original stimulus, through the mechanism of pairing neutral and original stimuli. For example, in this case, the woman shows emotional distress (conditioned response) at the sight of the entrance to her previous workplace (neutral stimulus) without the presence of verbal or other abuse (original stimulus). This type of behaviour is conditioned to a stimulus and warrants no repetition or excessive practice of a certain behaviour (as in the case of obsessive–compulsive disorder). However, it requires medical attention because it can lead to other physiological and psychiatric symptoms. The usual treatment intervention involves behavioural counselling therapy.

Depression
Depression is incorrect. A diagnosis of depression should be considered if a patient has persistent low mood or loss of interest or pleasure in their normal activities, alongside other symptoms such as disturbed sleep, loss of appetite, agitation, poor concentration and ideas of self-harm or suicide.

Obsessive–compulsive disorder
Obsessive-compulsive disorder is incorrect. This describes a condition where a patient suffers from obsessions - recurrent, persistent and intrusive thoughts that occur against their will and, if resisted, result in the patient experiencing anxiety and compulsions – irresistible impulses to complete particular activities that are usually triggered by obsessions.

Hypertension
Hypertension is incorrect. Hypertension or high blood pressure is considered in the general population as a blood pressure >140/85 mmHg and is typically asymptomatic.

Ischaemia
Ischaemia is incorrect. Ischaemia is the inadequate supply of blood to organs or tissues in the body, resulting in a lack of oxygen and glucose. If the patient was complaining of severe central chest pain that was associated with sweating and palpitations, ischaemia as a result of a myocardial infarction would be considered.

stem: A 42-year-old woman tells you she has developed fears of getting lost in the crowd and has become very anxious about going to open public places. She also says that she had experienced panic attacks previously when she went to a crowded shopping mall and has suffered these attacks intermittently since she was a teenager. She is physically healthy and so far has no history of mental illness. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Agoraphobia
Agoraphobia is an irrational fear of open spaces, crowds and unfamiliar settings. It is the most serious and common (50–80%) of all phobias, occurs more often in women than men and has a peak incidence in the early twenties. The onset is sudden and usually accompanied by panic attacks. There are cases where patients hardly go outside for years and agoraphobia like this may be severely disabling.

Social phobia
Social phobia is incorrect. Social phobia is the fear of interacting with people rather than a fear of open spaces.

Acrophobia
Acrophobia is incorrect. Acrophobia is an extreme or irrational fear of heights.

Bathophobia
Bathophobia is incorrect. This is the fear of depths. Phobic DisordersAn 18 year old woman comes to the psychiatric clinic for review. She attends with her mother who informs you that she has had problems with multiple hand washing and obsessive compulsive disorder type behavior with respect to visiting public toilets for the last 6 years. Apparently she had a number of infections between 11 and 12 years of age, and her mother feels that one of these may have triggered her symptoms.

Dissociative disorder
Dissociative disorder is incorrect. Dissociative disorders occur when patients somehow feel detached from their body or from reality, they are considered a defence mechanism against a period of psychological stress.

stem: A 25-year-old woman presents with problems of excessive worry about almost everything in her life, including her future plans. She has severe difficulty in concentrating, feelings of depression and sleep disturbances. Her job performance is affected because of this worry and restlessness. She also has problems developing social relationships and refuses invitations to almost any social gathering for work or for pleasure. How would you best describe her condition?
explanation:
Generalised anxiety disorder
Generalised anxiety disorder (GAD) is characterised by a persistent worry about almost everything on most days for at least 6 months. Symptoms include restlessness, fatigue, lack of concentration, sweating, palpitations, muscle tension and sleep disturbance. Treatment involves cognitive behavioural therapy and use of an SSRI appropriate for targeting GAD.

Phobic anxiety disorder
Phobic anxiety disorder is incorrect. Phobic anxiety disorder involves fear of a specific situation.

Acute stress reaction
Acute stress reaction is incorrect. Anxiety can be seen in response to an acute stressor, but we aren’t aware of a particular incident triggering the events described here.

Social phobia
Social phobia is incorrect. Social phobia would account for the difficulties in social relationships described here, but not the other features such as worry about future plans and money.

Panic disorder
Panic disorder is incorrect. Panic disorder is associated with specific panic attacks, rather than the generalized all pervasive worry which is described here.

stem: A 24-year-old woman was referred to the outpatient clinic with a skin disorder. She gave a three month history of sores and blisters over the legs and bony prominences which did not heal, thinning hair, and a sore mouth. She had a history of anorexia nervosa. On examination her pulse rate was 68bpm, blood pressure 106/72mmHg. She was underweight with fine lanugo hair over her body. Multiple sores were noted over the legs and bony prominences, there was diffuse hair loss from the scalp, and examination of the mouth showed glossitis. Which nutrient deficiency is likely to have caused her symptoms?
explanation:
Zinc
Zinc deficiency is common in patients with anorexia nervosa, and causes poor wound healing, hair loss and glossitis. Zinc is largely contained in red meat and shellfish, but is also present in some cereals and pulses. It is important to replace zinc as deficiency impairs patients’ ability to gain weight.

Copper
Copper is incorrect. Copper deficiency causes anaemia, neutropenia, and neurological sequelae such as peripheral neuropathy. It does not cause hair loss, poor healing and glossitis as seen in this case. Zinc deficiency is more likely to cause this.

Folic acid
Folic acid is incorrect. Folate deficiency leads to a megaloblastic anaemia; it does not cause poor healing and hair loss. It does cause glossitis. Folate deficiency is not especially common in anorexia nervosa; zinc deficiency is much more common and would be a better explanation for this patient’s symptoms.

Vitamin A
Vitamin A is incorrect. Vitamin A deficiency would cause night blindness, which this patient does not complain of. It does not cause poor healing, glossitis and hair loss. Zinc deficiency does cause these symptoms and is a more likely explanation

Vitamin C
Vitamin C is incorrect. Although vitamin C deficiency (scurvy) would give all of these symptoms, it is in fact uncommon in anorexia nervosa as it is so abundant in fresh fruit and vegetables. Zinc deficiency also produces these symptoms and signs, and is much more common in anorexic patients. Anorexia Nervosa A middle-aged librarian seeks therapy as he is lonely and unhappy. He describes a solitary life cataloguing books all day and then remaining alone all night and on weekends. He declines invitations for dinners, as he feels anxious when other people are around.

stem: A 50-year-old man presents with irritability, depression, poor short-term memory, and panic attacks one month following the death of his wife. His daughter, who attends with him, states that he constantly goes through her mother’s things and pores over old photographs of her. Which of the following is the patient exhibiting?
options: Grief: phase of disorganisation and despair
Grief: phase of reorganisation and repair
explanation:
Grief: phase of pining
Grief describes the thoughts, feelings and behaviours that accompany bereavement. Grief can be normal, where the symptoms gradually lessen in intensity and are followed by acceptance and readjustment. A typical ‘grief reaction’ lasts up to 12 months. An abnormal grief reaction is one that is very intense, prolonged, delayed/absent or associated with non-characteristic symptoms, such as hallucinatory experiences. Parkes and Bowlby outlined a four-phase model that described grief as a process involving a succession of behavioural signs and symptoms. The phase of pining, which usually follows the first stage of numbness, is characterised by preoccupation with the deceased in order to counteract feelings of separation anxiety. Anger, irritability and depressive features are common. Anxiety may escalate to hyperventilation and panic attacks.

Grief: phase of disorganisation and despair
Grief: phase of disorganisation and despair is incorrect. Parkes and Bowlby’s phase of disorganisation and despair is typically the third stage in the grief process. In this phase, the bereaved comes to accept the permanent loss and experiences restlessness and aimlessness. Most try to avoid being reminded of the deceased.

Grief: phase of numbness
Grief: phase of numbness is incorrect. Parkes and Bowlby’s phase of numbness describes the initial reaction to bereavement. It is characterised by shock and disbelief. Although there may be features of depression, anger or irritability, there are no symptoms in the stem to suggest specifically that the patient is exhibiting denial. The key feature in the stem is preoccupation with deceased – a feature that would not be typical for this phase.

Grief: phase of reorganisation and repair
Grief: phase of reorganization and repair is incorrect. The final phase of grief in Parkes and Bowlby’s model is reorganisation and recovery. Here, the individual engages in activities directed towards the future. There is no evidence of this in the stem and to have arrived at this phase after only one month is very unlikely.

Major depressive disorder
Major depressive disorder is incorrect. The diagnosis of major depressive disorder in DSM-V can be made after the bereavement. However, a normal grief reaction may co-exist with a major depressive episode and would be suggested by: abnormal perceptions, marked functional impairment, prominent psychomotor retardation, morbid preoccupation with guilt or worthlessness.

stem: A 20-year-old man with learning disability is noted on examination to have short stature and is morbidly obese. Carers report that he eats excessively all the time. What syndrome is the most likely cause for this patient’s symptoms?
explanation:
Prader–Willi syndrome
Prader-Willi syndrome is a rare condition with an estimated prevalence of approximately 1.2–1.3 per 10,000. Cytogenetic tests can detect a deletion on chromosome 15 (q11–13) in approximately 50–70% of cases. This syndrome is characterised by neonatal hypotonia, intellectual disability, short stature, obesity and cryptorchidism. The majority of the affected children have a mild to moderate degree of intellectual disability. Usually, between the ages of 1 and 4 years, they gradually develop hyperphagia, which eventually leads to gross obesity. These children also manifest developmental delay and limited sexual function due to hypogenitalism. Abnormal secondary sex characteristics, e.g. micropenis and cryptorchidism in males and amenorrhoea in females, are common. Other associated features in Prader–Willi syndrome include: small hands and feet, cleft palate, almond-shaped eyes, incurved feet, clubfoot, congenital hip dislocation, scoliosis, abnormalities in the knee and ankle joints and squint. Systemic abnormalities include diabetes, bowel obstruction, asthma, duodenal ulcer, rectal prolapse, heart disease, cor pulmonale, boils, deafness, renal stones, gall stones and hypothermia. Those with Prader–Willi syndrome can manifest severe behavioural problems associated with hyperphagia and self-injurious behaviour, particularly in the form of incessant spot picking and temper tantrums.

Down syndrome
Down syndrome is incorrect. Down syndrome (trisomy 21) causes learning disability but is characterised by brachycephaly, single palmar crease, upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthic folds, hypotonia, cardiovascular malformations in around 40% and development of Alzheimer’s disease in most by 50 years of age.

Tuberous sclerosis
Tuberous sclerosis is incorrect. Tuberous sclerosis is a genetic condition (two separate genes are known to cause the condition – one on chromosome 9 and the other on chromosome 16) that causes the growth of benign tumours in multiple organ systems and can cause learning disability. Clinical features of tuberous sclerosis include ash-leaf macules and shagreen patches on the skin, renal cysts, retinal hamartomas and seizures.

Lesch–Nyhan syndrome
Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is incorrect. Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is an X-linked recessive condition caused by an inborn error of purine metabolism, resulting in abnormally high levels of xanthine and uric acid in the blood of the affected person. A deficient production of hypoxanthine phosphoribosyltransferase is responsible for the abnormality in purine metabolism. This results in gout, renal problems, poor muscle control and learning disability, and is characterised by self-injurious behaviour in the majority of affected patients. A teenager presents with a 2-day history of anxiety, tremulousness and diaphoresis. He admits to the recent cessation of a drug, but will not reveal which drug he used. He has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure in the Emergency Department. Withdrawal of which drug is the most likely cause?

Fragile X syndrome
Fragile X syndrome is incorrect. Fragile X syndrome is an X-linked condition that results in learning disability. The observable clinical features associated with Fragile-X syndrome are subtle and often cannot be detected until the subject reaches adulthood. In adult life, affected individuals have a shorter than average height with a larger than average head circumference. Macro-orchidism is found in a proportion of adults with Fragile-X syndrome. Some adults have a characteristic facial appearance, i.e. a large forehead with supraorbital fullness, long face, long nose, prominent jaws, high arched palate and large ears resembling those of bats.

stem: A 57-year-old man, currently undergoing medical treatment for depression, is referred to the clinic. In the past three days has stood naked and rather agitated outside a local school proclaiming that he possesses a special power that will 'save children from the evil influences of sex and drugs'. He was insistent in this belief and had to be taken away by the police. Physical examination reveals a blood pressure of 135/72 mmHg, a pulse of 78 bpm, and a body mass index (BMI) of 24 kg/m 2. What is the most likely diagnosis cause of this latest episode?
explanation:
Mania
This patient has delusions of grandeur, believing that he possesses special powers to save the children, and has shown signs of psychomotor agitation, standing naked outside the local school. Against a background of previous depression, it seems most likely that he is suffering from a manic episode. Atypical antipsychotics and benzodiazepines are the mainstay of therapy for gaining control of an acute manic episode. Over the longer term, lithium is used as a mood stabiliser in patients with bipolar disorder.

Schizophrenia
Schizophrenia is incorrect. The delusions of grandeur fit with mania, and the absence of other features of schizophrenia such as thought broadcasting and thought insertion point us away from this as the diagnosis.

Borderline personality disorder
Borderline personality disorder is incorrect. Borderline personality disorder is characterized by inappropriate or extreme emotional reactions, impulsive behaviour, and unstable relationships.

Obsessive compulsive disorder
Obsessive compulsive disorder is incorrect. Obsessive compulsive disorder is associated with repetitive behaviours which pervade activities of daily living.

Conversion disorder
Conversion disorder is incorrect. Conversion disorder is characterized by the development of a symptom such as blindness or paralysis that cannot be explained by organic illness.

stem: A 19-year-old man comes to the psychiatry clinic for review. He has been asked to attend by the engineering firm where he is a modern apprentice. He has been suspended from work because he is unable to concentrate on completing tasks which are given to him, and has proved disruptive during lessons because he has a short attention span. Apparently this fits with a similar pattern of behaviour whilst at school over the past few years. He has failed to gain sufficient benefit from CBT to continue work. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation:
Methylphenidate
The picture of psychiatric symptoms here fits best with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, (ADHD). Treatment is similar to that proposed for children, using stimulant agents such as methylphenidate.

Amitriptyline
Amitriptyline is incorrect. Tricyclic anti-depressants are indicated in the treatment of depression, not in the treatment of ADHD.

Diazepam
Diazepam is incorrect. Stimulants are indicated in the treatment of ADHD, rather than benzodiazepines. Long term use of diazepam may also prove addictive.

MDMA
MDMA is incorrect. MDMA is a recreational drug also known as ecstasy, it has no role in the treatment of ADHD.

Sertraline
Sertraline is incorrect. Sertraline is an SSRI used in the treatment of depression and anxiety.

stem: You are taking a history from a 19-year-old man. He says he has trouble sleeping at night because thoughts about how to use his special powers are rushing through his head. He says he is able to read other people’s thoughts and sometimes feels able to control their hand movements. He knows this to be true because a passage in the Bible can be translated with a special code, and the translation explains he has these powers. He also says he hears voices talking about him. How is his delusion best categorised?
explanation:
Delusion of reference
The patient believes a passage in the Bible refers to him having special powers, which is a delusion of reference. A delusion is defined as a strongly held false belief that is not typical of the patient’s cultural or religious background. A patient will not acknowledge the belief as false despite evidence to contradict it, and will often change their other beliefs to keep their whole belief system consistent. Delusions can be categorised into different types: Delusions of Reference – belief that a special meaning lies behind something ‘innocent’ in the public domain, eg a song, book, newspaper or TV programme is about them; or the way objects are arranged in a room or cars parked in the street has a specific reference to them. Delusions of Control – belief that they are being controlled by an external force or having thoughts inserted, removed or broadcasted from their mind. They often cite things such as electricity, radio waves or aliens as the mediator. Delusions of Guilt – a false feeling of remorse or guilt that they have committed a horrible crime and should be punished; or are responsible for a disaster such as a flood or earthquake. Delusions of Replacement – when a patient believes a person or people in their life, eg their partner or close relative, have been replaced by an impostor who looks and talks exactly like that person. Paranoid Delusions – these are the most common type of delusions and often involve the theme of being followed, harassed or conspired against; or the belief that people or organisations (eg MI5, police, employer) are plotting to harm the patient. Grandiose Delusions – belief that they have exceptional talent, abilities, worth, or that they may be famous. For example, patients may believe themselves to be God, a billionaire or have superpowers.

Delusion of control
Deulsion of control is incorrect. The patient does not believe he himself is being controlled, but that he can control others.

Delusion of guilt
Delusion of guilt is incorrect. There are no delusions of guilt described.

Delusion of replacement
Delusion of replacement is incorrect. There are no delusions of replacement described.

Paranoid delusion
Paranoid delusion is incorrect. He does not display any paranoid ideas.

stem: You are referred a 48-year-old man who has been arrested by the police on suspicion of committing a number of aggravated robberies in the past few weeks. He is acting rather strangely, staring intently at you when you interview him, and the police feel he may be psychotic. You suspect he has Ganser syndrome. Which of the following is a feature of Ganser syndrome?
explanation:
Pseudohallucination
Ganser syndrome occurs where patients mimic the symptoms of a psychosis. One feature of Ganser syndrome is, therefore, pseudohallucination. Patients often have poor eye contact with prolonged periods of staring and giving approximate answers (vorbeireden). Other features of Ganser syndrome include: somatic conversion amnesia.

Delirium
Acute confusional state as characterized by delirium isn’t a feature of Ganser syndrome.

Areas of demyelination
Areas of demyelination are a feature of inflammatory disorders such as multiple sclerosis.

Frontal lobe atrophy
Frontal lobe atrophy is seen in patients with Pick’s disease.

Amyloid deposition
Amyloid deposition is most likely to be seen in Alzheimer’s disease.

stem: A 17-year-old woman is referred to the clinic with suspected anorexia nervosa. She has apparently been losing weight progressively over the past 6-12 months, and her BMI is now 16.5. Which of the following would you most expect to find when reviewing the patient’s history, examination and lab findings?
explanation:
Increased, excessive physical activity
The diagnostic criteria for anorexia nervosa are weight loss to more than 15% below expected weight, absence of three or more consecutive menstrual cycles and disturbance of body image. Methods of inducing extra weight loss are usually employed by patients with anorexia and these include starvation, postprandial vomiting, excessive physical exercise, purging with laxatives, diuretic use and amphetamine use.

Buccal pigmentation
Buccal pigmentation is incorrect. Buccal pigmentation is seen as a result of increased adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) production, which is a feature of hypoadrenalism.

Low plasma cortisol levels
Low plasma cortisol levels is incorrect. Cortisol levels are actually increased because of a stress response to starvation and weight loss.

Raised gonadotrophin levels
Raised gonadotrophin levels is incorrect. Gonadotrophin production almost ceases in patients with anorexia, accounting for the amenorrhoea. Anorexia Nervosa A 59-year-old man with hypertension presents with a six-month history of memory loss, aggression and social disinhibition. He has also been incontinent of urine on occasions. His hypertension was diagnosed many years earlier and he is managed with a combination of ramipril, amlodipine and indapamide. On examination his BP is 155/95 mmHg. Investigations reveal:

Hyperkalaemia
Hyperkalaemia is incorrect. Hypokalaemia is more likely to be seen because of abuse of purgatives or laxatives to drive weight loss.

stem: A 35-year-old man with a diagnosis of schizophrenia remains psychotic despite treatment with two different antipsychotic medications, from two different classes, both given for an adequate amount of time at an adequate dose. What would be the next best medication to prescribe for him?
explanation:
Clozapine
This patient has treatment-resistant schizophrenia; i.e. he has not responded to treatment with two different anti-psychotics. Clozapine is the drug of choice in treatment-resistant schizophrenia. Studies have shown that 30% of patients who have previously not responded to treatment with anti-psychotics significantly after six weeks’ treatment with clozapine. However, clozapine has side effects that include agranulocytosis and neutropenia, and therefore all patients on clozapine have to be registered with the Clozaril Patient Monitoring Service and have regular blood counts.

An oral typical anti-psychotic
An oral typical anti-psychotic is incorrect. This patient has already been treated with two different antipsychotic medications from two different classes, and still has ongoing symptoms.

A depot typical anti-psychotic
A depot typical antipsychotic is incorrect. This patient has already been treated with two different antipsychotic medications from two different classes and still has ongoing symptoms. Mode of delivery of the anti-psychotic will not affect the outcome unless there is an issue with compliance.

Mirtazapine
Mirtazapine is incorrect. This is a noradrenergic and specific serotonergic antidepressant used in the treatment of depression. Psychosis

A mood stabiliser
A mood stabiliser is incorrect. This would be used in the treatment of bipolar affective disorder.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with a long history of depression feels unwell after attending a cheese and wine tasting. She measures her blood pressure at home and it is 220/100 mmHg. Which antidepressant is she most likely to be on?
options: Serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) (eg venlafaxine)
explanation:
Monoamine oxidase inhibitors (MAOIs) (eg selegiline)
The patient is having a hypertensive crisis or ‘cheese reaction’. This is a potentially serious side-effect of the MAOIs and occurs when patients ingest foods with high amounts of tyramine. Tyramine is usually metabolised in the gastrointestinal (GI) tract by MAO, but due to MAOI, it enters the general circulation where it has direct sympathomimetic actions and increases the release of noradrenaline. This can cause vasoconstriction and a dangerous rise in blood pressure, as well as nausea, palpitations, headache and dilated pupils. In severe cases the reaction can lead to delirium, hyperpyrexia, cerebral haemorrhage and death. Foods high in tyramine include meat and yeast extracts, matured cheeses, red wine and broad beans. These foods should be restricted in the diet of patients taking MAOIs. Due to the number of side-effects, MAOIs are usually second- or third-line choices in treating depression.

Presynaptic α2-antagonists (eg mirtazapine)
Presynaptic α2-antagonists (eg mirtazapine) is incorrect as this class of drug works by increasing the release of noradrenaline from the presynaptic terminals. It does not lead to the reaction described above.

Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) (eg fluoxetine)
Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) (eg fluoxetine) is incorrect as SSRIs work by increasing serotonergic activity in the brain and do not cause this side-effect. They are frequently used as first-line antidepressants due to their better tolerability and safety in overdose.

Serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) (eg venlafaxine)
Serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs) (eg venlafaxine) is incorrect as drugs in this class are not associated with this reaction. Some three months after suffering a serious assault, a 45-year-old man complains of having vivid dreams of the incident, flashbacks of the assault and intrusive thoughts. He has noticed he is more ‘jumpy’ than before and avoids going out at night as it makes him anxious and reminds him of the attack.

Tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) (eg amitryptiline)
Tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs) (eg amitryptiline) is incorrect as TCAs work by inhibiting reuptake both of Chat They with AIdo Tutor serotonin and noradrenaline, so increasing the amount of neurotransmitter in the synaptic cleft. not cause the reaction described above, but they are particularly dangerous in overdose and can lead to cardiac arrhythmias and seizures.

stem: A 34-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department stating that he has been sent by God to heal the patients in the hospital. He tells you that he has been communicating with God for the last nine months (he believes he can hear God speaking to him) and he is now ready to carry out his work. He appears calm, but his speech is tangential, erratic and difficult to follow. Which one of the following is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Schizophrenia
This patient meets the DSM-5 criteria for a diagnosis of schizophrenia, which requires at least two of: delusions, hallucinations, disorganised speech, disorganised or catatonic behaviour and negative symptoms. Continuous signs of the disturbance must be present for at least six months, during which time the patient must experience at least one month of active symptoms with functional deterioration occurring over a significant amount of time.

Bipolar affective disorder
Bipolar affective disorder is incorrect. The most likely diagnosis based on the case vignette is schizophrenia. Bipolar affective disorder is characterised by predominant disturbances in affect or mood. Psychotic symptoms may be present but are congruent with mania or depression. This patient is clearly exhibiting delusions in addition to auditory hallucinations. There is no mention of mood disorder in the history and Chat therewith areAInoTutor comments on disturbed affect.

Cotard syndrome
Cotard syndrome is incorrect. Cotard syndrome is a rare psychiatric illness, the hallmark of which is nihilistic delusions concerning one’s own body, which range from believing that one is missing organs or limbs to the belief that one is dead. Clearly, this is not the diagnosis given the vignette.

Drug-induced psychosis
Drug-induced psychosis is incorrect. This patient meets the DSM-5 criteria for a diagnosis of schizophrenia. A diagnosis of drug-induced psychosis requires (1) evidence of psychosis (which is present in this case) and (2) evidence from the history, clinical exam or laboratory results that the symptoms developed during or within one month of substance intoxication/withdrawal, or that medication use is related to the disturbance by aetiology (which is not present in this case). Schizophrenia

Schizo-affective disorder
Schizo-affective disorder is incorrect. A diagnosis of schizo-affective disorder requires concurrent evidence of features of both schizophrenia and a mood disorder. There are no features of mood disorder in this case to support this and, as such, the diagnosis is most likely to be schizophrenia.

stem: A 50-year-old man presents to the Emerency Department with an anxiety attack. He tells you that it has been 6 months after the death of his wife. You chat to the patient and his friend about the passing of his wife. Which of the following is going to heighten your suspicion of an abnormal grief reaction?
options: A brief episode of seeing the dead person
No obvious grief reaction since the event
explanation:
No obvious grief reaction since the event
No obvious grief reaction since the event would constitute delayed grief.

A brief episode of seeing the dead person
A brief episode of seeing the dead person is incorrect. Visions of the dead person are very common after the passing of a loved one.

Poor concentration
Poor concentration is incorrect. Poor concentration, decreased appetite and poor sleep patterns are all features of a normal grief reaction.

Poor memory
Poor memory is incorrect. Poor memory, like other symptoms of depression is a common feature of a normal grief reaction.

Searching for the deceased
Searching for the deceased is incorrect. Searching for the deceased in their “usual haunt”, is also a feature of normal grief.

stem: A 50-year-old male comes to the clinic claiming his ears look large. He has 12 documented visits to medical services over the past year, all about this problem. On examination he is of completely normal appearance, with normal sized ears. This is explained to him, but he is absolutely insistent that they are too large. Apart from this he has no past medical history of note, and holds down a job running a small printing firm. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Body dysmorphia
Absolute belief that one part of the body is deformed, despite clear evidence that it is not, is typical of body dysmorphia. Patients may visit several physicians in succession, not happy with the opinion they receive each time they see the doctor, and may even undergo unnecessary plastic surgery. Those who have a family history of obsessive–compulsive disorder are at increased risk of body dysmorphia disorder. Psychotherapy is a mainstay of therapy for body dysmorphia disorder, with selective serotonin-reuptake inhibitors being of value in some patients.

Somatisation disorder
Somatisation disorder is incorrect. Somatisation disorder is considered when patients present with multiple different somatic symptoms for which no organic cause can be found, usually present for 2 years or more.

Obsessive–compulsive disorder
Obsessive-compulsive disorder is incorrect. Repeated cycles of behaviour which pervade activities of daily living, consistent with OCD are not reported in the scenario.

Depression
Depression is incorrect. There are no features in the scenario such as loss of appetite or early morning wakening to suggest a diagnosis of depression. Body Dysmorphic DisorderA 59-year-old woman who is taking long term lithium for bipolar disorder comes to the psychiatry clinic for review. She has been diagnosed with nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and the plan is to switch the lithium for an alternative.

Munchausen’s disease
Munchausen’s disease is incorrect. Munchausen’s disease implies that patients deliberately produce symptoms of an illness in themselves, there is no suggestion that the evolution of symptoms seen here is deliberate.

stem: After an automobile accident that kills her child but leaves her with only minor injuries, a mother appears very calm and says that she has no emotion. What mechanism is she using?
explanation:
Isolation
Isolation describes the separation of a thought from its attached emotional tone, thereby making it tolerable. It’s well described during highly stressful events such as the death of a loved one.

Derealisation
Derealisation is incorrect. Derealisation involves altering the perception of the external world that it somehow seems unreal or “make believe”.

Depersonalisation
Depersonalisation is incorrect. Depersonalisation involves the perception of being detached from self, and that the person concerned becomes an observer of events rather than being involved in them.

Disorientation
Disorientation is incorrect. Disorientation isn’t associated with the unnatural sense of calmness here.

Intellectualisation
Intellectualisation is incorrect. This involves over rationalizing the event concerned to drive a feeling of emotional detachment, which again isn’t seen here.

stem: A 21-year-old male medical student is admitted to the Emergency Department after behaving bizarrely. He had just returned from a 3 month attachment in South America during which he apparently began using cocaine after splitting up from his girlfriend. On arrival in the Emergency Department he is angry because he tells you that he has been brought to the department against his will, that he is the dean of the medical school and that there is nothing wrong with him. He also tells you his mind works 4 times faster than yours and that you will never win. His BP is 145/80 mmHg, pulse is 115/min and regular. No other significant findings are noted. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Drug induced psychosis
This behaviour is consistent with a manic episode, and may be related to cocaine abuse. The agitation and relative hypertension for a 21-year-old would also fit with stimulant drug use.

Adjustment disorder
Adjustment disorder is incorrect. Adjustment disorder is usually characterized by depressive symptoms associated with a stressful life event.

Bipolar disorder
Bipolar disorder is incorrect. Although presentation of bipolar disorder with a first episode of mania isn’t impossible at the age of 21, it’s more likely in this case the presentation is stimulant drug related.

Opiate withdrawal
Opiate withdrawal is incorrect. Opiate withdrawal is associated with agitation and anxiety, coupled with somatic symptoms such as sweating, muscle aches, abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting and diarrhoea.

Schizophrenia
Schizophrenia is incorrect. In the presence of recent onset cocaine use, drug induced psychosis is considered ahead of other option, including schizophrenia.

stem: A 20-year-old man presents with a history of delayed developmental milestones, problems with impulse control and an IQ of 65. His physical examination is unremarkable. He was in special education classes during his schooling. What is the most probable cause?
explanation:
Idiopathic
