They then display behaviours in an attempt to counteract the ‘fattening’ effects of food, such as self-induced vomiting, periods of starvation and diuretic abuse. Patients with bulimia are typically of normal weight. Around a third of individual who suffer from bulimia nervosa have a previous history of anorexia.

Body dysmorphic disorder
Body dysmorphic disorder is incorrect. This describes an anxiety disorder where an individual has a distorted view of their appearance and becomes obsessed worrying about a particular defect in their appearance that are not seen by others. Body dysmorphic disorder can be seen alongside individuals with anorexia bulimia Chator with nervosa, but is less likely than a diagnosis of bulimia nervosa in this case because of the presence of the other symptoms of bingeing, purging and diuretic abuse.

Anorexia nervosa
Anorexia nervosa is incorrect. This describes an eating disorder where individuals induce weight loss of >15% of normal weight resulting in BMI <17.5, and where individuals hold an over-valued idea that fatness is a dreadful state and will not allow their weight to rise above a very low threshold.

Generalised anxiety disorder
Generalised anxiety disorder is incorrect. The clinical features of generalised anxiety disorder are persistent and generalised symptoms of anxiety that occur across a range of daily circumstances, and are not related to particular events or circumstances. Bulimia Nervosa After an automobile accident that kills her child but leaves her with only minor injuries, a mother appears very calm and says that she has no emotion. What mechanism is she using?

Bingeing
Bingeing is incorrect. This refers to the behaviour of the excessive and compulsive consumption of food and overeating seen in bulimia nervosa, which is described here but, alongside the other symptoms described, a diagnosis of bulimia nervosa better fits this case.

stem: A 54-year-old divorced teacher who lives alone is seen 6 weeks after his second myocardial infarction (MI). He has a history of hypercholesterolaemia and diabetes; current medication includes simvastatin, omeprazole, amlodipine, digoxin, warfarin and glibenclamide. He is currently awaiting a further coronary angiography. On examination he has a pulse of 92 bpm, which is irregular, and evidence of biventricular failure; an ECG shows atrial fibrillation. He is depressed with sustained low mood, anhedonia, early morning waking, poor appetite and weight loss. He says the future is bleak, and after your assessment you feel he needs an antidepressant. Which one of the following would be most appropriate?
explanation:
Mirtazapine
Although selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) such as sertraline usually tend to be used first-line, NICE guidelines recommend avoiding SSRIs in patients on warfarin or heparin due to increased bleeding risk and consider mirtazapine instead.

Amitriptyline
Amitriptyline is incorrect. Amitriptyline (a tricyclic antidepressant [TCA]) should be used with caution in those with a recent MI or arrhythmias. TCAs have more side-effects than SSRIs, are dangerous in overdose and can lead to cardiac arrhythmias or prolongation of the QT interval. Amitriptyline is generally considered aAIsecondTutor line antidepressant unless its sedative effects are desired, such as where sleep disturbance and anxiety are predominant.

Dosulepin (dothiepin)
Dosulepin (dothiepin) is incorrect. Dosulepin (a TCA) is contraindicated in recent MI or heart block. Like amitryptyline it is dangerous in overdose, and cardiovascular side-effects include arrhythmias, postural hypotension and syncope. It tends to be used particularly when sedation is required, and is usually initiated by a specialist.

Sertraline
Sertraline is incorrect. Although sertraline (an SSRI) is often used first-line due to a good side-effect and safety profile, particularly in those with cardiovascular disease, NICE recommends avoiding SSRIs in patients on warfarin. If the patient was not on anticoagulation this would be the best answer.

Venlafaxine
Venlafaxine is incorrect. Venlafaxine (a serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor [SNRI]) is contraindicated in patients with heart disease or uncontrolled hypertension; it also has more side-effects than other drugs. NICE recommends it is used second-line after an initial antidepressant has been poorly tolerated, particularly for more severe depression.

stem: An 18 year old woman comes to the psychiatric clinic for review. She attends with her mother who informs you that she has had problems with multiple hand washing and obsessive compulsive disorder type behavior with respect to visiting public toilets for the last 6 years. Apparently she had a number of infections between 11 and 12 years of age, and her mother feels that one of these may have triggered her symptoms. Which of the following is associated with development of OCD?
explanation:
β-haemolytic streptococcal infection
A subgroup of patients with OCD has now been indentified who are characterised by prepubertal acute onset after group A β-haemolytic streptococcal pharyngitis. It has been postulated that the basal ganglia is involved in this process, a hypothesis that is supported by neuropsychological and neuroimaging evidence of basal ganglia dysfunction in both OCD and Sydenham’s chorea. In this case it’s likely that her initial symptoms of OCD have been reinforced over the intervening 6 years.

EBV infection
EBV infection is incorrect. EBV infection is recognised as a risk factor for the development of Hodgkin’s lymphoma.

Enterovirus infection
Enterovirus infection is incorrect. Enterovirus infection is associated with the development of Type 1 diabetes.

Influenza A infection
Influenza A infection is incorrect. Influenza infection is recognised to be associated with development of narcolepsy, as are some influenza vaccinations.

Staphylococcus aureus infection
Staphylococcus aureus infection is incorrect. Staphylococcus aureus infection is not thought to be associated with long-term sequelae.

stem: A 23-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department having been brought in by Police. He says that his wife has been unfaithful after seeing her talk to another man when they were out for dinner. He insists she does not want to be with him anymore and she cannot be trusted. He has no past medical history of note, smokes 20 cigarettes per day and drinks 8 pints of beer per week. Clinical examination is unremarkable. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Paranoid personality disorder
This type of picture, characterized by pathological jealousy and the absolute cast iron belief that his wife has been unfaithful, fits with a paranoid personality disorder.

Avoidant personality disorder
Avoidant personality disorder is incorrect. Patients suffering from an avoidant personality disorder suffer from shyness and are socially withdrawn.

Hypomania
Hypomania is incorrect. Although grandiose claims may be a feature of hypomania, as described here the pathological jealousy is more consistent with paranoid personality disorder.

Obsessive–compulsive personality disorder
Obsessive–compulsive personality disorder is incorrect. This is characterized by episodes of repeated ritualistic behavior.

Schizophrenia
Schizophrenia is incorrect. Features such as thought insertion, thought broadcasting and delusions of reference, which are seen in schizophrenia, do not feature here. Personality Disorders A 19 year old student is admitted under a court order for re-feeding. She has a diagnosis of anorexia nervosa, and her BMI is 15. Her BP is 100/60, pulse is 88 and regular. Abdomen is soft and non-tender. Investigations;.

stem: A 18-year-old man is referred to the mental health service. He has suffered with discipline issues at his previous school and has been excluded from 6th form college for defying the head teacher on multiple occasions. He gets along well with his peers and completes projects that he likes including a number of pieces for a school art exhibition. His developmental milestones are normal and he has no history of fighting, theft, or destruction of property. Mental status examination reveals an assertive teenager who tells the examiner that he does not wish to discuss his problems. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Oppositional defiant disorder
Oppositional defiant disorder involves problems in relating to authority figures. Such individuals get along well with their peers and have no other problems of conduct or development. Psychotherapy is the mainstay of therapy to allow individuals to modify their response in certain situations.

Intellectual disability
Intellectual disability is associated with delayed developmental milestones and other evidence of impaired intellectual ability, not seen here.

Conduct disorder
Conduct disorder is incorrect. Conduct disorder is characterised by violation of age-appropriate social norms, fighting, runaway behaviour, theft and destruction of property. Conduct disorder may follow oppositional defiant disorder.

Childhood disintegrative disorder
Childhood disintegrative disorder is incorrect. Childhood disintegrative disorder involves the development of severe disturbances in social, communicative and cognitive functions after a period of normal development.

Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder
Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder is incorrect. Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder is characterised by inattention, impulsivity and hyperactivity. Individuals with ADHD are unlikely to complete projects even if they are interested.

stem: A middle-aged woman with a single episode of major depressive disorder has responded well to imipramine after one month of treatment. What is the next step in the management of this case?
options: Continue the imipramine for 6 months then gradually downtitrate
Decrease imipramine gradually until she is medication-free, unless depression occurs
explanation:
Continue the imipramine for 6 months then gradually downtitrate
Maintenance therapy after a response to antidepressants should generally be continued at an effective dose for 6 months, with gradual down titration of dose prior to cessation of treatment.

Continue imipramine indefinitely
Continue imipramine indefinitely is incorrect. Given the episode of depression has resolved, there seems little reason to continue the medication for an indefinite period.

Decrease imipramine gradually until she is medication-free, unless depression occurs
Decrease imipramine gradually until she is medication free is incorrect. Studies suggest that tapering off medication after only one month is associated with increased risk of depression relapse.

Stop imipramine immediately
Stop imipramine immediately is incorrect. Although there has been a good response to therapy, rebound is likely if the medication is discontinued. Depression A 17-year-old male, who has difficulty concentrating on things for long periods of time and is hyperactive, has recently been prescribed a drug for treatment of his ‘hyperactivity’. What drug is most likely to have been prescribed?

Switch to fluoxetine
Switch to fluoxetine is incorrect. Given there has been a good initial response to imipramine, there is no indication to switch to an selective serotonin-reuptake inhibitor (SSRI).

stem: A 27-year-old woman presents to the General Practitioner with two episodes of agitation, pressured speech, grandiose delusions and disorganised behaviour. One episode occurred four years ago and lasted several weeks. She took anti-depressants for a period in her mid-20s when she became very low with no obvious cause. The current episode has lasted four weeks. Between episodes, she is generally happy, outgoing, and sociable. Mental status examination reveals increased psychomotor activity and impaired judgement. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Major depressive disorder with mood-congruent psychosis
explanation:
Bipolar disorder, manic phase
The presentation is suggestive of bipolar disorder, with the previous discrete episode of depression, and two subsequent episodes of mania. The normal level of functioning inbetween times fits with bipolar disorder rather than a more pervasive psychiatric disorder such as schizophrenia. A suitable mood stabilising agent should be considered, for example lamotrigine given that she is of child bearing age.

Brief psychotic disorder
Brief psychotic disorder is incorrect. Brief psychotic disorder lasts for less than 1 month and is not usually preceded by similar episodes.

Delusional disorder, erotomanic type
Delusional disorder, erotomanic type is incorrect. This is characterised by delusions about loving relationships with relative strangers.

Major depressive disorder with mood-congruent psychosis
Major depressive disorder with mood-congruent psychosis is incorrect. This is characterised by episodes of severe depression with hallucinations or delusions involving worthlessness, sickness, guilt, death and other depressive themes.

stem: A 17-year-old man with a diagnosis of Prader Willi syndrome comes to the clinic with his parents. He is holding down part time employment at a local warehouse, but is beginning to gain weight rapidly and he and his parents are concerned about food seeking behaviour. His BMI is elevated at 36. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial intervention?
explanation:
Limiting access to food
Although patients with Prader Willi may achieve a relatively high level of functioning and be able to hold down simple part time employment, they still find it impossible to control appetite when presented with access to food. As such the best way to limit weight gain is by limiting access to food.

Bupropion
Bupropion is incorrect. Although bupropion does limit appetite and is associated with modest weight reduction, it is likely to be ineffective in controlling weight gain associated with Prader Willi.

Cognitive behavioural therapy
Cognitive behavioural therapy, is incorrect. CBT may have a minor impact on appetite, unfortunately when presented with food it is still unlikely to impact on the appetite of patients with Prader Willi.

Gastric banding
Gastric banding is incorrect. Gastric banding only limits appetite in the short term in patients with Prader Willi. There are also a number of case reports of gastric rupture as a result of binge eating.

Liraglutide
Liraglutide is incorrect. Although liraglutide at a 3mg dose is licensed to treat obesity, there is little evidence to support its use in patients with Prader Willi. Genetic.

stem: A 63-year-old man is referred to the neurology clinic with worsening memory and confusion over the past few months. Which of the following symptoms would favour a diagnosis of vascular dementia over Alzheimer’s disease?
explanation:
Frequent seizures
Seizures are much more common in patients with vascular dementia compared to Alzheimer’s. This may well be because of neuronal irritability in areas where there is vascular compromise. A history of arteriosclerosis elsewhere and a history of hypertension are also likely.

Social disinhibition and irritability
Social disinhibition and irritability is incorrect. Social disinhibition is more likely to be seen in frontal lobe dementia syndromes.

Slow, insidious onset
Slow, insidious onset is incorrect. Vascular dementia has a more acute onset than Alzheimer’s disease. The cognitive impairment in vascular dementia progresses in a step-like manner, with acute exacerbations, often with acute confusion, followed by periods of stability; it is characteristically patchy.

Early loss of insight
Early loss of insight is incorrect. The basic personality may be well-preserved until late in the disease in vascular dementia (unlike the other dementias). Capacity for judgement may persist in vascular dementia, and insight may be preserved for some time, thus leading to anxiety and depression (rarely seen in Alzheimer's disease). Dementia

Disrupted sleep–wake cycle
Disrupted sleep-wake cycle is incorrect. Sleep wake cycle may be preserved until relatively late in multi-infarct dementia.

stem: A 25-year-old woman with no prior history of psychiatric problems presents with a 3-week episode of insomnia, increased psychomotor activity and impulsivity. There is no history of substance abuse, general medical problems, emotional stresses or depressive episodes. Laboratory tests for liver and thyroid functions are normal. Mental status examination reveals a well-oriented female with pressured speech and mood lability, but no psychotic symptoms. A diagnosis of mania is made. What is the approximate possibility that she may experience a similar episode later on in life?
explanation:
90% or greater
This patient's symptoms are most suggestive of a single episode of manic phase of a bipolar disorder. The lifetime chance of another episode is greater than 90% and the disorder often presents for the first time in the third decade of life.

10% or less
10% or less is incorrect. Even with therapy, a recurrence rate of 10% or less is optimistic with respect to mania even in patients who receive therapy with an agent such as lithium.

25%
25% is incorrect. Compliance with prophylactic mood stabilizers may significantly reduce recurrence rate, although younger age at first presentation is associated with increased rate of recurrence.

40%
40% is incorrect. 40% is the average recurrence rate at one year in patients suffering a first episode of mania.

70%
70% is incorrect. 77% represents the recurrence rate from an episode of mania at 6 months.

stem: A 45-year-old woman is started on citalopram for a first episode of depression. After 4 weeks she returns to the GP as she is feeling much better and wondering if she should stop the medication. For how long would you advise a single episode of depression should be treated after recovery?
explanation:
6 months
NICE recommends a single episode of depression should be treated for at least 6 months after recovery to reduce the risk of relapse. When a patient has taken antidepressants for 6 months after recovery, they should be reviewed to assess the need to continue, which should take into account the number of previous episodes and risk factors for relapse. If a person is at high risk of relapse (eg due to previous episodes, residual symptoms, physical health problems or ongoing psychosocial difficulties), NICE recommends they continue for 2 years.

6 weeks
6 weeks is incorrect. Stopping this early after recovery significantly increases the risk of relapse.

1 month
1 month is incorrect. Stopping this early after recovery significantly increases the risk of relapse.

3 months
3 months is incorrect. Stopping this early after recover significantly increases the risk of relapse. Depression

Stop when patient recovers
Stop when patient recovers is incorrect. If antidepressant treatment is stopped immediately on recovery, 50% of patients will experience a relapse of their depressive symptoms.

stem: A 19-year-old man presents to the General Practitioner with concerns that the lump he has discovered in his neck may be due to Hodgkin’s disease. A routine work-up is completely negative for underlying malignancy, and he is diagnosed with glandular fever. He continues to believe that he has a haematological malignancy and has presented three times over the past four months to the Haematology Service. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Illness anxiety disorder
Illness anxiety disorder is characterised by misinterpretation of the meaning of symptoms that does not respond to physician reassurance even after thorough medical assessment. The patient doesn’t derive any benefit from repeated presentation to clinical services.

Conversion disorder
Conversion disorder involves loss of sensory or motor nerve function in response to a potential psychological stressor.

Delusional disorder, somatic type
Delusional disorder, somatic type is associated with more bizarre and irrational somatic beliefs. The most common are the belief that one is infested with insects, emitting a foul smell, parts of the body are not functioning, belief that their body or parts of the body are misshapen or ugly, and that there are extra body parts.

Somatisation disorder
Somatisation disorder is characterised by multiple complaints involving different body systems, over a sustained period of time (up to two years).

Factitious disorder
Factitious disorder is where individuals deliberately reproduce symptoms of illness and have conscious control over them.

stem: A 35-year-old man was brought to hospital by the police. When asked by the police he was unable to recall his address, occupation or family details. He appeared calm and was not distressed. After several days his memory has improved completely, and he now tells you that his wife left him several days before he was picked up. He is suffering from no physical illness, injury or mental illness. Which of the following best describes his memory impairment?
explanation:
Dissociative amnesia
Dissociative amnesia is a type of amnesia where a patient seeks to avoid the stresses of their current life. The cause of such a disorder is the failure to cope with an extreme painful situation, e.g. marriage failure. Psychological trauma is severe enough to cause severe memory loss for the period of crisis and the episode begins and ends very suddenly. Behavioural therapy and anxiolytics may alleviate symptoms.

Korsakoff’s psychosis
Korsakoff’s psychosis is incorrect. Korsakoff’s is associated with short term memory loss and confabulation, which leads to often fantastical stories, and is associated with thiamine deficiency.

Anterograde amnesia
Anterograde amnesia is incorrect. Anterograde amnesia is the loss of ability to create new memories after an event, rather than the amnesia seen here.

Dementia
Dementia is incorrect. The sudden onset of memory loss coupled with rapid recovery is inconsistent with dementia.

Epilepsy
Epilepsy is incorrect. Temporal lobe epilepsy is more likely to present with automaton type behaviour rather than the frank memory loss seen here.

stem: A 62-year-old man presents with progressively worsening dementia. He has a history of hypertension and a previous myocardial infarction some 7 years earlier. His BP is 155/90 mmHg on examination, and his pulse is 65 beats/min and regular. You send him to the psychiatrist who diagnoses him with Lewy Body dementia. Which one of the following features is most likely to be associated with Lewy Body dementia?
explanation:
Fluctuating mental state
The three cardinal features that help to distinguish Lewy Body dementia from dementia of Alzheimer’s type include fluctuating cognitive function, varying levels of alertness, significant daytime somnolence. Visual hallucinations are also more common in Lewy Body dementia, and there is a strong association with parkinsonian motor features. The association with loss of dopaminergic neurones means that patients have significant sensitivity to neuroleptics. There may be significant improvement in memory loss in response to cholinesterase inhibitors.

Absence of extrapyramidal symptoms
Absence of extrapyramidal symptoms is incorrect. Features of Parkinson’s are usual in patients with lewy Body dementia because the two diseases share a common pathophysiology.

Poor concentration
Poor concentration is incorrect. Although poor concentration is a feature of a number of causes of dementia, it doesn’t differentiate Lewy Body dementia.

Rapid onset
Rapid onset is incorrect. Rapid onset is seen in Creutzfeld Jakob (CJD), and presents with ataxia, dementia and involuntary movements.

Auditory hallucinations
Auditory hallucinations is incorrect. Auditory hallucinations are seen in both Alzheimer’s and in Lewy body dementia, and hence don’t demarcate Lewy body disease vs other dementia subtypes.

stem: A 34-year-old man seeks treatment for depression. He has recently lost his job and is awaiting a divorce hearing. There is no past medical history of note, he drinks three bottles of wine per week. He feels hopelessness and despair with lethargy. He denies suicide plans, stating there is no point in suicide. At which time is the patient most likely to commit suicide?
options: When he admits his feelings of guilt
When he completes a course of ECT
After the first two doses of SSRI
In the second week after commencing treatment with an SSRI
explanation:
In the second week after commencing treatment with an SSRI
In the second week after commencing treatment with an SSRI is correct. In major depressive disorder, the greatest risk for suicide occurs after a partial response to antidepressants. Usually, energy and motivation return before a subjective improvement in mood occurs, and a patient who has been too apathetic to act on suicidal rumination may, at this point, attempt suicide.

When he admits his feelings of guilt
When he admits his feelings of guilt is incorrect. Allowing patients to vocalise negative thoughts during psychotherapy is not associated with increased risk of suicide.

When he completes a course of ECT
When he completes a course of ECT is incorrect. The response to electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) with respect to improvement in mood is rapid with some improvement even seen after the first session. It is not associated with increased risk of suicide.

After the first two doses of SSRI
After the first two doses of selective serotonin-reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) is incorrect. The greatest risk of suicide occurs a few days in to SSRI treatment, little response in terms of increased activity is seen after only two doses. Depression

When he develops antidepressant side-effects
When he develops antidepressant side-effects is incorrect. Antidepressant side effects are not associated with increased risk of suicide.

stem: A 33-year-old primiparous woman is 2 days post-partum, having delivered a normal baby boy. She has become increasingly anxious and has told the midwife she thinks the baby is ‘a changeling’. Careful evaluation fails to identify other bizarre beliefs, and she is continuing to care for the baby. Which one of the features below is most likely to reassure you that the patient is not psychotic?
options: The patient does not believe the thoughts to be hers
The patient has symptoms of anxiety
The patient says the thoughts are stupid and tries not to think them
explanation:
The patient says the thoughts are stupid and tries not to think them
This shows the patient has insight into her own obsessional thoughts. She accepts they are her own (ie arising internally), but realises they are unlikely to be true, are unwanted and tries to resist them. One of the markers of psychosis is delusional beliefs that are held with certainty, so are not resisted, and the patient lacks insight into their false nature. It is important to distinguish obsessional from psychotic phenomena as the risk to the mother and baby is far greater with the latter.

Absence of auditory hallucinations
Absence of auditory hallucinations is incorrect. Psychosis does not always have to include hallucinations; other symptoms of psychosis can include confusion, disorientation and delusions.

The patient does not believe the thoughts to be hers
The patient does not believe the thoughts to be hers is incorrect. If the patient believes the thoughts are not hers, this could be suggestive of a delusion of control or thought insertion (eg a belief they are having thoughts inserted into their mind). It could also suggest she is having hallucinations, which is why she does not believe the thoughts to be her own. Both of these would be more likely to occur in psychosis or could suggest an underlying diagnosis of schizophrenia as these are both first-rank symptoms.

The patient has symptoms of anxiety
The patient has symptoms of anxiety is incorrect. The presence of anxiety does not really help rule out a psychotic episode as it can occur as part of psychosis, and is also common to a degree in all new mothers.

The phenomenon is intermittent
The phenomenon is intermittent is incorrect. Symptoms can be intermittent and fluctuating in psychosis. Psychosis A 25-year-old woman with no prior history of psychiatric problems presents with a 3-week episode of insomnia, increased psychomotor activity and impulsivity. There is no history of substance abuse, general medical problems, emotional stresses or depressive episodes. Laboratory tests for liver and thyroid functions are normal. Mental status examination reveals a well-oriented female with pressured speech and mood lability, but no psychotic symptoms.

stem: A 17-year-old boy attends your clinic with his mother, having been referred with ‘developmental delay and learning disability, possible autism’. On assessment, you note the following: he has poor eye contact and little social interaction, hyperactivity, abnormal speech including repetition, and a long, thin face with large ears. On auscultation, there is a systolic click followed by a murmur. Given your suspicions of a unifying diagnosis, which of the following would be the best investigation to confirm this?
options: Molecular genetic testing of the FMR1 gene
explanation:
Molecular genetic testing of the FMR1 gene
The case vignette gives a detailed description of the phenotypic and behavioural features of fragile X syndrome. At a molecular level, fragile X syndrome is due to a trinucleotide repeat (CGG) in a fragment of DNA in the fragile X gene (FMR1) on the X chromosome. It is thought to be the most common cause of inherited learning disability, affecting 1 in 4000 males and 1 in 8000 females. It causes a varying degree of learning disability, developmental delay and sometimes a physical phenotype as described above. Additional features include large testicles after puberty, connective tissue disorder with joint laxity and flat feet. Genetic testing is the gold standard for diagnosis, and includes cytogenetics and southern blotting demonstrating the trinucleotide repeat. As with all cases of learning disability, the mainstay of management is family/carer education, social support, identification and treatment of associated complications and genetic counselling. Fragile X syndrome should be considered in all children with developmental delay of unknown cause.

EEG
EEG is incorrect. This patient has fragile X syndrome. Although around 20% of patients with fragile X syndrome have seizures, this is not a useful test for clinching the diagnosis of the presenting complaint (learning disability and developmental delay), but rather may be useful further down the line if seizures do develop.

Formal neuropsychology assessment
Formal neuropsychology assessment is incorrect. While formal cognitive and behavioural assessment via neuropsychology may help in identifying the severity and pattern of learning and behavioural difficulties seen in fragile X syndrome, this does not identify the underlying cause of the problem. Autism, which is an important differential diagnosis for fragile X syndrome, can be diagnosed with the help of neuropsychological assessment.

MRI brain
MRI brain is incorrect. MRI brain can be useful in the assessment of patients with learning disability of unknown cause, as it may reveal focal corresponding lesions. However, changes seen on MRI are often non-specific and there are no pathognomonic brain imaging features expected in a patient with fragile X syndrome. As such, it would not be the best investigation to reach a diagnosis in this case.

Trans-thoracic ECHO
Trans-thoracic ECHO is incorrect. A trans-thoracic ECHO is an important investigation for any patient presenting with a murmur not previously accounted for. The findings on cardiac auscultation in the case vignette suggest a mitral valve prolapse, which can be seen as part of the wider connective tissue disease sometimes seen in fragile X syndrome. Although this investigation is important and supportive, it will not confirm a diagnosis of fragile X syndrome. Genetic.

stem: A 40-year-old man with learning difficulties is noted on examination to have small stature and large head circumference, with a large jaw and ears and pale irises. What is the most likely diagnosis and cause of his learning difficulties?
explanation:
Fragile X syndrome
Fragile X syndrome is the most common hereditary cause of mental disability. This syndrome affects approximately 1 in 4425–6045 males and causes intellectual disability in 1 in 8000 females. It accounts for half of all X-linked mental disability cases and around 0.6% of the intellectually disabled population. The observable clinical features associated with Fragile-X syndrome are subtle and often cannot be detected until the subject reaches adulthood. In adult life, affected individuals have a shorter than average height with a larger than average head circumference. Macro-orchidism is found in a proportion of adults with fragile-X syndrome. Some adults have a characteristic facial appearance, i.e. a large forehead with supraorbital fullness, long face, long nose, prominent jaws, high arched palate and large ears - resembling those of bats. The characteristic eye abnormality is pale irises. The level of cognitive deficit varies widely among the subjects with fragile X syndrome. Recent studies have suggested, on average, a moderate to mild mean IQ of between 35 and 55 among affected boys and a lower mean IQ ranging from 20 to 40 among affected adult males. Between 30 and 50% of female carriers also show cognitive deficit. Associated conditions in Fragile X syndrome include: epilepsy - reported in about 25% of these individuals other medical conditions, such as strabismus, otitis media, sinusitis, joint dislocation, orthopaedic problems and apnoea.

Down syndrome
Down syndrome is incorrect. Down syndrome is the most common of all the genetic causes of mental disability (fragile X syndrome is the most common inherited cause). Down syndrome is caused by trisomy 21 and is not an inherited defect.

Tuberous sclerosis
Tuberous sclerosis is incorrect. This is a rare multi-system genetic condition resulting in benign tumours growing in the patient. Around 50% of patients with tuberous sclerosis have a degree of learning disability.

Prader–Willi syndrome
Prader-Willi syndrome is incorrect. This is a genetic condition resulting from the deletion/lack of function of genes on chromosome 15, and is characterized by symptoms including constant hunger/hyperphagia, restricted growth, hypogonadism and learning difficulties.

Lesch–Nyhan syndrome
Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is incorrect. This is an X-linked recessive condition caused by an inborn error of purine metabolism, resulting in abnormally high levels of xanthine and uric acid in the blood of the affected person. A deficient production of hypoxanthine phosphoribosyltransferase is responsible for the abnormality in purine metabolism. This results in gout, renal problems, poor muscle control and learning disability, and is characterised by self-injurious behaviour in the majority of affected patients. Genetic.

stem: A 70-year-old accountant has difficulty in concentrating on tasks and remembering recent events. He has found it difficult in practice to hold down his job over at least the past 18 months. Clinical examination and laboratory tests are normal. Mental status examination shows emotional lability, difficulty in naming common objects and a recall of only one out of three objects after five minutes. Which of the following could be the cause of his symptoms?
explanation:
Alzheimer’s dementia (AD)
There are a number of clues in the vignette. Demographically this patient’s age increases the risk of AD. In this history the slow onset of illness and the episodic memory loss are classical features of AD. Clinical examination and laboratory tests are often normal and are used to exclude other causes of dementia as opposed to confirm the diagnosis of AD. Mental state examination is also supportive of the condition, with loss of recall of familiar objects and delayed recall being affected early on. Treatment would involve holistic management of other medical or psychiatric problems and assessment for acetylcholinesterase inhibitors.

Alcoholic dementia
Alcohol-related dementia is incorrect. This is unlikely in this scenario as there is no evidence of chronic alcohol use from the vignette – there is no mention of alcohol or drug history, clinical examination showed no AIsigns Tutor of chronic alcohol use and laboratory results did not show any blood results consistent with alcohol use (GGT, LFTs, clotting. etc.). As compared to AD, alcohol-related cognitive impairment rarely presents without evidence of impaired motor function (especially cerebellar dysfunction). Korsakoff’s psychosis is a specific form of cognitive impairment presenting with profound anterograde memory loss and is related to thiamine deficiency. Korsakoff’s presents following an untreated acute phase of Wernicke’s encephalopathy (classic triad of ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and confusion). It is unlikely in this scenario given the long and slowly progressive history.

Cerebrovascular disease
Cerebrovascular disease-related cognitive impairment is incorrect. This is common in this age group but it is unlikely in this case. Cognitive impairment following a significant stroke would not be likely to present in this insidious manner and is unlikely to result in this pattern of memory impairment. Equally there is no evidence of CVA on neurological examination. Small vessel disease is possible, but this typically presents as ‘subcortical’ dementia with impaired attention and psychomotor retardation rather than episodic memory complaints.

Depression
Depression is incorrect. This is an important and reversible cause of dementia and probably the second most likely cause in this scenario. Depression can result in difficulties with memory, especially retrieval of episodic memory. Given time, however, most depressed patients can recall information as opposed to those with AD. Lability may be seen in depression, but consistently low mood is more common. Also, depression is more likely following retirement or a life event, but in this case cognitive impairment resulted in the loss of employment suggesting AD. Dementia Alzheimer’s dementia The symptoms are most suggestive of Alzheimer’s dementia, a most common cause in this age group It is characterised by a gradual onset of memory impairment and an absence of focal neurological disease Alcohol-related dementia Alcohol-related dementia is less likely in the absence of any history of excess alcohol intake In cerebrovascular disease Cerebrovascular dementia is less common than Alzheimer’s disease, and often has a more sudden onset and evidence of focal neurological or vascular disease Other notes Depression may cause difficulty in concentration but does not impair short-term memory Ageing alone does not cause problems with cognitive function Alzheimer’s Disease

Normal ageing
Normal ageing is incorrect. This would not be correct in this scenario given the functional impairment and clear cognitive symptoms. Equally, given the functional impairment a diagnosis of mild cognitive impairment is also not appropriate.

stem: An 18-year-old man who is an apprentice at a local aircraft factory comes to the psychiatry clinic for review. He has been flagged in a number of assessments for finding it difficult to stick to assigned tasks, is forgetful, and has poor time management. There has also been some trouble with irritability and leading others astray during group lessons. Apparently, he was also sanctioned for shouting out during a corporate presentation. A review of old school reports suggests he was unable to concentrate on detail and left with two grade Es at GCSE. Physical examination is entirely normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder
The features here, including difficulties with school attainment, problems with attention, completing tasks, and poor time management, are typical of ADHD persisting into adulthood. Conners' Adult ADHD Rating Scales (CAARS) and autistic spectrum rating scale (ASRS) are rating scales used to define the severity of symptoms related to ADHD in adulthood. Treatment is similar with agents such as methylphenidate.

Anti-social personality disorder
Anti-social personality disorder is incorrect. Antisocial personality disorder is defined by a pervasive and persistent disregard for morals, social norms, and the rights and feelings of others. Individuals with this personality disorder will typically have no compunction in exploiting others in harmful ways for their own gain or pleasure, and frequently manipulate and deceive other people. This doesn’t fit with the picture seen here.

Borderline personality disorder
Borderline personality disorder is incorrect. Borderline personality disorder is characterized by a pervasive pattern of instability in interpersonal relationships, self-image, and affect, as well as markedly impulsive behavior.

Narcissistic personality disorder
Narcissistic personality disorder is incorrect. Narcissistic personality disorder is characterized by persistent grandiosity, excessive need for admiration, and a disdain and lack of empathy for others.

Schizoid personality disorder
Schizoid personality disorder is incorrect. Schizoid personality disorder is characterized by a lack of interest in social relationships, a tendency towards a solitary or sheltered lifestyle, secretiveness, emotional coldness, and apathy.

stem: A 22-year-old man is being treated on the ward for a deep vein thrombosis in his left leg, which occurred after he had been injecting drugs of abuse into his femoral vein. He had been stable on a methadone programme at quite a high dose for 6 months, but he dropped out of this 10 days prior to his admission. The nurses ask you to see him at night because he has sweating, agitation, abdominal pain and diarrhoea. The only clinical findings on examination are a swollen left leg and a non-discharging sinus over the femoral vein; the abdomen is soft and rectal examination is normal. What is the most appropriate prescription for managing his diarrhoea?
explanation:
Loperamide
The described constellation of symptoms is typical of opiate withdrawal. Loperamide would be best as a partial opiate agonist such as loperamide that leads to a slowing of bowel transit without any significant central effects is the most appropriate choice. Patients on methadone are often difficult to prescribe for, as an appropriate prescription for withdrawal symptoms relies on reliable information about current dosing, supervision and timing of the most recent dose. Usually before a hospital pharmacy dispenses a dose of methadone, the correct prescription needs be confirmed by their dispensing community pharmacy or substance misuse key worker, which can be difficult out of hours. Without further information about this patient’s methadone prescriber, it is safer to give drugs aimed at specific symptoms until the community situation is clarified, particularly his reasons for leaving the programme.

Diazepam
Diazepam is incorrect. Diazepam would not help his diarrhoea.

Low-dose diamorphine
Low-dose diamorphine is incorrect. It is inappropriate to prescribe diamorphine to someone who has been a previous IV drug user. Only doctors with a special Home Office licence can prescribe diamorphine for treating opioid dependence.

Low-dose oramorph
Low-dose oramorph is incorrect. Could be an inappropriate choice to manage his symptoms. Drug Misuse and DependenceUsual dose methadone
Usual dose methadone is incorrect. Tolerance to large doses of methadone can subside within 3 days of the last dose, therefore respiratory depression can occur if large doses are re-prescribed. If the patient has not AI had Tutor methadone for 10 days, it should be reinitiated as if a new starter.

stem: A 45-year-old man with a history of paranoid schizophrenia is brought to the Emergency Department by the police, as he has been ‘behaving bizarrely’. There are no psychiatric beds available and he is admitted to the medical short-stay unit with continual monitoring from a psychiatric nurse. After sleeping throughout the day he appeared settled and cooperative, but overnight becomes extremely agitated. He screams that he can see ‘things crawling all over the walls’. He looks terrified and highly distractible and gazes intermittently at the walls. At times he appears drowsy and at others hyper-alert. He is disoriented in time and place but not person. A full physical examination was impossible but he looks tremulous, is sweating profusely, has normal upper limb tone and staggers across the cubicle with an ataxic gait. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Delerium tremens
This patient is exhibiting many of the characteristic features of a delirium, with fluctuating consciousness, global disturbance of cognition (disorientation, impaired perception and thinking), inattention, psychomotor agitation, reversal of sleep-wake cycle, and emotional disturbance. There are also additional features characteristic of specifically delirium tremens; these include: visual hallucinations, diaphoresis and tremulousness. An ataxic gait suggests recent alcohol intoxication or cerebellar disease as a result of long-standing alcohol abuse.

Exacerbation of his psychotic illness
Exacerbation of his psychotic illness is incorrect. Abnormalities of perception are fixed and persistent in schizophrenia. This patient’s symptoms are fluctuating, which would not be a feature of his existing illness. Furthermore, visual hallucinations are not typical.

Head injury
Head injury is incorrect. Whilst a head injury must be excluded in any acute change in behaviour, it would not typically cause sweating, tremors or visual hallucinations.

Korsakoff syndrome
Korsakoff syndrome is incorrect. This patient has little in the way of symptoms of Korsakoff. First, the history in the stem is relatively short: Korsakoff syndrome is a progressive and severe amnesic syndrome. Second, unlike this case, memory is preferentially affected with relative sparing of other cognitive functions. Third, there is no typical fluctuation in symptoms in Korsakoff. Alcohol Misuse and DependenceA 42-year-old woman tells you she has developed fears of getting lost in the crowd and has become very anxious about going to open public places. She also says that she had experienced panic attacks previously when she went to a crowded shopping mall and has suffered these attacks intermittently since she was a teenager. She is physically healthy and so far has no history of mental illness.

Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is incorrect. Whilst neuroleptic malignant syndrome can cause delirium and autonomic dysfunction, muscular rigidity is always present. Furthermore, it is much less common than delirium tremens and is not associated with an ataxic gait.

stem: A 39-year-old man with a 10-year history of alcoholism presents to his General Practitioner after successfully completing an inpatient drug rehabilitation programme. He is seeking advice on how to maintain his sobriety. What is the most appropriate advice to give him to prevent relapse?
options: Take disulfiram before going to parties where alcohol is served
Take naltrexone before attending parties, as even one drink will make him nauseous
Limit consumption to socially appropriate amounts
Join a local Alcoholics Anonymous group
Before attending a party, plan a definite number of drinks
explanation:
Join a local Alcoholics Anonymous group
Joining a local Alcoholics Anonymous group is the most appropriate advice for maintaining sobriety. Active participation in Alcoholics Anonymous, where total abstinence is mandatory, offers a structured support system that is crucial for preventing relapses. This program provides a community of individuals who share similar experiences and can offer emotional support. Additionally, Alcoholics Anonymous often includes access to counselling and psychological therapy, which further aids in maintaining long-term sobriety.

Take disulfiram before going to parties where alcohol is served
Taking disulfiram before going to parties where alcohol is served is incorrect. Disulfiram should only be taken under strict medical supervision because it can cause severe adverse effects, including potentially fatal reactions when alcohol is consumed. The drug induces intense vomiting and other unpleasant if Chatsymptoms with alcohol is ingested, but its use without medical oversight can be dangerous. It is not advisable as a standalone strategy for maintaining sobriety in social settings.

Take naltrexone before attending parties, as even one drink will make him nauseous
Taking naltrexone before attending parties, as even one drink will make him nauseous, is incorrect. Naltrexone is used to reduce cravings for alcohol but does not induce nausea when alcohol is consumed. Its primary function is to block the euphoric effects of alcohol, which can help reduce the desire to drink. However, relying solely on medication without additional support mechanisms is not the most effective strategy for maintaining long-term sobriety.

Limit consumption to socially appropriate amounts
Limiting consumption to socially appropriate amounts is incorrect. Individuals with a history of alcoholism usually have a high tolerance to alcohol, making it difficult for them to control their drinking once they start. This approach increases the risk of relapse, as even moderate drinking can quickly escalate into excessive consumption. For these individuals, complete abstinence is the safest and most effective strategy. 0

Before attending a party, plan a definite number of drinks
Seeking out new hobbies to replace drinking is a supportive strategy but not the most appropriate standalone advice. Engaging in new activities can help distract from the urge to drink and provide a sense of purpose. However, without a structured support system like Alcoholics Anonymous, this approach may not be sufficient to prevent relapse. New hobbies should be part of a comprehensive plan that includes professional counselling and community support.

stem: A 20-year-old patient, who has been having seizures, attends the clinic with his father. The patient has learning difficulties and on examination he has a number of skin lesions including white ash leaf-shaped macules, subcutaneous nodules, café-au-lait spots and subungual fibromas affecting his nails. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Tuberous sclerosis
The prevalence of tuberous sclerosis is about 1 in 7000–10,000. Linkage analysis has revealed two diseasedetermining genes, TSC1 and TSC2. TSC1 is linked to chromosome 9q34 and is responsible for about 40% of cases. TSC1 encodes for a protein called ‘hamartin’, which is believed to have a tumour-suppressant role. TSC2 is linked to chromosome 16p13 and encodes for tuberin, which functions as a guanosine triphosphataseactivating protein also with a putative tumour-suppressant role. It has been reported that TSC1 is less likely to cause mental disability. About 60% of cases of tuberose sclerosis are believed to be due to new mutations leading to dysfunction of hamartin and tuberin. Skin lesions in those affected include facial angiofibroma, adenoma sebaceum, white ash leaf-shaped macules, shagreen patches, depigmented naevi, subcutaneous nodules and café-au-lait spots. The nails of affected individuals show subungual fibromas, their teeth commonly have pitted enamel hypoplasia and their eyes can be affected by chromatic retinal patches, retinal tumours (phakomas) and hypopigmented iris spots. Neurological manifestations include infantile spasms, seizures and hydrocephaly secondary to cerebral glial nodules. Various tumours, e.g. myocardial rhabdomyoma, multiple bilateral renal angiomyolipoma, Wilms’ tumour, cardiac and olfactory hamartomas, ependymoma and astrocytoma, are common in this condition. Other features include renal cysts, hypertension and aortic aneurysm.

Down syndrome
Down syndrome is incorrect. Down syndrome (trisomy 21) causes learning disability but is characterised by brachycephaly, single palmar crease, upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthic folds, hypotonia, cardiovascular malformations in around 40% and development of Alzheimer’s disease in most by 50 years of age.

Prader–Willi syndrome
Prader-Willi syndrome is incorrect. This is a genetic condition resulting from the deletion/lack of function of genes on chromosome 15 and is characterised by symptoms including constant hunger/hyperphagia, restricted growth, hypogonadism and learning difficulties.

Lesch–Nyhan syndrome
Lesch–Nyhan syndrome is incorrect. Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is an X-linked recessive condition caused by an inborn error of purine metabolism, resulting in abnormally high levels of xanthine and uric acid in the blood of the affected person. A deficient production of hypoxanthine phosphoribosyltransferase is responsible for the abnormality in purine metabolism. This results in gout, renal problems, poor muscle control and learning disability, and is characterised by self-injurious behaviour in the majority of affected patients.

Fragile X syndrome.

stem: A 20-year-old male attends a clinic, along with his mother who is concerned that he has recently lost a significant amount of weight and appears to be exercising excessively. The patient refers to the fact that he hates how fat he is but does not feel he is over-exercising. His primary concern when you speak to him alone is that he has been having issues with impotency. On examination, he has a BMI of 17. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Anorexia nervosa
This describes an eating disorder where individuals induce weight loss of >15% of normal weight resulting in BMI <17.5, and where individuals hold an overvalued idea that fatness is a dreadful state and will not allow their weight to rise above a very low threshold. Epidemiological studies of anorexia nervosa have demonstrated a marked predominance of females over males, but it is becoming better recognised and diagnosed in males. Other epidemiological factors shown in anorexia nervosa include: a peak age of onset of 15 years an increased incidence in higher socioeconomic groups an increased incidence in Westernised countries (it seems that culture rather than race is important, as there is a high incidence in second-generation Asian girls) an increased incidence in high-risk professions, eg models, ballet dancers and jockeys.

Bulimia nervosa
Bulimia nervosa is incorrect. This describes an eating disorder where individuals have a persistent preoccupation with eating and have irresistible cravings for food resulting in episodes of binge eating. They then display behaviours in an attempt to counteract the ‘fattening’ effects of food, such as self-induced vomiting, periods of starvation and diuretic abuse. Around one third of individuals who suffer from bulimia nervosa have a previous history of anorexia.

Bingeing
Bingeing is incorrect. This refers to the behaviour of excessive and compulsive consumption of food and overeating seen in bulimia nervosa.

Generalised anxiety disorder
Generalised anxiety disorder is incorrect. Although anxiety is a common cause of impotence, the clinical features of generalised anxiety disorder are persistent and generalised symptoms of anxiety, which occur across a range of daily circumstances and are not related to particular events or circumstances. Anorexia Nervosa A 23-year-old woman suffers from excessive daytime sleepiness, including falling asleep at inappropriate moments such as at work or when eating. Which combination of four symptoms would be very suggestive of a diagnosis of narcolepsy?

Body dysmorphic disorder
Body dysmorphic disorder is incorrect, this describes an anxiety disorder where an individual has a distorted view of their appearance and becomes obsessed with worrying about particular defects in their appearance that are not seen by others. Body dysmorphic disorder can be seen in individuals with anorexia nervosa, but is less likely than a diagnosis of anorexia nervosa in this case as the patient’s view of his appearance is only one symptom alongside his weight loss and excessive exercise that are diagnostic of anorexia nervosa.

stem: A 19-year-old man who is wheelchair-bound and has severe learning difficulties is brought to the clinic as he has been noted by carers to be trying to hurt himself by biting his fingers and lips. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Lesch–Nyhan syndrome
Lesch-Nyhan syndrome is an X-linked recessive condition that almost exclusively affects boys. The incidence rate varies widely between 1 in 10,000 and 1 in 380,000 live births. The usual mode of inheritance is from a carrier mother to her affected son. The syndrome is caused by an inborn error of purine metabolism, resulting in abnormally high levels of xanthine and uric acid in the blood of the affected person. A deficient production of hypoxanthine phosphoribosyltransferase is responsible for the abnormality in purine metabolism. The gene locus for hypoxanthine phosphoribosyltransferase has recently been identified in the short arm of chromosome Xq26–27. Most affected children have severe mental disability, become wheelchair-bound and show increased tendon reflexes. Microcephaly is common, and approximately half of children develop epileptic seizures. The overall prognosis for this condition remains poor, with most affected subjects dying in early adulthood. Most children affected by Lesch–Nyhan syndrome show verbal and physical aggression. However, more characteristic problems, which are resistant to management, are the self-injurious behaviours that affect over 85% of these children. Most prominent self-injurious behaviours include biting of the lips, the inside of the mouth and the fingers. Other common self-injurious behaviours include thumping their ears and face, and hitting their head against objects. Various explanations of these self-injurious behaviours, such as malformation in the innervation of muscles, hyperexcitability of motor neurons and abnormalities in the basal ganglia D 1-receptor system (D 1 receptors are rich in hypoxanthine phosphoribosyltransferase), have been put forward, yet none has been proven unequivocally.

Down syndrome
Down syndrome is incorrect. Down syndrome is a genetic cause of learning disability caused by trisomy 21. Self-injurious behaviour is not typically associated with the condition.

Tuberous sclerosis
Tuberous sclerosis is incorrect. This is a rare multi-system genetic condition resulting in benign tumours growing in the patient. Around 50% of patients with tuberous sclerosis have a degree of learning disability, but the condition is not typically associated with self-injurious behaviour.

Prader–Willi syndrome
Prader-Willi syndrome is incorrect. This is a genetic condition resulting from the deletion/lack of function of genes on chromosome 15, and is characterised symptoms including constant hunger/hyperphagia, restricted growth, hypogonadism and learning difficulties. Self-injurious behaviour may also be seen with other inherited conditions that lead to learning disability, including Prader-Willi, although it is most often a feature of LeschNyhan syndrome.

Fragile X syndrome
Fragile X syndrome is incorrect. Fragile X syndrome is an X-linked condition resulting in mental disability. The condition is not typically associated with self-injurious behaviour. stem: A 52-year-old man is reported to have serious problems in developing social relationships. He is self-centred, arrogant, aggressively violent at times, exaggerates his abilities and fantasises that he is superior to others. His wife has suffered several mental breakdowns related to his selfishness and lack of empathy and remorse. From his medical history, you have ascertained that he is not suffering from any physical illnesses, although his mental health status remains to be investigated. What is the most likely psychiatric diagnosis?
explanation:
Narcissistic personality disorder
Narcissistic personality disorder is characterised by false beliefs about oneself being successful and perfect. This patient is self-centred and intensely selfish in his relationship with others; he uses others to satisfy his own desires and lacks empathy and remorse. The patient uses others for his/her personal gains using his/her personal charisma. Narcissistic personality disorder is similar to antisocial personality disorder, except that narcissistic personality disorder does not tend to manifest severe criminal behaviour; rather it is concentrated on self-serving interests, and is thus mainly a form of deviant covert behaviour. However, the tendency to commit criminal activities cannot be ruled out, especially if this concerns self-promotion. Treatment involves long-term intervention and community rehabilitation programmes. ICD-10 defines a personality disorder as a severe disturbance in the characterological condition and behavioural tendencies of the individual, usually involving several areas of the personality and nearly always associated with considerable personal and social disruption.

Antisocial personality disorder
Antisocial personality disorder is incorrect. Antisocial personality disorder is characterised by impulsive, irresponsible and criminal behaviour. Individuals often show a disregard for normal social Chat behaviour, manipulate with or violate the rights of others and lack concern or guilt and often blame other people for the problems in their lives.

Histrionic personality disorder
Histrionic personality disorder is incorrect. Histrionic personality disorder is characterised by the overwhelming need to be noticed and gain attention from others. They may display excessive emotions, seek constant reassurance and approval from others and appear self-centred and show little care for other people.

Schizoid personality disorder
Schizoid personality disorder is incorrect. Schizoid personality disorder is characterised by a detached individual who avoids making close social contact with others; they often complete activities in isolation, do not have or desire close relationships and are uninterested in others’ opinions of themselves.

Dependent personality disorder
Dependent personality disorder is incorrect. Dependent personality disorder is characterised by an individual who feels they are unable to be independent. They show an excessive need for others to look after them or make decisions for them, have a constant fear of being left alone and feel the need to start new relationships as soon as an old relationship ends.

stem: The risk of successful suicide is higher in which one of the following individuals?
options: A 45-year-old woman with a history of paracetamol overdose
A married man with two children who has taken a paracetamol overdose
A 50-year-old man with prior suicide attempts
A 30-year-old man recently diagnosed with a positive HIV test
A 25-year-old woman with a history of cocaine, tricyclic and alcohol overdose
explanation:
A 50-year-old man with prior suicide attempts
A variety of factors are associated with an increased risk of suicide. In this case male sex and repeated previous attempts, predispose him to a successful attempt in the future.

A 45-year-old woman with a history of paracetamol overdose
A 45-year-old woman with a history of paracetamol overdose is incorrect. The non-violent nature of her selfharm attempt and her female sex are associated with lower risk of successful suicide.

A married man with two children who has taken a paracetamol overdose
A married man with two children who has taken a paracetamol overdose is incorrect. Lower risk status is associated with marriage, and a paracetamol overdose constitutes a non-violent self-harm episode.

A 30-year-old man recently diagnosed with a positive HIV test
A 30-year-old man recently diagnosed with a positive HIV test is incorrect. Although chronic illness and disability is associated with increased risk of successful suicide, a recent positive HIV test isn’t associated with significantly increased risk. Suicidal Ideation and SuicideA 25-year-old woman with a history of cocaine, tricyclic and alcohol overdose
A 25-year-old woman with a history of cocaine, tricyclic and alcohol overdose is incorrect. Younger age at onset of the event, and female sex are associated with lower risk of successful suicide versus the other scenarios mentioned here.

stem: A 19-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner with his mother who reports a 6-month history of unusual behaviour. He now spends most of his time alone, has taken up smoking cannabis on weekends and drinks 5–10 cans of beer per week. In the last two months, he has accused his mother of trying to poison him and has put silver foil over the windows in his room to stop the government controlling his thoughts. He is reluctant to give a more detailed history due to suspicions towards the medical team and refuses to be examined. Which of the following is the most likely reason for this presentation?
explanation:
Schizophrenia
This man displays several characteristic symptoms of insidious-onset schizophrenia and is in the typical age group for this diagnosis. Diagnosis is typically before the age of 35. Initial presentation before the onset of delusions and hallucinations may be subtle. Typical symptoms include: personality change, and becoming increasingly withdrawn and introverted; deterioration in performance at school or work; self-neglect; and paranoid and delusional ideas. This can be associated with psychomotor dysfunction such as blunted or flat affect. According to the International Classification of Diseases, 11th revision (ICD-11), the diagnosis of schizophrenia requires at least two symptoms to be present, and must include one core symptoms such as delusions, thought insertion, thought withdrawal, hallucinations or thought disorder (commonly exhibited by disordered speech).

Alcohol withdrawal
Features of alcohol withdrawal include agitation, sweating and tachycardia, which may progress to delirium tremens and alcohol withdrawal-related seizures. Alcohol withdrawal is an acute process and does not account for this patient’s more prolonged presentation. Delirium tremens is a rapid onset of confusion with associated tactile hallucinations, due to hyperexcitability of the gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) and N-methyl-Daspartate (NMDA) pathways with alcohol withdrawal.

Bipolar disorder
Bipolar disorder is a mood disorder that is characterised by occurrence of manic, mixed and hypomanic symptoms, with alternative episodes of depression. Paranoia, suspicious behaviour and delusions are not usual features of depression, although they may be present in mania. More common symptoms, however, include elated mood, impulsive and risky behaviour and pressured speech. The absence of a history of previous depression and the focus on paranoid delusions make schizophrenia more likely.

Drug-induced psychosis
Typically, the onset of drug-induced psychosis is more acute. The history described in the vignette is that of a young man with a gradual onset of symptoms over a more prolonged period of time. The vignette also suggests the use of psychoactive substances since symptoms began. This man’s symptoms are more typical of schizophrenia.

Personality disorder
Although this patient’s symptoms do have some overlap with some of the personality disorders (paranoid, schizoid or schizotypal), the extent of his symptoms and the fact that there seems to have been a recent change in his behaviour are more suggestive of schizophrenia. Individuals with a schizoid personality disorder are unlikely to experience paranoia or hallucinations.

stem: A 43-year-old woman presents complaining of fever over the last week. She has multiple scars over both wrists, and scars are also noted on her abdomen. She is apyrexial during her brief stay on the ward, and a urine specimen she provides has +2 of blood but no growth in the lab. She soon leaves the hospital against medical advice. She has a large set of medical records, with previous admissions on at least six occasions over the past 2 years for abdominal pain, and is also known to other local hospitals. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Factitious disorder
Factitious disorders (previously known as Munchausen syndrome) are the intentional production or feigning of physical or psychological symptoms. In contrast to malingering, there is no apparent secondary gain except a need to be taken care of (primary gain). Examples include: self-harm, self-neglect (eg failure to control diabetes) or fabrication of recurrent symptoms or disease (eg fever, pain, haematuria (adding blood to urine), injecting bacteria to produce infection, taking medications to induce psychiatric symptoms). Patients often present to multiple hospitals, have an abnormally detailed grasp of medical terminology and often discharge themselves before full investigation or treatment is complete. There may also be coexistent medication abuse (eg sedatives or painkillers).

Borderline personality disorder
Borderline personality disorder is incorrect. Apart from possible self-harm, this woman’s symptoms do not fit with borderline personality disorder: unpredictable behaviour, emotional outbursts, rapid fluctuations in emotional state, unstable personal relationships and a strong tendency towards suicidal thinking.

Conversion disorder
Conversion disorder is incorrect. A conversion disorder is when a person has symptoms and signs affecting voluntary motor or sensory function that cannot be explained by a medical condition (ie medically unexplained symptoms). In conversion disorder, the symptoms are unintentional and the person is not aware they are producing them; in contrast, in factitious disorder, the symptoms are intentionally produced. The symptoms of conversion disorder are thought to be associated with psychological factors such as conflict or stress. Examples include: unexplained blindness, paralysis, swallowing difficulties, non-epileptic seizures.

Malingering
Malingering is incorrect. Malingering is the intentional and fraudulent feigning or exaggeration of symptoms for external gain (eg financial, insurance claims or to relieve themselves of other duties such as employment, prison, military service). In contrast, in factitious disorder, there is no apparent secondary gain. Factitious DisorderFabricated or induced illness
Fabricated or induced illness is incorrect. This is when a parent or carer deliberately fabricates symptoms or signs of illness for their child or dependent for their own personal gain. This may lead to repeated, unnecessary investigations and treatment of a child or dependent. This is a form of child abuse.

stem: A 52-year-old man is admitted to hospital with chronic alcohol abuse and symptoms of cognitive decline. He is unable to remember what he does for a job, although he can remember his name, certain dates and his recent meals. He also suffers from short-term memory loss, for example after reading a newspaper didn’t appear to recall the stories accurately, but instead made up fantastic explanations to fit the stories in the paper. How would you best describe his memory impairment?
explanation:
Korsakoff syndrome
Korsakoff's syndrome is an abnormal mental state in which memory and learning are affected out of all proportion to other cognitive functions in an otherwise alert and responsive patient. This occurs as a result of nutritional depletion, notably thiamine deficiency. Thiamine deficiency is more common in those with alcohol dependence owing to their poor nutritional intake and problems of malabsorption. Many cases are diagnosed after an episode of Wernicke’s encephalopathy, although some may present insidiously where patients haven’t previously utilized medical services.

Wernicke’s encephalopathy
Wernicke’s encephalopathy is incorrect. Acute Wernicke’s presents with confusion, ataxia, nystagmus and ophthalmoplegia. Not all these features are always present, and the ophthalmoplegia responds rapidly to treatment with high-dose thiamine. The condition is occasionally seen in pregnant women with Chat hyperemesis, with as well as in alcoholics.

Anterograde amnesia
Anterograde amnesia is incorrect. Simple anterograde amnesia is not correct, given that this patient shows clear evidence of confabulation, an important pointer to Korsakoff’s.

Retrograde amnesia
Retrograde amnesia is incorrect. Retrograde amnesia involves the loss of memory for events before the onset of an injury or disease.

Autism spectrum disorder.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner with complaints of persistent sadness, difficulty sleeping, and feeling detached from others for the past three months following the death of her husband a year ago. She reports feeling guilty about not being able to save him despite knowing there was nothing she could have done. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Persistent complex bereavement disorder
Persistent complex bereavement disorder involves prolonged grief reactions to the loss of a loved one that occurred at least a year ago for adults and significantly impairs daily life activities well beyond what is considered a culturally appropriate duration for grieving. The patient's ongoing severe emotional distress focused on loss-specific themes such as guilt about failing to save her husband, along with persistent sadness and loneliness for at least the last month before the diagnosis aligns well with prolonged grief disorder.

Adjustment disorder
Adjustment disorder involves emotional or behavioural symptoms in response to an identifiable stressor occurring within three months of the onset of the stressor. While this patient’s symptoms are related a toTutor specific event (the death of her husband), the onset of the stressor is beyond six months, which is more consistent with another diagnosis.

Bereavement
Bereavement is a normal reaction to loss, typically involving feelings of sadness and longing for the deceased, but usually resolves over time without significant impairment in daily functioning. Although this patient’s situation began as bereavement, her persistent functional impairment and severe guilt suggest a more complicated form.

Major depressive disorder
Major depressive disorder (MDD) includes at least five symptoms, such as depressed mood, anhedonia, weight changes, sleep disturbances and feelings of worthlessness lasting for two weeks or more. While she does exhibit some MDD features like sadness and difficulty sleeping, her intense preoccupation with grief-specific aspects like guilt over not saving her husband points towards another condition. A political figure is engaged in a television debate with an opponent. As his anxiety mounts, he loses his calm, interrupts his opponent and attacks his character. He finally throws down his papers and walks away angrily. What is the defence mechanism associated with this reaction?

Post-traumatic stress disorder
Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) requires exposure to actual or threatened death or serious injury followed by intrusive memories/flashbacks, avoidance behaviours and heightened arousal lasting longer than one month. This patient’s symptomatology lacks hallmark PTSD features such as recurrent distressing dreams or hypervigilance linked directly to experiencing trauma rather than prolonged grief processes.

stem: A patient with schizophrenia is started on haloperidol, but 1 week later he complains of a feeling of restlessness and an inability to sit still since starting his medication. What is this side-effect called?
explanation:
Akathisia
This patient’s symptoms are an example of an extrapyramidal side-effect (EPS) that often occurs with the older ‘typical’ anti-psychotics such as haloperidol or chlorpromazine. There are four types of EPS (akathisia, dystonias, Parkinsonism and tardive dyskinesias); akathisia is the most common type. It presents as motor restlessness with an unpleasant, compelling urge to move and inability to sit still (eg foot stamping when seated, constant crossing and uncrossing of legs or pacing up and down). It is important not to mistake akathisia for psychotic agitation, as the treatment of akathisia is to reduce the antipsychotic dose: any further increase in dose is likely to make the symptoms worse. Although akathisia usually occurs in the first 2 weeks of taking a neuroleptic drug, it may also begin after several months’ treatment.

Dystonic reaction
Dystonic reaction is incorrect. Dystonias are the involuntary contractions of major muscle groups (egAI eye Tutor muscles, leading to oculogyric crisis; neck muscles, leading to torticollis; etc).

Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Neurileptic malignant syndrome is incorrect. Neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) is a serious, rare idiosyncratic reaction occurring in response to neuroleptic therapy. It is characterised by hyperthermia, fluctuating conscious level, muscular rigidity, autonomic dysfunction, tachycardia, labile blood pressure and urinary incontinence. It can be potentially fatal. Treatment includes stopping the causative drug and supportive care, usually in an intensive therapy unit setting.

Parkinsonism
Parkinsonism is incorrect. Parkinsonian symptoms include mask-like facies, resting tremor, rigidity, shuffling gait and bradykinesia.

Tardive dyskinesia
Tardive dyskinesia is incorrect. Tardive dyskinesias are involuntary movements, particularly of the face and sometimes trunk: examples include protruding and twisting of the tongue, pouting or lip smacking, chewing movements, etc. They usually occur after many years of treatment with antipsychotic medication and would be unusual to develop after 1 week.
